40 def _remove_optimizer_parameters(kwds):
41 """
42 Remove the optimizer-related keyword arguments 'loc', 'scale' and
43 'optimizer' from `kwds`. Then check that `kwds` is empty, and
44 raise `TypeError("Unknown arguments: %s." % kwds)` if it is not.
45  
46 This function is used in the fit method of distributions that override
47 the default method and do not use the default optimization code.
48  
49 `kwds` is modified in-place.
50 """
51 kwds.pop('loc', None)
52 kwds.pop('scale', None)
53 kwds.pop('optimizer', None)
54 kwds.pop('method', None)
55 if kwds:
56 raise TypeError(f"Unknown arguments: {kwds}.")
57  
58  
59 def _call_super_mom(fun):
60 # If fit method is overridden only for MLE and doesn't specify what to do
61 # if method == 'mm' or with censored data, this decorator calls the generic
62 # implementation.
63 @wraps(fun)
64 def wrapper(self, data, *args, **kwds):
65 method = kwds.get('method', 'mle').lower()
66 censored = isinstance(data, CensoredData)
67 if method == 'mm' or (censored and data.num_censored() > 0):
68 return super(type(self), self).fit(data, *args, **kwds)
69 else:
70 if censored:
71 # data is an instance of CensoredData, but actually holds
72 # no censored values, so replace it with the array of
73 # uncensored values.
74 data = data._uncensored
75 return fun(self, data, *args, **kwds)
76  
77 return wrapper
78  
79  
80 def _get_left_bracket(fun, rbrack, lbrack=None):
81 # find left bracket for `root_scalar`. A guess for lbrack may be provided.
82 lbrack = lbrack or rbrack - 1
83 diff = rbrack - lbrack
84  
85 # if there is no sign change in `fun` between the brackets, expand
86 # rbrack - lbrack until a sign change occurs
87 def interval_contains_root(lbrack, rbrack):
88 # return true if the signs disagree.
89 return np.sign(fun(lbrack)) != np.sign(fun(rbrack))
90  
91 while not interval_contains_root(lbrack, rbrack):
92 diff *= 2
93 lbrack = rbrack - diff
94  
95 msg = ("The solver could not find a bracket containing a "
96 "root to an MLE first order condition.")
97 if np.isinf(lbrack):
98 raise FitSolverError(msg)
99  
100 return lbrack
101

103 class ksone_gen(rv_continuous):
104 r"""Kolmogorov-Smirnov one-sided test statistic distribution.
105  
106 This is the distribution of the one-sided Kolmogorov-Smirnov (KS)
107 statistics :math:`D_n^+` and :math:`D_n^-`
108 for a finite sample size ``n >= 1`` (the shape parameter).
109  
110 %(before_notes)s
111  
112 See Also
113 --------
114 kstwobign, kstwo, kstest
115  
116 Notes
117 -----
118 :math:`D_n^+` and :math:`D_n^-` are given by
119  
120 .. math::
121  
122 D_n^+ &= \text{sup}_x (F_n(x) - F(x)),\\
123 D_n^- &= \text{sup}_x (F(x) - F_n(x)),\\
124  
125 where :math:`F` is a continuous CDF and :math:`F_n` is an empirical CDF.
126 `ksone` describes the distribution under the null hypothesis of the KS test
127 that the empirical CDF corresponds to :math:`n` i.i.d. random variates
128 with CDF :math:`F`.
129  
130 %(after_notes)s
131  
132 References
133 ----------
134 .. [1] Birnbaum, Z. W. and Tingey, F.H. "One-sided confidence contours
135 for probability distribution functions", The Annals of Mathematical
136 Statistics, 22(4), pp 592-596 (1951).
137  
138 Examples
139 --------
140 >>> import numpy as np
141 >>> from scipy.stats import ksone
142 >>> import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
143 >>> fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 1)
144  
145 Display the probability density function (``pdf``):
146  
147 >>> n = 1e+03
148 >>> x = np.linspace(ksone.ppf(0.01, n),
149 ... ksone.ppf(0.99, n), 100)
150 >>> ax.plot(x, ksone.pdf(x, n),
151 ... 'r-', lw=5, alpha=0.6, label='ksone pdf')
152  
153 Alternatively, the distribution object can be called (as a function)
154 to fix the shape, location and scale parameters. This returns a "frozen"
155 RV object holding the given parameters fixed.
156  
157 Freeze the distribution and display the frozen ``pdf``:
158  
159 >>> rv = ksone(n)
160 >>> ax.plot(x, rv.pdf(x), 'k-', lw=2, label='frozen pdf')
161 >>> ax.legend(loc='best', frameon=False)
162 >>> plt.show()
163  
164 Check accuracy of ``cdf`` and ``ppf``:
165  
166 >>> vals = ksone.ppf([0.001, 0.5, 0.999], n)
167 >>> np.allclose([0.001, 0.5, 0.999], ksone.cdf(vals, n))
168 True
169  
170 """
171 def _argcheck(self, n):
172 return (n >= 1) & (n == np.round(n))
173  
174 def _shape_info(self):
175 return [_ShapeInfo("n", True, (1, np.inf), (True, False))]
176  
177 def _pdf(self, x, n):
178 return -scu._smirnovp(n, x)
179  
180 def _cdf(self, x, n):
181 return scu._smirnovc(n, x)
182  
183 def _sf(self, x, n):
184 return sc.smirnov(n, x)
185  
186 def _ppf(self, q, n):
187 return scu._smirnovci(n, q)
188  
189 def _isf(self, q, n):
190 return sc.smirnovi(n, q)
191  
192  
193 ksone = ksone_gen(a=0.0, b=1.0, name='ksone')
194

196 class kstwo_gen(rv_continuous):
197 r"""Kolmogorov-Smirnov two-sided test statistic distribution.
198  
199 This is the distribution of the two-sided Kolmogorov-Smirnov (KS)
200 statistic :math:`D_n` for a finite sample size ``n >= 1``
201 (the shape parameter).
202  
203 %(before_notes)s
204  
205 See Also
206 --------
207 kstwobign, ksone, kstest
208  
209 Notes
210 -----
211 :math:`D_n` is given by
212  
213 .. math::
214  
215 D_n = \text{sup}_x |F_n(x) - F(x)|
216  
217 where :math:`F` is a (continuous) CDF and :math:`F_n` is an empirical CDF.
218 `kstwo` describes the distribution under the null hypothesis of the KS test
219 that the empirical CDF corresponds to :math:`n` i.i.d. random variates
220 with CDF :math:`F`.
221  
222 %(after_notes)s
223  
224 References
225 ----------
226 .. [1] Simard, R., L'Ecuyer, P. "Computing the Two-Sided
227 Kolmogorov-Smirnov Distribution", Journal of Statistical Software,
228 Vol 39, 11, 1-18 (2011).
229  
230 Examples
231 --------
232 >>> import numpy as np
233 >>> from scipy.stats import kstwo
234 >>> import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
235 >>> fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 1)
236  
237 Display the probability density function (``pdf``):
238  
239 >>> n = 10
240 >>> x = np.linspace(kstwo.ppf(0.01, n),
241 ... kstwo.ppf(0.99, n), 100)
242 >>> ax.plot(x, kstwo.pdf(x, n),
243 ... 'r-', lw=5, alpha=0.6, label='kstwo pdf')
244  
245 Alternatively, the distribution object can be called (as a function)
246 to fix the shape, location and scale parameters. This returns a "frozen"
247 RV object holding the given parameters fixed.
248  
249 Freeze the distribution and display the frozen ``pdf``:
250  
251 >>> rv = kstwo(n)
252 >>> ax.plot(x, rv.pdf(x), 'k-', lw=2, label='frozen pdf')
253 >>> ax.legend(loc='best', frameon=False)
254 >>> plt.show()
255  
256 Check accuracy of ``cdf`` and ``ppf``:
257  
258 >>> vals = kstwo.ppf([0.001, 0.5, 0.999], n)
259 >>> np.allclose([0.001, 0.5, 0.999], kstwo.cdf(vals, n))
260 True
261  
262 """
263 def _argcheck(self, n):
264 return (n >= 1) & (n == np.round(n))
265  
266 def _shape_info(self):
267 return [_ShapeInfo("n", True, (1, np.inf), (True, False))]
268  
269 def _get_support(self, n):
270 return (0.5/(n if not isinstance(n, Iterable) else np.asanyarray(n)),
271 1.0)
272  
273 def _pdf(self, x, n):
274 return kolmognp(n, x)
275  
276 def _cdf(self, x, n):
277 return kolmogn(n, x)
278  
279 def _sf(self, x, n):
280 return kolmogn(n, x, cdf=False)
281  
282 def _ppf(self, q, n):
283 return kolmogni(n, q, cdf=True)
284  
285 def _isf(self, q, n):
286 return kolmogni(n, q, cdf=False)
287  
288  
289 # Use the pdf, (not the ppf) to compute moments
290 kstwo = kstwo_gen(momtype=0, a=0.0, b=1.0, name='kstwo')

393 class norm_gen(rv_continuous):
394 r"""A normal continuous random variable.
395  
396 The location (``loc``) keyword specifies the mean.
397 The scale (``scale``) keyword specifies the standard deviation.
398  
399 %(before_notes)s
400  
401 Notes
402 -----
403 The probability density function for `norm` is:
404  
405 .. math::
406  
407 f(x) = \frac{\exp(-x^2/2)}{\sqrt{2\pi}}
408  
409 for a real number :math:`x`.
410  
411 %(after_notes)s
412  
413 %(example)s
414  
415 """
416 def _shape_info(self):
417 return []
418  
419 def _rvs(self, size=None, random_state=None):
420 return random_state.standard_normal(size)
421  
422 def _pdf(self, x):
423 # norm.pdf(x) = exp(-x**2/2)/sqrt(2*pi)
424 return _norm_pdf(x)
425  
426 def _logpdf(self, x):
427 return _norm_logpdf(x)
428  
429 def _cdf(self, x):
430 return _norm_cdf(x)
431  
432 def _logcdf(self, x):
433 return _norm_logcdf(x)
434  
435 def _sf(self, x):
436 return _norm_sf(x)
437  
438 def _logsf(self, x):
439 return _norm_logsf(x)
440  
441 def _ppf(self, q):
442 return _norm_ppf(q)
443  
444 def _isf(self, q):
445 return _norm_isf(q)
446  
447 def _stats(self):
448 return 0.0, 1.0, 0.0, 0.0
449  
450 def _entropy(self):
451 return 0.5*(np.log(2*np.pi)+1)
452  
453 @_call_super_mom
454 @replace_notes_in_docstring(rv_continuous, notes="""\
455 For the normal distribution, method of moments and maximum likelihood
456 estimation give identical fits, and explicit formulas for the estimates
457 are available.
458 This function uses these explicit formulas for the maximum likelihood
459 estimation of the normal distribution parameters, so the
460 `optimizer` and `method` arguments are ignored.\n\n""")
461 def fit(self, data, **kwds):
462 floc = kwds.pop('floc', None)
463 fscale = kwds.pop('fscale', None)
464  
465 _remove_optimizer_parameters(kwds)
466  
467 if floc is not None and fscale is not None:
468 # This check is for consistency with `rv_continuous.fit`.
469 # Without this check, this function would just return the
470 # parameters that were given.
471 raise ValueError("All parameters fixed. There is nothing to "
472 "optimize.")
473  
474 data = np.asarray(data)
475  
476 if not np.isfinite(data).all():
477 raise ValueError("The data contains non-finite values.")
478  
479 if floc is None:
480 loc = data.mean()
481 else:
482 loc = floc
483  
484 if fscale is None:
485 scale = np.sqrt(((data - loc)**2).mean())
486 else:
487 scale = fscale
488  
489 return loc, scale
490  
491 def _munp(self, n):
492 """
493 @returns Moments of standard normal distribution for integer n >= 0
494  
495 See eq. 16 of https://arxiv.org/abs/1209.4340v2
496 """
497 if n == 0:
498 return 1.
499 if n % 2 == 0:
500 return sc.factorial2(int(n) - 1)
501 else:
502 return 0.
503  
504  
505 norm = norm_gen(name='norm')

508 class alpha_gen(rv_continuous):
509 r"""An alpha continuous random variable.
510  
511 %(before_notes)s
512  
513 Notes
514 -----
515 The probability density function for `alpha` ([1]_, [2]_) is:
516  
517 .. math::
518  
519 f(x, a) = \frac{1}{x^2 \Phi(a) \sqrt{2\pi}} *
520 \exp(-\frac{1}{2} (a-1/x)^2)
521  
522 where :math:`\Phi` is the normal CDF, :math:`x > 0`, and :math:`a > 0`.
523  
524 `alpha` takes ``a`` as a shape parameter.
525  
526 %(after_notes)s
527  
528 References
529 ----------
530 .. [1] Johnson, Kotz, and Balakrishnan, "Continuous Univariate
531 Distributions, Volume 1", Second Edition, John Wiley and Sons,
532 p. 173 (1994).
533 .. [2] Anthony A. Salvia, "Reliability applications of the Alpha
534 Distribution", IEEE Transactions on Reliability, Vol. R-34,
535 No. 3, pp. 251-252 (1985).
536  
537 %(example)s
538  
539 """
540 _support_mask = rv_continuous._open_support_mask
541  
542 def _shape_info(self):
543 return [_ShapeInfo("a", False, (0, np.inf), (False, False))]
544  
545 def _pdf(self, x, a):
546 # alpha.pdf(x, a) = 1/(x**2*Phi(a)*sqrt(2*pi)) * exp(-1/2 * (a-1/x)**2)
547 return 1.0/(x**2)/_norm_cdf(a)*_norm_pdf(a-1.0/x)
548  
549 def _logpdf(self, x, a):
550 return -2*np.log(x) + _norm_logpdf(a-1.0/x) - np.log(_norm_cdf(a))
551  
552 def _cdf(self, x, a):
553 return _norm_cdf(a-1.0/x) / _norm_cdf(a)
554  
555 def _ppf(self, q, a):
556 return 1.0/np.asarray(a - _norm_ppf(q*_norm_cdf(a)))
557  
558 def _stats(self, a):
559 return [np.inf]*2 + [np.nan]*2
560  
561  
562 alpha = alpha_gen(a=0.0, name='alpha')
563

659 class FitDataError(ValueError):
660 """Raised when input data is inconsistent with fixed parameters."""
661 # This exception is raised by, for example, beta_gen.fit when both floc
662 # and fscale are fixed and there are values in the data not in the open
663 # interval (floc, floc+fscale).
664 def __init__(self, distr, lower, upper):
665 self.args = (
666 "Invalid values in `data`. Maximum likelihood "
667 f"estimation with {distr!r} requires that {lower!r} < "
668 f"(x - loc)/scale < {upper!r} for each x in `data`.",
669 )
670  
671  
672 class FitSolverError(FitError):
673 """
674 Raised when a solver fails to converge while fitting a distribution.
675 """
676 # This exception is raised by, for example, beta_gen.fit when
677 # optimize.fsolve returns with ier != 1.
678 def __init__(self, mesg):
679 emsg = "Solver for the MLE equations failed to converge: "
680 emsg += mesg.replace('\n', '')
681 self.args = (emsg,)
682  
683  
684 def _beta_mle_a(a, b, n, s1):
685 # The zeros of this function give the MLE for `a`, with
686 # `b`, `n` and `s1` given. `s1` is the sum of the logs of
687 # the data. `n` is the number of data points.
688 psiab = sc.psi(a + b)
689 func = s1 - n * (-psiab + sc.psi(a))
690 return func
691  
692  
693 def _beta_mle_ab(theta, n, s1, s2):
694 # Zeros of this function are critical points of
695 # the maximum likelihood function. Solving this system
696 # for theta (which contains a and b) gives the MLE for a and b
697 # given `n`, `s1` and `s2`. `s1` is the sum of the logs of the data,
698 # and `s2` is the sum of the logs of 1 - data. `n` is the number
699 # of data points.
700 a, b = theta
701 psiab = sc.psi(a + b)
702 func = [s1 - n * (-psiab + sc.psi(a)),
703 s2 - n * (-psiab + sc.psi(b))]
704 return func
705  
706  
707 class beta_gen(rv_continuous):
708 r"""A beta continuous random variable.
709  
710 %(before_notes)s
711  
712 Notes
713 -----
714 The probability density function for `beta` is:
715

880 if f0 is not None:

884

899 # Compute the MLE for a and b by solving _beta_mle_ab.

904 )

963 class betaprime_gen(rv_continuous):
964 r"""A beta prime continuous random variable.
965  
966 %(before_notes)s
967  
968 Notes
969 -----
970 The probability density function for `betaprime` is:
971  
972 .. math::
973  
974 f(x, a, b) = \frac{x^{a-1} (1+x)^{-a-b}}{\beta(a, b)}
975  
976 for :math:`x >= 0`, :math:`a > 0`, :math:`b > 0`, where
977 :math:`\beta(a, b)` is the beta function (see `scipy.special.beta`).
978  
979 `betaprime` takes ``a`` and ``b`` as shape parameters.
980  
981 The distribution is related to the `beta` distribution as follows:
982 If :math:`X` follows a beta distribution with parameters :math:`a, b`,
983 then :math:`Y = X/(1-X)` has a beta prime distribution with
984 parameters :math:`a, b` ([1]_).
985  
986 The beta prime distribution is a reparametrized version of the
987 F distribution. The beta prime distribution with shape parameters
988 ``a`` and ``b`` and ``scale = s`` is equivalent to the F distribution
989 with parameters ``d1 = 2*a``, ``d2 = 2*b`` and ``scale = (a/b)*s``.
990 For example,
991  
992 >>> from scipy.stats import betaprime, f
993 >>> x = [1, 2, 5, 10]
994 >>> a = 12
995 >>> b = 5
996 >>> betaprime.pdf(x, a, b, scale=2)
997 array([0.00541179, 0.08331299, 0.14669185, 0.03150079])
998 >>> f.pdf(x, 2*a, 2*b, scale=(a/b)*2)
999 array([0.00541179, 0.08331299, 0.14669185, 0.03150079])
1000  
1001 %(after_notes)s
1002  
1003 References
1004 ----------
1005 .. [1] Beta prime distribution, Wikipedia,
1006 https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beta_prime_distribution
1007  
1008 %(example)s
1009  
1010 """

1012

1014 ia = _ShapeInfo("a", False, (0, np.inf), (False, False))
1015 ib = _ShapeInfo("b", False, (0, np.inf), (False, False))
1016 return [ia, ib]

1021 return u1 / u2

1077 class bradford_gen(rv_continuous):

1080 %(before_notes)s
1081  
1082 Notes
1083 -----
1084 The probability density function for `bradford` is:
1085  
1086 .. math::
1087  
1088 f(x, c) = \frac{c}{\log(1+c) (1+cx)}
1089  
1090 for :math:`0 <= x <= 1` and :math:`c > 0`.
1091  
1092 `bradford` takes ``c`` as a shape parameter for :math:`c`.
1093  
1094 %(after_notes)s
1095  
1096 %(example)s
1097  
1098 """

1100 return [_ShapeInfo("c", False, (0, np.inf), (False, False))]
1101  
1102 def _pdf(self, x, c):
1103 # bradford.pdf(x, c) = c / (k * (1+c*x))
1104 return c / (c*x + 1.0) / sc.log1p(c)
1105  
1106 def _cdf(self, x, c):
1107 return sc.log1p(c*x) / sc.log1p(c)
1108  
1109 def _ppf(self, q, c):
1110 return sc.expm1(q * sc.log1p(c)) / c

1115 mu2 = ((c+2.0)*k-2.0*c)/(2*c*k*k)

1117 g2 = None
1118 if 's' in moments:
1119 g1 = np.sqrt(2)*(12*c*c-9*c*k*(c+2)+2*k*k*(c*(c+3)+3))

1122 g2 = (c**3*(k-3)*(k*(3*k-16)+24)+12*k*c*c*(k-4)*(k-3) +
1123 6*c*k*k*(3*k-14) + 12*k**3)
1124 g2 /= 3*c*(c*(k-2)+2*k)**2
1125 return mu, mu2, g1, g2

1128 k = np.log(1+c)
1129 return k/2.0 - np.log(c/k)

1147 -----
1148 The probability density function for `burr` is:
1149  
1150 .. math::
1151  
1152 f(x; c, d) = c d \frac{x^{-c - 1}}
1153 {{(1 + x^{-c})}^{d + 1}}

1155 for :math:`x >= 0` and :math:`c, d > 0`.

1157 `burr` takes ``c`` and ``d`` as shape parameters for :math:`c` and
1158 :math:`d`.

1161 specifically, it is equation (11) in Burr's paper [1]_. The distribution
1162 is also commonly referred to as the Dagum distribution [2]_. If the
1163 parameter :math:`c < 1` then the mean of the distribution does not
1164 exist and if :math:`c < 2` the variance does not exist [2]_.
1165 The PDF is finite at the left endpoint :math:`x = 0` if :math:`c * d >= 1`.

1748 r"""A double gamma continuous random variable.

1755 Notes

1757 The probability density function for `dgamma` is:
1758  
1759 .. math::
1760  
1761 f(x, a) = \frac{1}{2\Gamma(a)} |x|^{a-1} \exp(-|x|)
1762  
1763 for a real number :math:`x` and :math:`a > 0`. :math:`\Gamma` is the
1764 gamma function (`scipy.special.gamma`).

1766 `dgamma` takes ``a`` as a shape parameter for :math:`a`.

1768 %(after_notes)s
1769  
1770 References
1771 ----------

1773 Distributions, Volume 1", Second Edition, John Wiley and Sons
1774 (1994).
1775  
1776 %(example)s
1777  
1778 """
1779 def _shape_info(self):
1780 return [_ShapeInfo("a", False, (0, np.inf), (False, False))]
1781

1783 u = random_state.uniform(size=size)

1827 class dpareto_lognorm_gen(rv_continuous):
1828 r"""A double Pareto lognormal continuous random variable.
1829  
1830 %(before_notes)s
1831  
1832 Notes
1833 -----
1834 The probability density function for `dpareto_lognorm` is:
1835  
1836 .. math::
1837  
1838 f(x, \mu, \sigma, \alpha, \beta) =
1839 \frac{\alpha \beta}{(\alpha + \beta) x}
1840 \phi\left( \frac{\log x - \mu}{\sigma} \right)
1841 \left( R(y_1) + R(y_2) \right)
1842  
1843 where :math:`R(t) = \frac{1 - \Phi(t)}{\phi(t)}`,
1844 :math:`\phi` and :math:`\Phi` are the normal PDF and CDF, respectively,
1845 :math:`y_1 = \alpha \sigma - \frac{\log x - \mu}{\sigma}`,
1846 and :math:`y_2 = \beta \sigma + \frac{\log x - \mu}{\sigma}`
1847 for real numbers :math:`x` and :math:`\mu`, :math:`\sigma > 0`,
1848 :math:`\alpha > 0`, and :math:`\beta > 0` [1]_.
1849  
1850 `dpareto_lognorm` takes
1851 ``u`` as a shape parameter for :math:`\mu`,
1852 ``s`` as a shape parameter for :math:`\sigma`,
1853 ``a`` as a shape parameter for :math:`\alpha`, and
1854 ``b`` as a shape parameter for :math:`\beta`.
1855  
1856 A random variable :math:`X` distributed according to the PDF above
1857 can be represented as :math:`X = U \frac{V_1}{V_2}` where :math:`U`,
1858 :math:`V_1`, and :math:`V_2` are independent, :math:`U` is lognormally
1859 distributed such that :math:`\log U \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)`, and
1860 :math:`V_1` and :math:`V_2` follow Pareto distributions with parameters
1861 :math:`\alpha` and :math:`\beta`, respectively [2]_.

1965 class dweibull_gen(rv_continuous):
1966 r"""A double Weibull continuous random variable.
1967  
1968 %(before_notes)s
1969  
1970 Notes
1971 -----
1972 The probability density function for `dweibull` is given by
1973  
1974 .. math::
1975  
1976 f(x, c) = c / 2 |x|^{c-1} \exp(-|x|^c)
1977  
1978 for a real number :math:`x` and :math:`c > 0`.
1979  
1980 `dweibull` takes ``c`` as a shape parameter for :math:`c`.
1981  
1982 %(after_notes)s
1983  
1984 %(example)s
1985  
1986 """
1987 def _shape_info(self):
1988 return [_ShapeInfo("c", False, (0, np.inf), (False, False))]
1989  
1990 def _rvs(self, c, size=None, random_state=None):
1991 u = random_state.uniform(size=size)
1992 w = weibull_min.rvs(c, size=size, random_state=random_state)
1993 return w * (np.where(u >= 0.5, 1, -1))
1994  
1995 def _pdf(self, x, c):
1996 # dweibull.pdf(x, c) = c / 2 * abs(x)**(c-1) * exp(-abs(x)**c)
1997 ax = abs(x)
1998 Px = c / 2.0 * ax**(c-1.0) * np.exp(-ax**c)
1999 return Px
2000  
2001 def _logpdf(self, x, c):
2002 ax = abs(x)
2003 return np.log(c) - np.log(2.0) + sc.xlogy(c - 1.0, ax) - ax**c
2004  
2005 def _cdf(self, x, c):
2006 Cx1 = 0.5 * np.exp(-abs(x)**c)
2007 return np.where(x > 0, 1 - Cx1, Cx1)
2008  
2009 def _ppf(self, q, c):
2010 fac = 2. * np.where(q <= 0.5, q, 1. - q)
2011 fac = np.power(-np.log(fac), 1.0 / c)
2012 return np.where(q > 0.5, fac, -fac)
2013  
2014 def _sf(self, x, c):
2015 half_weibull_min_sf = 0.5 * stats.weibull_min._sf(np.abs(x), c)
2016 return np.where(x > 0, half_weibull_min_sf, 1 - half_weibull_min_sf)
2017  
2018 def _isf(self, q, c):
2019 double_q = 2. * np.where(q <= 0.5, q, 1. - q)
2020 weibull_min_isf = stats.weibull_min._isf(double_q, c)
2021 return np.where(q > 0.5, -weibull_min_isf, weibull_min_isf)
2022  
2023 def _munp(self, n, c):
2024 return (1 - (n % 2)) * sc.gamma(1.0 + 1.0 * n / c)
2025  
2026 # since we know that all odd moments are zeros, return them at once.
2027 # returning Nones from _stats makes the public stats call _munp
2028 # so overall we're saving one or two gamma function evaluations here.
2029 def _stats(self, c):
2030 return 0, None, 0, None
2031  
2032 def _entropy(self, c):
2033 h = stats.weibull_min._entropy(c) - np.log(0.5)
2034 return h
2035  
2036  
2037 dweibull = dweibull_gen(name='dweibull')

2040 class expon_gen(rv_continuous):

2101 @_call_super_mom
2102 @replace_notes_in_docstring(rv_continuous, notes="""\
2103 When `method='MLE'`,
2104 this function uses explicit formulas for the maximum likelihood
2105 estimation of the exponential distribution parameters, so the
2106 `optimizer`, `loc` and `scale` keyword arguments are
2107 ignored.\n\n""")
2108 def fit(self, data, *args, **kwds):
2109 if len(args) > 0:
2110 raise TypeError("Too many arguments.")
2111  
2112 floc = kwds.pop('floc', None)
2113 fscale = kwds.pop('fscale', None)
2114  
2115 _remove_optimizer_parameters(kwds)
2116  
2117 if floc is not None and fscale is not None:
2118 # This check is for consistency with `rv_continuous.fit`.
2119 raise ValueError("All parameters fixed. There is nothing to "
2120 "optimize.")
2121  
2122 data = np.asarray(data)
2123  
2124 if not np.isfinite(data).all():
2125 raise ValueError("The data contains non-finite values.")
2126  
2127 data_min = data.min()
2128  
2129 if floc is None:
2130 # ML estimate of the location is the minimum of the data.
2131 loc = data_min
2132 else:
2133 loc = floc
2134 if data_min < loc:
2135 # There are values that are less than the specified loc.
2136 raise FitDataError("expon", lower=floc, upper=np.inf)
2137  
2138 if fscale is None:
2139 # ML estimate of the scale is the shifted mean.
2140 scale = data.mean() - loc
2141 else:
2142 scale = fscale
2143  
2144 # We expect the return values to be floating point, so ensure it
2145 # by explicitly converting to float.
2146 return float(loc), float(scale)
2147  
2148  
2149 expon = expon_gen(a=0.0, name='expon')

2152 class exponnorm_gen(rv_continuous):
2153 r"""An exponentially modified Normal continuous random variable.
2154  
2155 Also known as the exponentially modified Gaussian distribution [1]_.
2156  
2157 %(before_notes)s
2158  
2159 Notes
2160 -----
2161 The probability density function for `exponnorm` is:
2162  
2163 .. math::
2164  
2165 f(x, K) = \frac{1}{2K} \exp\left(\frac{1}{2 K^2} - x / K \right)
2166 \text{erfc}\left(-\frac{x - 1/K}{\sqrt{2}}\right)
2167  
2168 where :math:`x` is a real number and :math:`K > 0`.
2169  
2170 It can be thought of as the sum of a standard normal random variable
2171 and an independent exponentially distributed random variable with rate
2172 ``1/K``.
2173  
2174 %(after_notes)s
2175  
2176 An alternative parameterization of this distribution (for example, in
2177 the Wikipedia article [1]_) involves three parameters, :math:`\mu`,
2178 :math:`\lambda` and :math:`\sigma`.
2179  
2180 In the present parameterization this corresponds to having ``loc`` and
2181 ``scale`` equal to :math:`\mu` and :math:`\sigma`, respectively, and
2182 shape parameter :math:`K = 1/(\sigma\lambda)`.
2183  
2184 .. versionadded:: 0.16.0
2185  
2186 References
2187 ----------
2188 .. [1] Exponentially modified Gaussian distribution, Wikipedia,
2189 https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exponentially_modified_Gaussian_distribution
2190  
2191 %(example)s
2192  
2193 """
2194 def _shape_info(self):
2195 return [_ShapeInfo("K", False, (0, np.inf), (False, False))]
2196  
2197 def _rvs(self, K, size=None, random_state=None):
2198 expval = random_state.standard_exponential(size) * K
2199 gval = random_state.standard_normal(size)
2200 return expval + gval
2201  
2202 def _pdf(self, x, K):
2203 return np.exp(self._logpdf(x, K))
2204  
2205 def _logpdf(self, x, K):
2206 invK = 1.0 / K
2207 exparg = invK * (0.5 * invK - x)
2208 return exparg + _norm_logcdf(x - invK) - np.log(K)
2209  
2210 def _cdf(self, x, K):
2211 invK = 1.0 / K
2212 expval = invK * (0.5 * invK - x)
2213 logprod = expval + _norm_logcdf(x - invK)
2214 return _norm_cdf(x) - np.exp(logprod)
2215  
2216 def _sf(self, x, K):
2217 invK = 1.0 / K
2218 expval = invK * (0.5 * invK - x)
2219 logprod = expval + _norm_logcdf(x - invK)
2220 return _norm_cdf(-x) + np.exp(logprod)
2221  
2222 def _stats(self, K):
2223 K2 = K * K
2224 opK2 = 1.0 + K2
2225 skw = 2 * K**3 * opK2**(-1.5)
2226 krt = 6.0 * K2 * K2 * opK2**(-2)
2227 return K, opK2, skw, krt
2228  
2229  
2230 exponnorm = exponnorm_gen(name='exponnorm')
2231  
2232  
2233 def _pow1pm1(x, y):
2234 """
2235 Compute (1 + x)**y - 1.
2236  
2237 Uses expm1 and xlog1py to avoid loss of precision when
2238 (1 + x)**y is close to 1.
2239  
2240 Note that the inverse of this function with respect to x is
2241 ``_pow1pm1(x, 1/y)``. That is, if
2242  
2243 t = _pow1pm1(x, y)
2244  
2245 then
2246  
2247 x = _pow1pm1(t, 1/y)
2248 """
2249 return np.expm1(sc.xlog1py(y, x))
2250  
2251  
2252 class exponweib_gen(rv_continuous):
2253 r"""An exponentiated Weibull continuous random variable.
2254  
2255 %(before_notes)s
2256  
2257 See Also
2258 --------
2259 weibull_min, numpy.random.Generator.weibull
2260  
2261 Notes
2262 -----
2263 The probability density function for `exponweib` is:
2264  
2265 .. math::
2266  
2267 f(x, a, c) = a c [1-\exp(-x^c)]^{a-1} \exp(-x^c) x^{c-1}
2268  
2269 and its cumulative distribution function is:
2270  
2271 .. math::
2272  
2273 F(x, a, c) = [1-\exp(-x^c)]^a
2274  
2275 for :math:`x > 0`, :math:`a > 0`, :math:`c > 0`.
2276  
2277 `exponweib` takes :math:`a` and :math:`c` as shape parameters:
2278  
2279 * :math:`a` is the exponentiation parameter,
2280 with the special case :math:`a=1` corresponding to the
2281 (non-exponentiated) Weibull distribution `weibull_min`.
2282 * :math:`c` is the shape parameter of the non-exponentiated Weibull law.
2283  
2284 %(after_notes)s
2285  
2286 References
2287 ----------
2288 https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exponentiated_Weibull_distribution
2289  
2290 %(example)s
2291  
2292 """
2293 def _shape_info(self):
2294 ia = _ShapeInfo("a", False, (0, np.inf), (False, False))
2295 ic = _ShapeInfo("c", False, (0, np.inf), (False, False))
2296 return [ia, ic]
2297  
2298 def _pdf(self, x, a, c):
2299 # exponweib.pdf(x, a, c) =
2300 # a * c * (1-exp(-x**c))**(a-1) * exp(-x**c)*x**(c-1)
2301 return np.exp(self._logpdf(x, a, c))
2302  
2303 def _logpdf(self, x, a, c):
2304 negxc = -x**c
2305 exm1c = -sc.expm1(negxc)
2306 logp = (np.log(a) + np.log(c) + sc.xlogy(a - 1.0, exm1c) +
2307 negxc + sc.xlogy(c - 1.0, x))
2308 return logp
2309  
2310 def _cdf(self, x, a, c):
2311 exm1c = -sc.expm1(-x**c)
2312 return exm1c**a
2313  
2314 def _ppf(self, q, a, c):
2315 return (-sc.log1p(-q**(1.0/a)))**np.asarray(1.0/c)
2316  
2317 def _sf(self, x, a, c):
2318 return -_pow1pm1(-np.exp(-x**c), a)
2319  
2320 def _isf(self, p, a, c):
2321 return (-np.log(-_pow1pm1(-p, 1/a)))**(1/c)
2322  
2323  
2324 exponweib = exponweib_gen(a=0.0, name='exponweib')
2325  
2326  
2327 class exponpow_gen(rv_continuous):
2328 r"""An exponential power continuous random variable.
2329  
2330 %(before_notes)s
2331  
2332 Notes
2333 -----
2334 The probability density function for `exponpow` is:
2335  
2336 .. math::
2337  
2338 f(x, b) = b x^{b-1} \exp(1 + x^b - \exp(x^b))
2339  
2340 for :math:`x \ge 0`, :math:`b > 0`. Note that this is a different
2341 distribution from the exponential power distribution that is also known
2342 under the names "generalized normal" or "generalized Gaussian".
2343  
2344 `exponpow` takes ``b`` as a shape parameter for :math:`b`.
2345  
2346 %(after_notes)s
2347  
2348 References
2349 ----------
2350 http://www.math.wm.edu/~leemis/chart/UDR/PDFs/Exponentialpower.pdf
2351  
2352 %(example)s
2353  
2354 """
2355 def _shape_info(self):
2356 return [_ShapeInfo("b", False, (0, np.inf), (False, False))]
2357  
2358 def _pdf(self, x, b):
2359 # exponpow.pdf(x, b) = b * x**(b-1) * exp(1 + x**b - exp(x**b))
2360 return np.exp(self._logpdf(x, b))
2361  
2362 def _logpdf(self, x, b):
2363 xb = x**b
2364 f = 1 + np.log(b) + sc.xlogy(b - 1.0, x) + xb - np.exp(xb)
2365 return f
2366  
2367 def _cdf(self, x, b):
2368 return -sc.expm1(-sc.expm1(x**b))
2369  
2370 def _sf(self, x, b):
2371 return np.exp(-sc.expm1(x**b))
2372  
2373 def _isf(self, x, b):
2374 return (sc.log1p(-np.log(x)))**(1./b)
2375  
2376 def _ppf(self, q, b):
2377 return pow(sc.log1p(-sc.log1p(-q)), 1.0/b)
2378

2383 class fatiguelife_gen(rv_continuous):
2384 r"""A fatigue-life (Birnbaum-Saunders) continuous random variable.
2385  
2386 %(before_notes)s
2387  
2388 Notes
2389 -----
2390 The probability density function for `fatiguelife` is:
2391  
2392 .. math::
2393  
2394 f(x, c) = \frac{x+1}{2c\sqrt{2\pi x^3}} \exp(-\frac{(x-1)^2}{2x c^2})
2395  
2396 for :math:`x >= 0` and :math:`c > 0`.
2397  
2398 `fatiguelife` takes ``c`` as a shape parameter for :math:`c`.
2399  
2400 %(after_notes)s
2401  
2402 References
2403 ----------
2404 .. [1] "Birnbaum-Saunders distribution",
2405 https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birnbaum-Saunders_distribution
2406  
2407 %(example)s
2408  
2409 """
2410 _support_mask = rv_continuous._open_support_mask
2411  
2412 def _shape_info(self):
2413 return [_ShapeInfo("c", False, (0, np.inf), (False, False))]
2414  
2415 def _rvs(self, c, size=None, random_state=None):
2416 z = random_state.standard_normal(size)
2417 x = 0.5*c*z
2418 x2 = x*x
2419 t = 1.0 + 2*x2 + 2*x*np.sqrt(1 + x2)
2420 return t
2421  
2422 def _pdf(self, x, c):
2423 # fatiguelife.pdf(x, c) =
2424 # (x+1) / (2*c*sqrt(2*pi*x**3)) * exp(-(x-1)**2/(2*x*c**2))
2425 return np.exp(self._logpdf(x, c))
2426  
2427 def _logpdf(self, x, c):
2428 return (np.log(x+1) - (x-1)**2 / (2.0*x*c**2) - np.log(2*c) -
2429 0.5*(np.log(2*np.pi) + 3*np.log(x)))
2430  
2431 def _cdf(self, x, c):
2432 return _norm_cdf(1.0 / c * (np.sqrt(x) - 1.0/np.sqrt(x)))
2433  
2434 def _ppf(self, q, c):
2435 tmp = c * _norm_ppf(q)
2436 return 0.25 * (tmp + np.sqrt(tmp**2 + 4))**2
2437  
2438 def _sf(self, x, c):
2439 return _norm_sf(1.0 / c * (np.sqrt(x) - 1.0/np.sqrt(x)))
2440  
2441 def _isf(self, q, c):
2442 tmp = -c * _norm_ppf(q)
2443 return 0.25 * (tmp + np.sqrt(tmp**2 + 4))**2
2444  
2445 def _stats(self, c):
2446 # NB: the formula for kurtosis in wikipedia seems to have an error:
2447 # it's 40, not 41. At least it disagrees with the one from Wolfram
2448 # Alpha. And the latter one, below, passes the tests, while the wiki
2449 # one doesn't So far I didn't have the guts to actually check the
2450 # coefficients from the expressions for the raw moments.
2451 c2 = c*c
2452 mu = c2 / 2.0 + 1.0
2453 den = 5.0 * c2 + 4.0
2454 mu2 = c2*den / 4.0
2455 g1 = 4 * c * (11*c2 + 6.0) / np.power(den, 1.5)
2456 g2 = 6 * c2 * (93*c2 + 40.0) / den**2.0
2457 return mu, mu2, g1, g2
2458  
2459  
2460 fatiguelife = fatiguelife_gen(a=0.0, name='fatiguelife')
2461  
2462  
2463 class foldcauchy_gen(rv_continuous):
2464 r"""A folded Cauchy continuous random variable.
2465  
2466 %(before_notes)s
2467  
2468 Notes
2469 -----
2470 The probability density function for `foldcauchy` is:
2471  
2472 .. math::
2473  
2474 f(x, c) = \frac{1}{\pi (1+(x-c)^2)} + \frac{1}{\pi (1+(x+c)^2)}
2475  
2476 for :math:`x \ge 0` and :math:`c \ge 0`.
2477  
2478 `foldcauchy` takes ``c`` as a shape parameter for :math:`c`.
2479  
2480 %(example)s
2481  
2482 """
2483 def _argcheck(self, c):
2484 return c >= 0
2485  
2486 def _shape_info(self):
2487 return [_ShapeInfo("c", False, (0, np.inf), (True, False))]
2488  
2489 def _rvs(self, c, size=None, random_state=None):
2490 return abs(cauchy.rvs(loc=c, size=size,
2491 random_state=random_state))
2492  
2493 def _pdf(self, x, c):
2494 # foldcauchy.pdf(x, c) = 1/(pi*(1+(x-c)**2)) + 1/(pi*(1+(x+c)**2))
2495 return 1.0/np.pi*(1.0/(1+(x-c)**2) + 1.0/(1+(x+c)**2))
2496  
2497 def _cdf(self, x, c):
2498 return 1.0/np.pi*(np.arctan(x-c) + np.arctan(x+c))
2499  
2500 def _sf(self, x, c):
2501 # 1 - CDF(x, c) = 1 - (atan(x - c) + atan(x + c))/pi
2502 # = ((pi/2 - atan(x - c)) + (pi/2 - atan(x + c)))/pi
2503 # = (acot(x - c) + acot(x + c))/pi
2504 # = (atan2(1, x - c) + atan2(1, x + c))/pi
2505 return (np.arctan2(1, x - c) + np.arctan2(1, x + c))/np.pi
2506  
2507 def _stats(self, c):
2508 return np.inf, np.inf, np.nan, np.nan
2509  
2510  
2511 foldcauchy = foldcauchy_gen(a=0.0, name='foldcauchy')
2512

2514 class f_gen(rv_continuous):
2515 r"""An F continuous random variable.
2516  
2517 For the noncentral F distribution, see `ncf`.
2518  
2519 %(before_notes)s
2520  
2521 See Also
2522 --------
2523 ncf
2524  
2525 Notes
2526 -----
  • E501 Line too long (87 > 79 characters)
2527 The F distribution with :math:`df_1 > 0` and :math:`df_2 > 0` degrees of freedom is
  • E501 Line too long (83 > 79 characters)
2528 the distribution of the ratio of two independent chi-squared distributions with
2529 :math:`df_1` and :math:`df_2` degrees of freedom, after rescaling by
2530 :math:`df_2 / df_1`.
2531  
2532 The probability density function for `f` is:
2533  
2534 .. math::
2535  
2536 f(x, df_1, df_2) = \frac{df_2^{df_2/2} df_1^{df_1/2} x^{df_1 / 2-1}}
2537 {(df_2+df_1 x)^{(df_1+df_2)/2}
2538 B(df_1/2, df_2/2)}
2539  
2540 for :math:`x > 0`.
2541  
  • E501 Line too long (85 > 79 characters)
2542 `f` accepts shape parameters ``dfn`` and ``dfd`` for :math:`df_1`, the degrees of
  • E501 Line too long (83 > 79 characters)
2543 freedom of the chi-squared distribution in the numerator, and :math:`df_2`, the
  • E501 Line too long (88 > 79 characters)
2544 degrees of freedom of the chi-squared distribution in the denominator, respectively.
2545  
2546 %(after_notes)s
2547  
2548 %(example)s
2549  
2550 """
2551 def _shape_info(self):
2552 idfn = _ShapeInfo("dfn", False, (0, np.inf), (False, False))
2553 idfd = _ShapeInfo("dfd", False, (0, np.inf), (False, False))
2554 return [idfn, idfd]
2555  
2556 def _rvs(self, dfn, dfd, size=None, random_state=None):
2557 return random_state.f(dfn, dfd, size)
2558  
2559 def _pdf(self, x, dfn, dfd):
2560 # df2**(df2/2) * df1**(df1/2) * x**(df1/2-1)
2561 # F.pdf(x, df1, df2) = --------------------------------------------
2562 # (df2+df1*x)**((df1+df2)/2) * B(df1/2, df2/2)
2563 return np.exp(self._logpdf(x, dfn, dfd))
2564  
2565 def _logpdf(self, x, dfn, dfd):
2566 n = 1.0 * dfn
2567 m = 1.0 * dfd
2568 lPx = (m/2 * np.log(m) + n/2 * np.log(n) + sc.xlogy(n/2 - 1, x)
2569 - (((n+m)/2) * np.log(m + n*x) + sc.betaln(n/2, m/2)))
2570 return lPx
2571  
2572 def _cdf(self, x, dfn, dfd):
2573 return sc.fdtr(dfn, dfd, x)
2574  
2575 def _sf(self, x, dfn, dfd):
2576 return sc.fdtrc(dfn, dfd, x)
2577  
2578 def _ppf(self, q, dfn, dfd):
2579 return sc.fdtri(dfn, dfd, q)
2580  
2581 def _stats(self, dfn, dfd):
2582 v1, v2 = 1. * dfn, 1. * dfd
2583 v2_2, v2_4, v2_6, v2_8 = v2 - 2., v2 - 4., v2 - 6., v2 - 8.
2584  
2585 mu = xpx.apply_where(
2586 v2 > 2, (v2, v2_2),
2587 lambda v2, v2_2: v2 / v2_2,
2588 fill_value=np.inf)
2589  
2590 mu2 = xpx.apply_where(
2591 v2 > 4, (v1, v2, v2_2, v2_4),
2592 lambda v1, v2, v2_2, v2_4:
2593 2 * v2 * v2 * (v1 + v2_2) / (v1 * v2_2**2 * v2_4),
2594 fill_value=np.inf)
2595  
2596 g1 = xpx.apply_where(
2597 v2 > 6, (v1, v2_2, v2_4, v2_6),
2598 lambda v1, v2_2, v2_4, v2_6:
2599 (2 * v1 + v2_2) / v2_6 * np.sqrt(v2_4 / (v1 * (v1 + v2_2))),
2600 fill_value=np.nan)
2601 g1 *= np.sqrt(8.)
2602  
2603 g2 = xpx.apply_where(
2604 v2 > 8, (g1, v2_6, v2_8),
2605 lambda g1, v2_6, v2_8: (8 + g1 * g1 * v2_6) / v2_8,
2606 fill_value=np.nan)
2607 g2 *= 3. / 2.
2608  
2609 return mu, mu2, g1, g2
2610  
2611 def _entropy(self, dfn, dfd):
2612 # the formula found in literature is incorrect. This one yields the
2613 # same result as numerical integration using the generic entropy
2614 # definition. This is also tested in tests/test_conntinous_basic
2615 half_dfn = 0.5 * dfn
2616 half_dfd = 0.5 * dfd
2617 half_sum = 0.5 * (dfn + dfd)
2618  
2619 return (np.log(dfd) - np.log(dfn) + sc.betaln(half_dfn, half_dfd) +
2620 (1 - half_dfn) * sc.psi(half_dfn) - (1 + half_dfd) *
2621 sc.psi(half_dfd) + half_sum * sc.psi(half_sum))
2622  
2623  
2624 f = f_gen(a=0.0, name='f')
2625  
2626

2635 class foldnorm_gen(rv_continuous):
2636 r"""A folded normal continuous random variable.
2637  
2638 %(before_notes)s
2639  
2640 Notes
2641 -----
2642 The probability density function for `foldnorm` is:
2643  
2644 .. math::
2645  
2646 f(x, c) = \sqrt{2/\pi} cosh(c x) \exp(-\frac{x^2+c^2}{2})
2647  
2648 for :math:`x \ge 0` and :math:`c \ge 0`.
2649  
2650 `foldnorm` takes ``c`` as a shape parameter for :math:`c`.
2651  
2652 %(after_notes)s
2653  
2654 %(example)s
2655  
2656 """
2657 def _argcheck(self, c):
2658 return c >= 0
2659  
2660 def _shape_info(self):
2661 return [_ShapeInfo("c", False, (0, np.inf), (True, False))]
2662  
2663 def _rvs(self, c, size=None, random_state=None):
2664 return abs(random_state.standard_normal(size) + c)
2665  
2666 def _pdf(self, x, c):
2667 # foldnormal.pdf(x, c) = sqrt(2/pi) * cosh(c*x) * exp(-(x**2+c**2)/2)
2668 return _norm_pdf(x + c) + _norm_pdf(x-c)
2669  
2670 def _cdf(self, x, c):
2671 sqrt_two = np.sqrt(2)
2672 return 0.5 * (sc.erf((x - c)/sqrt_two) + sc.erf((x + c)/sqrt_two))
2673  
2674 def _sf(self, x, c):
2675 return _norm_sf(x - c) + _norm_sf(x + c)
2676  
2677 def _stats(self, c):
2678 # Regina C. Elandt, Technometrics 3, 551 (1961)
2679 # https://www.jstor.org/stable/1266561
2680 #
2681 c2 = c*c
2682 expfac = np.exp(-0.5*c2) / np.sqrt(2.*np.pi)
2683  
2684 mu = 2.*expfac + c * sc.erf(c/np.sqrt(2))
2685 mu2 = c2 + 1 - mu*mu
2686  
2687 g1 = 2. * (mu*mu*mu - c2*mu - expfac)
2688 g1 /= np.power(mu2, 1.5)
2689  
2690 g2 = c2 * (c2 + 6.) + 3 + 8.*expfac*mu
2691 g2 += (2. * (c2 - 3.) - 3. * mu**2) * mu**2
2692 g2 = g2 / mu2**2.0 - 3.
2693  
2694 return mu, mu2, g1, g2
2695  
2696  
2697 foldnorm = foldnorm_gen(a=0.0, name='foldnorm')
2698

2700 class weibull_min_gen(rv_continuous):
2701 r"""Weibull minimum continuous random variable.
2702  
2703 The Weibull Minimum Extreme Value distribution, from extreme value theory
2704 (Fisher-Gnedenko theorem), is also often simply called the Weibull
2705 distribution. It arises as the limiting distribution of the rescaled
2706 minimum of iid random variables.
2707  
2708 %(before_notes)s
2709  
2710 See Also
2711 --------
2712 weibull_max, numpy.random.Generator.weibull, exponweib
2713  
2714 Notes
2715 -----
2716 The probability density function for `weibull_min` is:
2717  
2718 .. math::
2719  
2720 f(x, c) = c x^{c-1} \exp(-x^c)
2721  
2722 for :math:`x > 0`, :math:`c > 0`.
2723  
2724 `weibull_min` takes ``c`` as a shape parameter for :math:`c`.
2725 (named :math:`k` in Wikipedia article and :math:`a` in
2726 ``numpy.random.weibull``). Special shape values are :math:`c=1` and
2727 :math:`c=2` where Weibull distribution reduces to the `expon` and
2728 `rayleigh` distributions respectively.
2729  
2730 Suppose ``X`` is an exponentially distributed random variable with
2731 scale ``s``. Then ``Y = X**k`` is `weibull_min` distributed with shape
2732 ``c = 1/k`` and scale ``s**k``.
2733  
2734 %(after_notes)s
2735  
2736 References
2737 ----------
2738 https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weibull_distribution
2739  
2740 https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fisher-Tippett-Gnedenko_theorem
2741  
2742 %(example)s
2743  
2744 """
2745 def _shape_info(self):
2746 return [_ShapeInfo("c", False, (0, np.inf), (False, False))]
2747  
2748 def _pdf(self, x, c):
2749 # weibull_min.pdf(x, c) = c * x**(c-1) * exp(-x**c)
2750 return c*pow(x, c-1)*np.exp(-pow(x, c))
2751  
2752 def _logpdf(self, x, c):
2753 return np.log(c) + sc.xlogy(c - 1, x) - pow(x, c)
2754  
2755 def _cdf(self, x, c):
2756 return -sc.expm1(-pow(x, c))
2757  
2758 def _ppf(self, q, c):
2759 return pow(-sc.log1p(-q), 1.0/c)
2760  
2761 def _sf(self, x, c):
2762 return np.exp(self._logsf(x, c))
2763  
2764 def _logsf(self, x, c):
2765 return -pow(x, c)
2766  
2767 def _isf(self, q, c):
2768 return (-np.log(q))**(1/c)
2769  
2770 def _munp(self, n, c):
2771 return sc.gamma(1.0+n*1.0/c)
2772  
2773 def _entropy(self, c):
2774 return -_EULER / c - np.log(c) + _EULER + 1
2775  
2776 @extend_notes_in_docstring(rv_continuous, notes="""\
2777 If ``method='mm'``, parameters fixed by the user are respected, and the
2778 remaining parameters are used to match distribution and sample moments
2779 where possible. For example, if the user fixes the location with
2780 ``floc``, the parameters will only match the distribution skewness and
2781 variance to the sample skewness and variance; no attempt will be made
2782 to match the means or minimize a norm of the errors.
2783 \n\n""")
2784 def fit(self, data, *args, **kwds):
2785  
2786 if isinstance(data, CensoredData):
2787 if data.num_censored() == 0:
2788 data = data._uncensor()
2789 else:
2790 return super().fit(data, *args, **kwds)
2791  
2792 if kwds.pop('superfit', False):
2793 return super().fit(data, *args, **kwds)
2794  
2795 # this extracts fixed shape, location, and scale however they
2796 # are specified, and also leaves them in `kwds`
2797 data, fc, floc, fscale = _check_fit_input_parameters(self, data,
2798 args, kwds)
2799 method = kwds.get("method", "mle").lower()
2800  
2801 # See https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weibull_distribution#Moments for
2802 # moment formulas.
2803 def skew(c):
2804 gamma1 = sc.gamma(1+1/c)
2805 gamma2 = sc.gamma(1+2/c)
2806 gamma3 = sc.gamma(1+3/c)
2807 num = 2 * gamma1**3 - 3*gamma1*gamma2 + gamma3
2808 den = (gamma2 - gamma1**2)**(3/2)
2809 return num/den
2810  
2811 # For c in [1e2, 3e4], population skewness appears to approach
2812 # asymptote near -1.139, but past c > 3e4, skewness begins to vary
2813 # wildly, and MoM won't provide a good guess. Get out early.
2814 s = stats.skew(data)
2815 max_c = 1e4
2816 s_min = skew(max_c)
2817 if s < s_min and method != "mm" and fc is None and not args:
2818 return super().fit(data, *args, **kwds)
2819  
2820 # If method is method of moments, we don't need the user's guesses.
2821 # Otherwise, extract the guesses from args and kwds.
2822 if method == "mm":
2823 c, loc, scale = None, None, None
2824 else:
2825 c = args[0] if len(args) else None
2826 loc = kwds.pop('loc', None)
2827 scale = kwds.pop('scale', None)
2828  
2829 if fc is None and c is None: # not fixed and no guess: use MoM
2830 # Solve for c that matches sample distribution skewness to sample
2831 # skewness.
2832 # we start having numerical issues with `weibull_min` with
2833 # parameters outside this range - and not just in this method.
2834 # We could probably improve the situation by doing everything
2835 # in the log space, but that is for another time.
2836 c = root_scalar(lambda c: skew(c) - s, bracket=[0.02, max_c],
2837 method='bisect').root
2838 elif fc is not None: # fixed: use it
2839 c = fc
2840  
2841 if fscale is None and scale is None:
2842 v = np.var(data)
2843 scale = np.sqrt(v / (sc.gamma(1+2/c) - sc.gamma(1+1/c)**2))
2844 elif fscale is not None:
2845 scale = fscale
2846  
2847 if floc is None and loc is None:
2848 m = np.mean(data)
2849 loc = m - scale*sc.gamma(1 + 1/c)
2850 elif floc is not None:
2851 loc = floc
2852  
2853 if method == 'mm':
2854 return c, loc, scale
2855 else:
2856 # At this point, parameter "guesses" may equal the fixed parameters
2857 # in kwds. No harm in passing them as guesses, too.
2858 return super().fit(data, c, loc=loc, scale=scale, **kwds)
2859  
2860  
2861 weibull_min = weibull_min_gen(a=0.0, name='weibull_min')
2862  
2863  
2864 class truncweibull_min_gen(rv_continuous):
2865 r"""A doubly truncated Weibull minimum continuous random variable.
2866  
2867 %(before_notes)s
2868  
2869 See Also
2870 --------
2871 weibull_min, truncexpon
2872  
2873 Notes
2874 -----
2875 The probability density function for `truncweibull_min` is:
2876  
2877 .. math::
2878  
2879 f(x, a, b, c) = \frac{c x^{c-1} \exp(-x^c)}{\exp(-a^c) - \exp(-b^c)}
2880  
2881 for :math:`a < x <= b`, :math:`0 \le a < b` and :math:`c > 0`.
2882  
2883 `truncweibull_min` takes :math:`a`, :math:`b`, and :math:`c` as shape
2884 parameters.
2885  
2886 Notice that the truncation values, :math:`a` and :math:`b`, are defined in
2887 standardized form:
2888  
2889 .. math::
2890  
2891 a = (u_l - loc)/scale
2892 b = (u_r - loc)/scale
2893  
2894 where :math:`u_l` and :math:`u_r` are the specific left and right
2895 truncation values, respectively. In other words, the support of the
2896 distribution becomes :math:`(a*scale + loc) < x <= (b*scale + loc)` when
2897 :math:`loc` and/or :math:`scale` are provided.
2898  
2899 %(after_notes)s
2900  
2901 References
2902 ----------
2903  
2904 .. [1] Rinne, H. "The Weibull Distribution: A Handbook". CRC Press (2009).
2905  
2906 %(example)s
2907  
2908 """
2909 def _argcheck(self, c, a, b):
2910 return (a >= 0.) & (b > a) & (c > 0.)
2911  
2912 def _shape_info(self):
2913 ic = _ShapeInfo("c", False, (0, np.inf), (False, False))
2914 ia = _ShapeInfo("a", False, (0, np.inf), (True, False))
2915 ib = _ShapeInfo("b", False, (0, np.inf), (False, False))
2916 return [ic, ia, ib]
2917  
2918 def _fitstart(self, data):
2919 # Arbitrary, but default a=b=c=1 is not valid
2920 return super()._fitstart(data, args=(1, 0, 1))
2921  
2922 def _get_support(self, c, a, b):
2923 return a, b
2924  
2925 def _pdf(self, x, c, a, b):
2926 denum = (np.exp(-pow(a, c)) - np.exp(-pow(b, c)))
2927 return (c * pow(x, c-1) * np.exp(-pow(x, c))) / denum
2928  
2929 def _logpdf(self, x, c, a, b):
2930 logdenum = np.log(np.exp(-pow(a, c)) - np.exp(-pow(b, c)))
2931 return np.log(c) + sc.xlogy(c - 1, x) - pow(x, c) - logdenum
2932  
2933 def _cdf(self, x, c, a, b):
2934 num = (np.exp(-pow(a, c)) - np.exp(-pow(x, c)))
2935 denum = (np.exp(-pow(a, c)) - np.exp(-pow(b, c)))
2936 return num / denum
2937  
2938 def _logcdf(self, x, c, a, b):
2939 lognum = np.log(np.exp(-pow(a, c)) - np.exp(-pow(x, c)))
2940 logdenum = np.log(np.exp(-pow(a, c)) - np.exp(-pow(b, c)))
2941 return lognum - logdenum
2942  
2943 def _sf(self, x, c, a, b):
2944 num = (np.exp(-pow(x, c)) - np.exp(-pow(b, c)))
2945 denum = (np.exp(-pow(a, c)) - np.exp(-pow(b, c)))
2946 return num / denum
2947  
2948 def _logsf(self, x, c, a, b):
2949 lognum = np.log(np.exp(-pow(x, c)) - np.exp(-pow(b, c)))
2950 logdenum = np.log(np.exp(-pow(a, c)) - np.exp(-pow(b, c)))
2951 return lognum - logdenum
2952  
2953 def _isf(self, q, c, a, b):
2954 return pow(
2955 -np.log((1 - q) * np.exp(-pow(b, c)) + q * np.exp(-pow(a, c))), 1/c
2956 )
2957  
2958 def _ppf(self, q, c, a, b):
2959 return pow(
2960 -np.log((1 - q) * np.exp(-pow(a, c)) + q * np.exp(-pow(b, c))), 1/c
2961 )
2962  
2963 def _munp(self, n, c, a, b):
2964 gamma_fun = sc.gamma(n/c + 1.) * (
2965 sc.gammainc(n/c + 1., pow(b, c)) - sc.gammainc(n/c + 1., pow(a, c))
2966 )
2967 denum = (np.exp(-pow(a, c)) - np.exp(-pow(b, c)))
2968 return gamma_fun / denum
2969  
2970  
2971 truncweibull_min = truncweibull_min_gen(name='truncweibull_min')
2972 truncweibull_min._support = ('a', 'b')
2973  
2974  
2975 class weibull_max_gen(rv_continuous):
2976 r"""Weibull maximum continuous random variable.
2977  
2978 The Weibull Maximum Extreme Value distribution, from extreme value theory
2979 (Fisher-Gnedenko theorem), is the limiting distribution of rescaled
2980 maximum of iid random variables. This is the distribution of -X
2981 if X is from the `weibull_min` function.
2982  
2983 %(before_notes)s
2984  
2985 See Also
2986 --------
2987 weibull_min
2988  
2989 Notes
2990 -----
2991 The probability density function for `weibull_max` is:
2992  
2993 .. math::
2994  
2995 f(x, c) = c (-x)^{c-1} \exp(-(-x)^c)
2996  
2997 for :math:`x < 0`, :math:`c > 0`.
2998  
2999 `weibull_max` takes ``c`` as a shape parameter for :math:`c`.
3000  
3001 %(after_notes)s
3002  
3003 References
3004 ----------
3005 https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weibull_distribution
3006  
3007 https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fisher-Tippett-Gnedenko_theorem

3049 class genlogistic_gen(rv_continuous):
3050 r"""A generalized logistic continuous random variable.
3051  
3052 %(before_notes)s
3053  
3054 Notes
3055 -----
3056 The probability density function for `genlogistic` is:
3057  
3058 .. math::
3059  
3060 f(x, c) = c \frac{\exp(-x)}
3061 {(1 + \exp(-x))^{c+1}}
3062  
3063 for real :math:`x` and :math:`c > 0`. In literature, different
  • E501 Line too long (81 > 79 characters)
3064 generalizations of the logistic distribution can be found. This is the type 1
3065 generalized logistic distribution according to [1]_. It is also referred to
3066 as the skew-logistic distribution [2]_.
3067  
3068 `genlogistic` takes ``c`` as a shape parameter for :math:`c`.
3069  
3070 %(after_notes)s
3071  
3072 References
3073 ----------
3074 .. [1] Johnson et al. "Continuous Univariate Distributions", Volume 2,
3075 Wiley. 1995.
3076 .. [2] "Generalized Logistic Distribution", Wikipedia,
3077 https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generalized_logistic_distribution
3078  
3079 %(example)s
3080  
3081 """
3082 def _shape_info(self):
3083 return [_ShapeInfo("c", False, (0, np.inf), (False, False))]
3084  
3085 def _pdf(self, x, c):
3086 # genlogistic.pdf(x, c) = c * exp(-x) / (1 + exp(-x))**(c+1)
3087 return np.exp(self._logpdf(x, c))
3088  
3089 def _logpdf(self, x, c):
3090 # Two mathematically equivalent expressions for log(pdf(x, c)):
3091 # log(pdf(x, c)) = log(c) - x - (c + 1)*log(1 + exp(-x))
3092 # = log(c) + c*x - (c + 1)*log(1 + exp(x))
3093 mult = -(c - 1) * (x < 0) - 1
3094 absx = np.abs(x)
3095 return np.log(c) + mult*absx - (c+1) * sc.log1p(np.exp(-absx))
3096  
3097 def _cdf(self, x, c):
3098 Cx = (1+np.exp(-x))**(-c)
3099 return Cx
3100  
3101 def _logcdf(self, x, c):
3102 return -c * np.log1p(np.exp(-x))
3103  
3104 def _ppf(self, q, c):
3105 return -np.log(sc.powm1(q, -1.0/c))
3106  
3107 def _sf(self, x, c):
3108 return -sc.expm1(self._logcdf(x, c))
3109  
3110 def _isf(self, q, c):
3111 return self._ppf(1 - q, c)
3112  
3113 def _stats(self, c):
3114 mu = _EULER + sc.psi(c)
3115 mu2 = np.pi*np.pi/6.0 + sc.zeta(2, c)
3116 g1 = -2*sc.zeta(3, c) + 2*_ZETA3
3117 g1 /= np.power(mu2, 1.5)
3118 g2 = np.pi**4/15.0 + 6*sc.zeta(4, c)
3119 g2 /= mu2**2.0
3120 return mu, mu2, g1, g2

3123 return xpx.apply_where(
3124 c < 8e6, c,
3125 lambda c: -np.log(c) + sc.psi(c + 1) + _EULER + 1,
3126 # asymptotic expansion: psi(c) ~ log(c) - 1 / (2 * c)
3127 # a = -log(c) + psi(c + 1)
3128 # = -log(c) + psi(c) + 1 / c
3129 # ~ -log(c) + log(c) - 1 / (2 * c) + 1 / c
3130 # = 1 / (2 * c)
3131 lambda c: 1 / (2 * c) + _EULER + 1)

3134 genlogistic = genlogistic_gen(name='genlogistic')

3498 def _digammainv(y):
3499 """Inverse of the digamma function (real positive arguments only).
3500  
3501 This function is used in the `fit` method of `gamma_gen`.
3502 The function uses either optimize.fsolve or optimize.newton
3503 to solve `sc.digamma(x) - y = 0`. There is probably room for
3504 improvement, but currently it works over a wide range of y:
3505  
3506 >>> import numpy as np
3507 >>> rng = np.random.default_rng()
3508 >>> y = 64*rng.standard_normal(1000000)
3509 >>> y.min(), y.max()
3510 (-311.43592651416662, 351.77388222276869)
3511 >>> x = [_digammainv(t) for t in y]
3512 >>> np.abs(sc.digamma(x) - y).max()
3513 1.1368683772161603e-13
3514

3518 def func(x):
3519 return sc.digamma(x) - y
3520  
3521 if y > -0.125:
3522 x0 = np.exp(y) + 0.5
3523 if y < 10:
3524 # Some experimentation shows that newton reliably converges
3525 # must faster than fsolve in this y range. For larger y,
3526 # newton sometimes fails to converge.
3527 value = optimize.newton(func, x0, tol=1e-10)
3528 return value
3529 elif y > -3:
3530 x0 = np.exp(y/2.332) + 0.08661
3531 else:
3532 x0 = 1.0 / (-y - _em)
3533  
3534 value, info, ier, mesg = optimize.fsolve(func, x0, xtol=1e-11,
3535 full_output=True)
3536 if ier != 1:
3537 raise RuntimeError(f"_digammainv: fsolve failed, y = {y!r}")
3538  
3539 return value[0]

3548 class gamma_gen(rv_continuous):
3549 r"""A gamma continuous random variable.
3550  
3551 %(before_notes)s
3552  
3553 See Also
3554 --------
3555 erlang, expon
3556  
3557 Notes
3558 -----
3559 The probability density function for `gamma` is:
3560  
3561 .. math::
3562  
3563 f(x, a) = \frac{x^{a-1} e^{-x}}{\Gamma(a)}
3564  
3565 for :math:`x \ge 0`, :math:`a > 0`. Here :math:`\Gamma(a)` refers to the
3566 gamma function.
3567  
3568 `gamma` takes ``a`` as a shape parameter for :math:`a`.
3569  
3570 When :math:`a` is an integer, `gamma` reduces to the Erlang
3571 distribution, and when :math:`a=1` to the exponential distribution.
3572  
3573 Gamma distributions are sometimes parameterized with two variables,
3574 with a probability density function of:
3575  
3576 .. math::
3577  
3578 f(x, \alpha, \beta) =
3579 \frac{\beta^\alpha x^{\alpha - 1} e^{-\beta x }}{\Gamma(\alpha)}
3580  
3581 Note that this parameterization is equivalent to the above, with
3582 ``scale = 1 / beta``.
3583  
3584 %(after_notes)s
3585  
3586 %(example)s
3587  
3588 """
3589 def _shape_info(self):
3590 return [_ShapeInfo("a", False, (0, np.inf), (False, False))]
3591  
3592 def _rvs(self, a, size=None, random_state=None):
3593 return random_state.standard_gamma(a, size)
3594  
3595 def _pdf(self, x, a):
3596 # gamma.pdf(x, a) = x**(a-1) * exp(-x) / gamma(a)
3597 return np.exp(self._logpdf(x, a))
3598  
3599 def _logpdf(self, x, a):
3600 return sc.xlogy(a-1.0, x) - x - sc.gammaln(a)
3601  
3602 def _cdf(self, x, a):
3603 return sc.gammainc(a, x)
3604  
3605 def _sf(self, x, a):
3606 return sc.gammaincc(a, x)
3607  
3608 def _ppf(self, q, a):
3609 return sc.gammaincinv(a, q)
3610  
3611 def _isf(self, q, a):
3612 return sc.gammainccinv(a, q)
3613  
3614 def _stats(self, a):
3615 return a, a, 2.0/np.sqrt(a), 6.0/a
3616  
3617 def _munp(self, n, a):
3618 return sc.poch(a, n)
3619  
3620 def _entropy(self, a):
3621  
3622 def regular_formula(a):
3623 return sc.psi(a) * (1-a) + a + sc.gammaln(a)
3624  
3625 def asymptotic_formula(a):
3626 # plug in above formula the expansions:
3627 # psi(a) ~ ln(a) - 1/2a - 1/12a^2 + 1/120a^4
3628 # gammaln(a) ~ a * ln(a) - a - 1/2 * ln(a) + 1/2 ln(2 * pi) +
3629 # 1/12a - 1/360a^3
3630 return (0.5 * (1. + np.log(2*np.pi) + np.log(a)) - 1/(3 * a)
3631 - (a**-2.)/12 - (a**-3.)/90 + (a**-4.)/120)
3632  
3633 return xpx.apply_where(a < 250, a, regular_formula, asymptotic_formula)
3634  
3635 def _fitstart(self, data):
3636 # The skewness of the gamma distribution is `2 / np.sqrt(a)`.
3637 # We invert that to estimate the shape `a` using the skewness
3638 # of the data. The formula is regularized with 1e-8 in the
3639 # denominator to allow for degenerate data where the skewness
3640 # is close to 0.
3641 if isinstance(data, CensoredData):
3642 data = data._uncensor()
3643 sk = _skew(data)
3644 a = 4 / (1e-8 + sk**2)
3645 return super()._fitstart(data, args=(a,))
3646  
3647 @extend_notes_in_docstring(rv_continuous, notes="""\
3648 When the location is fixed by using the argument `floc`
3649 and `method='MLE'`, this
3650 function uses explicit formulas or solves a simpler numerical
3651 problem than the full ML optimization problem. So in that case,
3652 the `optimizer`, `loc` and `scale` arguments are ignored.
3653 \n\n""")
3654 def fit(self, data, *args, **kwds):
3655 floc = kwds.get('floc', None)
3656 method = kwds.get('method', 'mle')
3657  
3658 if (isinstance(data, CensoredData) or
3659 floc is None and method.lower() != 'mm'):
3660 # loc is not fixed or we're not doing standard MLE.
3661 # Use the default fit method.
3662 return super().fit(data, *args, **kwds)
3663  
3664 # We already have this value, so just pop it from kwds.
3665 kwds.pop('floc', None)
3666  
3667 f0 = _get_fixed_fit_value(kwds, ['f0', 'fa', 'fix_a'])
3668 fscale = kwds.pop('fscale', None)
3669  
3670 _remove_optimizer_parameters(kwds)
3671  
3672 if f0 is not None and floc is not None and fscale is not None:
3673 # This check is for consistency with `rv_continuous.fit`.
3674 # Without this check, this function would just return the
3675 # parameters that were given.
3676 raise ValueError("All parameters fixed. There is nothing to "
3677 "optimize.")
3678  
3679 # Fixed location is handled by shifting the data.
3680 data = np.asarray(data)
3681  
3682 if not np.isfinite(data).all():
3683 raise ValueError("The data contains non-finite values.")
3684  
3685 # Use explicit formulas for mm (gh-19884)
3686 if method.lower() == 'mm':
3687 m1 = np.mean(data)
3688 m2 = np.var(data)
3689 m3 = np.mean((data - m1) ** 3)
3690 a, loc, scale = f0, floc, fscale
3691 # Three unknowns
3692 if a is None and loc is None and scale is None:
3693 scale = m3 / (2 * m2)
3694 # Two unknowns
3695 if loc is None and scale is None:
3696 scale = np.sqrt(m2 / a)
3697 if a is None and scale is None:
3698 scale = m2 / (m1 - loc)
3699 if a is None and loc is None:
3700 a = m2 / (scale ** 2)
3701 # One unknown
3702 if a is None:
3703 a = (m1 - loc) / scale
3704 if loc is None:
3705 loc = m1 - a * scale
3706 if scale is None:
3707 scale = (m1 - loc) / a
3708 return a, loc, scale
3709  
3710 # Special case: loc is fixed.
3711  
3712 # NB: data == loc is ok if a >= 1; the below check is more strict.
3713 if np.any(data <= floc):
3714 raise FitDataError("gamma", lower=floc, upper=np.inf)
3715  
3716 if floc != 0:
3717 # Don't do the subtraction in-place, because `data` might be a
3718 # view of the input array.
3719 data = data - floc
3720 xbar = data.mean()
3721  
3722 # Three cases to handle:
3723 # * shape and scale both free
3724 # * shape fixed, scale free
3725 # * shape free, scale fixed
3726  
3727 if fscale is None:
3728 # scale is free
3729 if f0 is not None:
3730 # shape is fixed
3731 a = f0
3732 else:
3733 # shape and scale are both free.
3734 # The MLE for the shape parameter `a` is the solution to:
3735 # np.log(a) - sc.digamma(a) - np.log(xbar) +
3736 # np.log(data).mean() = 0
3737 s = np.log(xbar) - np.log(data).mean()
3738 aest = (3-s + np.sqrt((s-3)**2 + 24*s)) / (12*s)
3739 xa = aest*(1-0.4)
3740 xb = aest*(1+0.4)
3741 a = optimize.brentq(lambda a: np.log(a) - sc.digamma(a) - s,
3742 xa, xb, disp=0)
3743  
3744 # The MLE for the scale parameter is just the data mean
3745 # divided by the shape parameter.
3746 scale = xbar / a
3747 else:
3748 # scale is fixed, shape is free
3749 # The MLE for the shape parameter `a` is the solution to:
3750 # sc.digamma(a) - np.log(data).mean() + np.log(fscale) = 0
3751 c = np.log(data).mean() - np.log(fscale)
3752 a = _digammainv(c)
3753 scale = fscale
3754  
3755 return a, floc, scale
3756  
3757  
3758 gamma = gamma_gen(a=0.0, name='gamma')
3759  
3760  
3761 class erlang_gen(gamma_gen):
3762 """An Erlang continuous random variable.
3763  
3764 %(before_notes)s
3765  
3766 See Also
3767 --------
3768 gamma
3769  
3770 Notes
3771 -----
3772 The Erlang distribution is a special case of the Gamma distribution, with
3773 the shape parameter `a` an integer. Note that this restriction is not
3774 enforced by `erlang`. It will, however, generate a warning the first time
3775 a non-integer value is used for the shape parameter.
3776  
3777 Refer to `gamma` for examples.
3778  
3779 """
3780  
3781 def _argcheck(self, a):
3782 allint = np.all(np.floor(a) == a)
3783 if not allint:
3784 # An Erlang distribution shouldn't really have a non-integer
3785 # shape parameter, so warn the user.
3786 message = ('The shape parameter of the erlang distribution '
3787 f'has been given a non-integer value {a!r}.')
3788 warnings.warn(message, RuntimeWarning, stacklevel=3)
3789 return a > 0
3790  
3791 def _shape_info(self):
3792 return [_ShapeInfo("a", True, (1, np.inf), (True, False))]
3793  
3794 def _fitstart(self, data):
3795 # Override gamma_gen_fitstart so that an integer initial value is
3796 # used. (Also regularize the division, to avoid issues when
3797 # _skew(data) is 0 or close to 0.)
3798 if isinstance(data, CensoredData):
3799 data = data._uncensor()
3800 a = int(4.0 / (1e-8 + _skew(data)**2))
3801 return super(gamma_gen, self)._fitstart(data, args=(a,))
3802  
3803 # Trivial override of the fit method, so we can monkey-patch its
3804 # docstring.
3805 @extend_notes_in_docstring(rv_continuous, notes="""\
3806 The Erlang distribution is generally defined to have integer values
3807 for the shape parameter. This is not enforced by the `erlang` class.
3808 When fitting the distribution, it will generally return a non-integer
3809 value for the shape parameter. By using the keyword argument
3810 `f0=<integer>`, the fit method can be constrained to fit the data to
3811 a specific integer shape parameter.""")
3812 def fit(self, data, *args, **kwds):
3813 return super().fit(data, *args, **kwds)
3814  
3815  
3816 erlang = erlang_gen(a=0.0, name='erlang')
3817

3819 class gengamma_gen(rv_continuous):
3820 r"""A generalized gamma continuous random variable.
3821  
3822 %(before_notes)s
3823  
3824 See Also
3825 --------
3826 gamma, invgamma, weibull_min
3827  
3828 Notes
3829 -----
3830 The probability density function for `gengamma` is ([1]_):
3831  
3832 .. math::
3833  
3834 f(x, a, c) = \frac{|c| x^{c a-1} \exp(-x^c)}{\Gamma(a)}
3835  
3836 for :math:`x \ge 0`, :math:`a > 0`, and :math:`c \ne 0`.
3837 :math:`\Gamma` is the gamma function (`scipy.special.gamma`).
3838  
3839 `gengamma` takes :math:`a` and :math:`c` as shape parameters.
3840  
3841 %(after_notes)s
3842  
3843 References
3844 ----------
3845 .. [1] E.W. Stacy, "A Generalization of the Gamma Distribution",
3846 Annals of Mathematical Statistics, Vol 33(3), pp. 1187--1192.
3847  
3848 %(example)s
3849  
3850 """
3851 def _argcheck(self, a, c):
3852 return (a > 0) & (c != 0)
3853  
3854 def _shape_info(self):
3855 ia = _ShapeInfo("a", False, (0, np.inf), (False, False))
3856 ic = _ShapeInfo("c", False, (-np.inf, np.inf), (False, False))
3857 return [ia, ic]
3858  
3859 def _pdf(self, x, a, c):
3860 return np.exp(self._logpdf(x, a, c))
3861  
3862 def _logpdf(self, x, a, c):
3863 return xpx.apply_where(
3864 (x != 0) | (c > 0), (x, c),
  • E501 Line too long (88 > 79 characters)
3865 lambda x, c: (np.log(abs(c)) + sc.xlogy(c*a - 1, x) - x**c - sc.gammaln(a)),
3866 fill_value=-np.inf)
3867  
3868 def _cdf(self, x, a, c):
3869 xc = x**c
3870 val1 = sc.gammainc(a, xc)
3871 val2 = sc.gammaincc(a, xc)
3872 return np.where(c > 0, val1, val2)
3873  
3874 def _rvs(self, a, c, size=None, random_state=None):
3875 r = random_state.standard_gamma(a, size=size)
3876 return r**(1./c)
3877  
3878 def _sf(self, x, a, c):
3879 xc = x**c
3880 val1 = sc.gammainc(a, xc)
3881 val2 = sc.gammaincc(a, xc)
3882 return np.where(c > 0, val2, val1)
3883  
3884 def _ppf(self, q, a, c):
3885 val1 = sc.gammaincinv(a, q)
3886 val2 = sc.gammainccinv(a, q)
3887 return np.where(c > 0, val1, val2)**(1.0/c)
3888  
3889 def _isf(self, q, a, c):
3890 val1 = sc.gammaincinv(a, q)
3891 val2 = sc.gammainccinv(a, q)
3892 return np.where(c > 0, val2, val1)**(1.0/c)
3893  
3894 def _munp(self, n, a, c):
3895 # Pochhammer symbol: sc.pocha,n) = gamma(a+n)/gamma(a)
3896 return sc.poch(a, n*1.0/c)
3897  
3898 def _entropy(self, a, c):
3899 def regular(a, c):
3900 val = sc.psi(a)
3901 A = a * (1 - val) + val / c
3902 B = sc.gammaln(a) - np.log(abs(c))
3903 h = A + B
3904 return h
3905  
3906 def asymptotic(a, c):
3907 # using asymptotic expansions for gammaln and psi (see gh-18093)
3908 return (norm._entropy() - np.log(a)/2
3909 - np.log(np.abs(c)) + (a**-1.)/6 - (a**-3.)/90
3910 + (np.log(a) - (a**-1.)/2 - (a**-2.)/12 + (a**-4.)/120)/c)
3911  
3912 return xpx.apply_where(a >= 200, (a, c), asymptotic, regular)
3913  
3914  
3915 gengamma = gengamma_gen(a=0.0, name='gengamma')
3916

3918 class genhalflogistic_gen(rv_continuous):
3919 r"""A generalized half-logistic continuous random variable.
3920  
3921 %(before_notes)s
3922  
3923 Notes
3924 -----
3925 The probability density function for `genhalflogistic` is:
3926  
3927 .. math::
3928  
3929 f(x, c) = \frac{2 (1 - c x)^{1/(c-1)}}{[1 + (1 - c x)^{1/c}]^2}
3930  
3931 for :math:`0 \le x \le 1/c`, and :math:`c > 0`.
3932  
3933 `genhalflogistic` takes ``c`` as a shape parameter for :math:`c`.
3934  
3935 %(after_notes)s
3936  
3937 %(example)s
3938  
3939 """
3940 def _shape_info(self):
3941 return [_ShapeInfo("c", False, (0, np.inf), (False, False))]
3942  
3943 def _get_support(self, c):
3944 return self.a, 1.0/c
3945  
3946 def _pdf(self, x, c):
3947 # genhalflogistic.pdf(x, c) =
3948 # 2 * (1-c*x)**(1/c-1) / (1+(1-c*x)**(1/c))**2
3949 limit = 1.0/c
3950 tmp = np.asarray(1-c*x)
3951 tmp0 = tmp**(limit-1)
3952 tmp2 = tmp0*tmp
3953 return 2*tmp0 / (1+tmp2)**2
3954  
3955 def _cdf(self, x, c):
3956 limit = 1.0/c
3957 tmp = np.asarray(1-c*x)
3958 tmp2 = tmp**(limit)
3959 return (1.0-tmp2) / (1+tmp2)
3960  
3961 def _ppf(self, q, c):
3962 return 1.0/c*(1-((1.0-q)/(1.0+q))**c)
3963  
3964 def _entropy(self, c):
3965 return 2 - (2*c+1)*np.log(2)
3966  
3967  
3968 genhalflogistic = genhalflogistic_gen(a=0.0, name='genhalflogistic')

3971 class genhyperbolic_gen(rv_continuous):
3972 r"""A generalized hyperbolic continuous random variable.
3973  
3974 %(before_notes)s
3975  
3976 See Also
3977 --------
3978 t, norminvgauss, geninvgauss, laplace, cauchy
3979  
3980 Notes
3981 -----
3982 The probability density function for `genhyperbolic` is:
3983  
3984 .. math::
3985  
3986 f(x, p, a, b) =
3987 \frac{(a^2 - b^2)^{p/2}}
3988 {\sqrt{2\pi}a^{p-1/2}
3989 K_p\Big(\sqrt{a^2 - b^2}\Big)}
3990 e^{bx} \times \frac{K_{p - 1/2}
3991 (a \sqrt{1 + x^2})}
3992 {(\sqrt{1 + x^2})^{1/2 - p}}
3993  
3994 for :math:`x, p \in ( - \infty; \infty)`,
3995 :math:`|b| < a` if :math:`p \ge 0`,
3996 :math:`|b| \le a` if :math:`p < 0`.
3997 :math:`K_{p}(.)` denotes the modified Bessel function of the second
3998 kind and order :math:`p` (`scipy.special.kv`)
3999  
4000 `genhyperbolic` takes ``p`` as a tail parameter,
4001 ``a`` as a shape parameter,
4002 ``b`` as a skewness parameter.
4003  
4004 %(after_notes)s
4005  
4006 The original parameterization of the Generalized Hyperbolic Distribution
4007 is found in [1]_ as follows
4008  
4009 .. math::
4010  
4011 f(x, \lambda, \alpha, \beta, \delta, \mu) =
4012 \frac{(\gamma/\delta)^\lambda}{\sqrt{2\pi}K_\lambda(\delta \gamma)}
4013 e^{\beta (x - \mu)} \times \frac{K_{\lambda - 1/2}
4014 (\alpha \sqrt{\delta^2 + (x - \mu)^2})}
4015 {(\sqrt{\delta^2 + (x - \mu)^2} / \alpha)^{1/2 - \lambda}}
4016  
4017 for :math:`x \in ( - \infty; \infty)`,
4018 :math:`\gamma := \sqrt{\alpha^2 - \beta^2}`,
4019 :math:`\lambda, \mu \in ( - \infty; \infty)`,
4020 :math:`\delta \ge 0, |\beta| < \alpha` if :math:`\lambda \ge 0`,
4021 :math:`\delta > 0, |\beta| \le \alpha` if :math:`\lambda < 0`.
4022  
4023 The location-scale-based parameterization implemented in
4024 SciPy is based on [2]_, where :math:`a = \alpha\delta`,
4025 :math:`b = \beta\delta`, :math:`p = \lambda`,
4026 :math:`scale=\delta` and :math:`loc=\mu`
4027  
4028 Moments are implemented based on [3]_ and [4]_.
4029  
4030 For the distributions that are a special case such as Student's t,
4031 it is not recommended to rely on the implementation of genhyperbolic.
4032 To avoid potential numerical problems and for performance reasons,
4033 the methods of the specific distributions should be used.
4034  
4035 References
4036 ----------
4037 .. [1] O. Barndorff-Nielsen, "Hyperbolic Distributions and Distributions
4038 on Hyperbolae", Scandinavian Journal of Statistics, Vol. 5(3),
4039 pp. 151-157, 1978. https://www.jstor.org/stable/4615705
4040  
4041 .. [2] Eberlein E., Prause K. (2002) The Generalized Hyperbolic Model:
4042 Financial Derivatives and Risk Measures. In: Geman H., Madan D.,
4043 Pliska S.R., Vorst T. (eds) Mathematical Finance - Bachelier
4044 Congress 2000. Springer Finance. Springer, Berlin, Heidelberg.
4045 :doi:`10.1007/978-3-662-12429-1_12`
4046  
4047 .. [3] Scott, David J, Würtz, Diethelm, Dong, Christine and Tran,
4048 Thanh Tam, (2009), Moments of the generalized hyperbolic
4049 distribution, MPRA Paper, University Library of Munich, Germany,
4050 https://EconPapers.repec.org/RePEc:pra:mprapa:19081.
4051  
4052 .. [4] E. Eberlein and E. A. von Hammerstein. Generalized hyperbolic
4053 and inverse Gaussian distributions: Limiting cases and approximation
4054 of processes. FDM Preprint 80, April 2003. University of Freiburg.
4055 https://freidok.uni-freiburg.de/fedora/objects/freidok:7974/datastreams/FILE1/content
4056  
4057 %(example)s
4058  
4059 """
4060  
4061 def _argcheck(self, p, a, b):
4062 return (np.logical_and(np.abs(b) < a, p >= 0)
4063 | np.logical_and(np.abs(b) <= a, p < 0))
4064  
4065 def _shape_info(self):
4066 ip = _ShapeInfo("p", False, (-np.inf, np.inf), (False, False))
4067 ia = _ShapeInfo("a", False, (0, np.inf), (True, False))
4068 ib = _ShapeInfo("b", False, (-np.inf, np.inf), (False, False))
4069 return [ip, ia, ib]
4070  
4071 def _fitstart(self, data):
4072 # Arbitrary, but the default p = a = b = 1 is not valid; the
4073 # distribution requires |b| < a if p >= 0.
4074 return super()._fitstart(data, args=(1, 1, 0.5))
4075  
4076 def _logpdf(self, x, p, a, b):
4077 # kve instead of kv works better for large values of p
4078 # and smaller values of sqrt(a^2 - b^2)
4079 @np.vectorize
4080 def _logpdf_single(x, p, a, b):
4081 return _stats.genhyperbolic_logpdf(x, p, a, b)
4082  
4083 return _logpdf_single(x, p, a, b)
4084  
4085 def _pdf(self, x, p, a, b):
4086 # kve instead of kv works better for large values of p
4087 # and smaller values of sqrt(a^2 - b^2)
4088 @np.vectorize
4089 def _pdf_single(x, p, a, b):
4090 return _stats.genhyperbolic_pdf(x, p, a, b)
4091  
4092 return _pdf_single(x, p, a, b)
4093  
4094 # np.vectorize isn't currently designed to be used as a decorator,
4095 # so use a lambda instead. This allows us to decorate the function
4096 # with `np.vectorize` and still provide the `otypes` parameter.
4097 @lambda func: np.vectorize(func, otypes=[np.float64])
4098 @staticmethod
4099 def _integrate_pdf(x0, x1, p, a, b):
4100 """
4101 Integrate the pdf of the genhyberbolic distribution from x0 to x1.
4102 This is a private function used by _cdf() and _sf() only; either x0
4103 will be -inf or x1 will be inf.
4104 """
4105 user_data = np.array([p, a, b], float).ctypes.data_as(ctypes.c_void_p)
4106 llc = LowLevelCallable.from_cython(_stats, '_genhyperbolic_pdf',
4107 user_data)
4108 d = np.sqrt((a + b)*(a - b))
4109 mean = b/d * sc.kv(p + 1, d) / sc.kv(p, d)
4110 epsrel = 1e-10
4111 epsabs = 0
4112 if x0 < mean < x1:
4113 # If the interval includes the mean, integrate over the two
4114 # intervals [x0, mean] and [mean, x1] and add. If we try to do
4115 # the integral in one call of quad and the non-infinite endpoint
4116 # is far in the tail, quad might return an incorrect result
4117 # because it does not "see" the peak of the PDF.
4118 intgrl = (integrate.quad(llc, x0, mean,
4119 epsrel=epsrel, epsabs=epsabs)[0]
4120 + integrate.quad(llc, mean, x1,
4121 epsrel=epsrel, epsabs=epsabs)[0])
4122 else:
4123 intgrl = integrate.quad(llc, x0, x1,
4124 epsrel=epsrel, epsabs=epsabs)[0]
4125 if np.isnan(intgrl):
4126 msg = ("Infinite values encountered in scipy.special.kve. "
4127 "Values replaced by NaN to avoid incorrect results.")
4128 warnings.warn(msg, RuntimeWarning, stacklevel=3)
4129 return max(0.0, min(1.0, intgrl))
4130  
4131 def _cdf(self, x, p, a, b):
4132 return self._integrate_pdf(-np.inf, x, p, a, b)
4133  
4134 def _sf(self, x, p, a, b):
4135 return self._integrate_pdf(x, np.inf, p, a, b)
4136  
4137 def _rvs(self, p, a, b, size=None, random_state=None):
4138 # note: X = b * V + sqrt(V) * X has a
4139 # generalized hyperbolic distribution
4140 # if X is standard normal and V is
4141 # geninvgauss(p = p, b = t2, loc = loc, scale = t3)
4142 t1 = np.float_power(a, 2) - np.float_power(b, 2)
4143 # b in the GIG
4144 t2 = np.float_power(t1, 0.5)
4145 # scale in the GIG
4146 t3 = np.float_power(t1, - 0.5)
4147 gig = geninvgauss.rvs(
4148 p=p,
4149 b=t2,
4150 scale=t3,
4151 size=size,
4152 random_state=random_state
4153 )
4154 normst = norm.rvs(size=size, random_state=random_state)
4155  
4156 return b * gig + np.sqrt(gig) * normst
4157  
4158 def _stats(self, p, a, b):
4159 # https://mpra.ub.uni-muenchen.de/19081/1/MPRA_paper_19081.pdf
4160 # https://freidok.uni-freiburg.de/fedora/objects/freidok:7974/datastreams/FILE1/content
4161 # standardized moments
4162 p, a, b = np.broadcast_arrays(p, a, b)
4163 t1 = np.float_power(a, 2) - np.float_power(b, 2)
4164 t1 = np.float_power(t1, 0.5)
4165 t2 = np.float_power(1, 2) * np.float_power(t1, - 1)
4166 integers = np.linspace(0, 4, 5)
4167 # make integers perpendicular to existing dimensions
4168 integers = integers.reshape(integers.shape + (1,) * p.ndim)
4169 b0, b1, b2, b3, b4 = sc.kv(p + integers, t1)
4170 r1, r2, r3, r4 = (b / b0 for b in (b1, b2, b3, b4))
4171  
4172 m = b * t2 * r1
4173 v = (
4174 t2 * r1 + np.float_power(b, 2) * np.float_power(t2, 2) *
4175 (r2 - np.float_power(r1, 2))
4176 )
4177 m3e = (
4178 np.float_power(b, 3) * np.float_power(t2, 3) *
4179 (r3 - 3 * b2 * b1 * np.float_power(b0, -2) +
4180 2 * np.float_power(r1, 3)) +
4181 3 * b * np.float_power(t2, 2) *
4182 (r2 - np.float_power(r1, 2))
4183 )
4184 s = m3e * np.float_power(v, - 3 / 2)
4185 m4e = (
4186 np.float_power(b, 4) * np.float_power(t2, 4) *
4187 (r4 - 4 * b3 * b1 * np.float_power(b0, - 2) +
4188 6 * b2 * np.float_power(b1, 2) * np.float_power(b0, - 3) -
4189 3 * np.float_power(r1, 4)) +
4190 np.float_power(b, 2) * np.float_power(t2, 3) *
4191 (6 * r3 - 12 * b2 * b1 * np.float_power(b0, - 2) +
4192 6 * np.float_power(r1, 3)) +
4193 3 * np.float_power(t2, 2) * r2
4194 )
4195 k = m4e * np.float_power(v, -2) - 3
4196  
4197 return m, v, s, k
4198  
4199  
4200 genhyperbolic = genhyperbolic_gen(name='genhyperbolic')
