7108 with np.errstate(divide='ignore'):
7109 return _LOG_SQRT_2_OVER_PI + 2*np.log(x) - 0.5*x*x
7110  
7111 def _cdf(self, x):
7112 return sc.gammainc(1.5, x*x/2.0)
7113  
7114 def _ppf(self, q):
7115 return np.sqrt(2*sc.gammaincinv(1.5, q))
7116  
7117 def _sf(self, x):
7118 return sc.gammaincc(1.5, x*x/2.0)
7119  
7120 def _isf(self, q):
7121 return np.sqrt(2*sc.gammainccinv(1.5, q))
7122  
7123 def _stats(self):
7124 val = 3*np.pi-8
7125 return (2*np.sqrt(2.0/np.pi),
7126 3-8/np.pi,
7127 np.sqrt(2)*(32-10*np.pi)/val**1.5,
7128 (-12*np.pi*np.pi + 160*np.pi - 384) / val**2.0)
7129  
7130 def _entropy(self):
7131 return _EULER + 0.5*np.log(2*np.pi)-0.5
7132  
7133  
7134 maxwell = maxwell_gen(a=0.0, name='maxwell')
7135  
7136  
7137 class mielke_gen(rv_continuous):
7138 r"""A Mielke Beta-Kappa / Dagum continuous random variable.
7139  
7140 %(before_notes)s
7141  
7142 Notes
7143 -----
7144 The probability density function for `mielke` is:
7145  
7146 .. math::
7147  
7148 f(x, k, s) = \frac{k x^{k-1}}{(1+x^s)^{1+k/s}}
7149  
7150 for :math:`x > 0` and :math:`k, s > 0`. The distribution is sometimes
7151 called Dagum distribution ([2]_). It was already defined in [3]_, called
7152 a Burr Type III distribution (`burr` with parameters ``c=s`` and
7153 ``d=k/s``).
7154  
7155 `mielke` takes ``k`` and ``s`` as shape parameters.
7156  
7157 %(after_notes)s
7158  
7159 References
7160 ----------
7161 .. [1] Mielke, P.W., 1973 "Another Family of Distributions for Describing
7162 and Analyzing Precipitation Data." J. Appl. Meteor., 12, 275-280
7163 .. [2] Dagum, C., 1977 "A new model for personal income distribution."
7164 Economie Appliquee, 33, 327-367.
7165 .. [3] Burr, I. W. "Cumulative frequency functions", Annals of
7166 Mathematical Statistics, 13(2), pp 215-232 (1942).
7167  
7168 %(example)s
7169  
7170 """
7171 def _shape_info(self):
7172 ik = _ShapeInfo("k", False, (0, np.inf), (False, False))
7173 i_s = _ShapeInfo("s", False, (0, np.inf), (False, False))
7174 return [ik, i_s]
7175  
7176 def _pdf(self, x, k, s):
7177 return k*x**(k-1.0) / (1.0+x**s)**(1.0+k*1.0/s)
7178  
7179 def _logpdf(self, x, k, s):
7180 # Allow x=0 without 'divide by zero' warnings.
7181 with np.errstate(divide='ignore'):
7182 return np.log(k) + np.log(x)*(k - 1) - np.log1p(x**s)*(1 + k/s)
7183  
7184 def _cdf(self, x, k, s):
7185 return x**k / (1.0+x**s)**(k*1.0/s)
7186  
7187 def _ppf(self, q, k, s):
7188 qsk = pow(q, s*1.0/k)
7189 return pow(qsk/(1.0-qsk), 1.0/s)
7190  
7191 def _munp(self, n, k, s):
7192 def nth_moment(n, k, s):
7193 # n-th moment is defined for -k < n < s
7194 return sc.gamma((k+n)/s)*sc.gamma(1-n/s)/sc.gamma(k/s)
7195  
7196 return xpx.apply_where(n < s, (n, k, s), nth_moment, fill_value=np.inf)
7197  
7198  
7199 mielke = mielke_gen(a=0.0, name='mielke')
7200  
7201  
7202 class kappa4_gen(rv_continuous):
7203 r"""Kappa 4 parameter distribution.
7204  
7205 %(before_notes)s
7206  
7207 Notes
7208 -----
7209 The probability density function for kappa4 is:
7210  
7211 .. math::
7212  
7213 f(x, h, k) = (1 - k x)^{1/k - 1} (1 - h (1 - k x)^{1/k})^{1/h-1}
7214  
7215 if :math:`h` and :math:`k` are not equal to 0.
7216  
7217 If :math:`h` or :math:`k` are zero then the pdf can be simplified:
7218  
7219 h = 0 and k != 0::
7220  
7221 kappa4.pdf(x, h, k) = (1.0 - k*x)**(1.0/k - 1.0)*
7222 exp(-(1.0 - k*x)**(1.0/k))
7223  
7224 h != 0 and k = 0::
7225  
7226 kappa4.pdf(x, h, k) = exp(-x)*(1.0 - h*exp(-x))**(1.0/h - 1.0)
7227  
7228 h = 0 and k = 0::
7229  
7230 kappa4.pdf(x, h, k) = exp(-x)*exp(-exp(-x))
7231  
7232 kappa4 takes :math:`h` and :math:`k` as shape parameters.
7233  
7234 The kappa4 distribution returns other distributions when certain
7235 :math:`h` and :math:`k` values are used.
7236  
7237 +------+-------------+----------------+------------------+
7238 | h | k=0.0 | k=1.0 | -inf<=k<=inf |
7239 +======+=============+================+==================+
7240 | -1.0 | Logistic | | Generalized |
7241 | | | | Logistic(1) |
7242 | | | | |
7243 | | logistic(x) | | |
7244 +------+-------------+----------------+------------------+
7245 | 0.0 | Gumbel | Reverse | Generalized |
7246 | | | Exponential(2) | Extreme Value |
7247 | | | | |
7248 | | gumbel_r(x) | | genextreme(x, k) |
7249 +------+-------------+----------------+------------------+
7250 | 1.0 | Exponential | Uniform | Generalized |
7251 | | | | Pareto |
7252 | | | | |
7253 | | expon(x) | uniform(x) | genpareto(x, -k) |
7254 +------+-------------+----------------+------------------+
7255  
7256 (1) There are at least five generalized logistic distributions.
7257 Four are described here:
7258 https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generalized_logistic_distribution
7259 The "fifth" one is the one kappa4 should match which currently
7260 isn't implemented in scipy:
7261 https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talk:Generalized_logistic_distribution
7262 https://www.mathwave.com/help/easyfit/html/analyses/distributions/gen_logistic.html
7263 (2) This distribution is currently not in scipy.
7264  
7265 References
7266 ----------
7267 J.C. Finney, "Optimization of a Skewed Logistic Distribution With Respect
7268 to the Kolmogorov-Smirnov Test", A Dissertation Submitted to the Graduate
7269 Faculty of the Louisiana State University and Agricultural and Mechanical
7270 College, (August, 2004),
7271 https://digitalcommons.lsu.edu/gradschool_dissertations/3672
7272  
7273 J.R.M. Hosking, "The four-parameter kappa distribution". IBM J. Res.
7274 Develop. 38 (3), 25 1-258 (1994).
7275  
7276 B. Kumphon, A. Kaew-Man, P. Seenoi, "A Rainfall Distribution for the Lampao
7277 Site in the Chi River Basin, Thailand", Journal of Water Resource and
7278 Protection, vol. 4, 866-869, (2012).
7279 :doi:`10.4236/jwarp.2012.410101`
7280  
7281 C. Winchester, "On Estimation of the Four-Parameter Kappa Distribution", A
7282 Thesis Submitted to Dalhousie University, Halifax, Nova Scotia, (March
7283 2000).
7284 http://www.nlc-bnc.ca/obj/s4/f2/dsk2/ftp01/MQ57336.pdf
7285  
7286 %(after_notes)s
7287  
7288 %(example)s
7289  
7290 """
7291 def _argcheck(self, h, k):
7292 shape = np.broadcast_arrays(h, k)[0].shape
7293 return np.full(shape, fill_value=True)
7294  
7295 def _shape_info(self):
7296 ih = _ShapeInfo("h", False, (-np.inf, np.inf), (False, False))
7297 ik = _ShapeInfo("k", False, (-np.inf, np.inf), (False, False))
7298 return [ih, ik]
7299  
7300 def _get_support(self, h, k):
7301 condlist = [np.logical_and(h > 0, k > 0),
7302 np.logical_and(h > 0, k == 0),
7303 np.logical_and(h > 0, k < 0),
7304 np.logical_and(h <= 0, k > 0),
7305 np.logical_and(h <= 0, k == 0),
7306 np.logical_and(h <= 0, k < 0)]
7307  
7308 def f0(h, k):
7309 return (1.0 - np.float_power(h, -k))/k
7310  
7311 def f1(h, k):
7312 return np.log(h)
7313  
7314 def f3(h, k):
7315 a = np.empty(np.shape(h))
7316 a[:] = -np.inf
7317 return a
7318  
7319 def f5(h, k):
7320 return 1.0/k
7321  
7322 _a = _lazyselect(condlist,
7323 [f0, f1, f0, f3, f3, f5],
7324 [h, k],
7325 default=np.nan)
7326  
7327 def f0(h, k):
7328 return 1.0/k
7329  
7330 def f1(h, k):
7331 a = np.empty(np.shape(h))
7332 a[:] = np.inf
7333 return a
7334  
7335 _b = _lazyselect(condlist,
7336 [f0, f1, f1, f0, f1, f1],
7337 [h, k],
7338 default=np.nan)
7339 return _a, _b
7340  
7341 def _pdf(self, x, h, k):
7342 # kappa4.pdf(x, h, k) = (1.0 - k*x)**(1.0/k - 1.0)*
7343 # (1.0 - h*(1.0 - k*x)**(1.0/k))**(1.0/h-1)
7344 return np.exp(self._logpdf(x, h, k))
7345  
7346 def _logpdf(self, x, h, k):
7347 condlist = [np.logical_and(h != 0, k != 0),
7348 np.logical_and(h == 0, k != 0),
7349 np.logical_and(h != 0, k == 0),
7350 np.logical_and(h == 0, k == 0)]
7351  
7352 def f0(x, h, k):
7353 '''pdf = (1.0 - k*x)**(1.0/k - 1.0)*(
7354 1.0 - h*(1.0 - k*x)**(1.0/k))**(1.0/h-1.0)
7355 logpdf = ...
7356 '''
7357 return (sc.xlog1py(1.0/k - 1.0, -k*x) +
7358 sc.xlog1py(1.0/h - 1.0, -h*(1.0 - k*x)**(1.0/k)))
7359  
7360 def f1(x, h, k):
7361 '''pdf = (1.0 - k*x)**(1.0/k - 1.0)*np.exp(-(
7362 1.0 - k*x)**(1.0/k))
7363 logpdf = ...
7364 '''
7365 return sc.xlog1py(1.0/k - 1.0, -k*x) - (1.0 - k*x)**(1.0/k)
7366  
7367 def f2(x, h, k):
7368 '''pdf = np.exp(-x)*(1.0 - h*np.exp(-x))**(1.0/h - 1.0)
7369 logpdf = ...
7370 '''
7371 return -x + sc.xlog1py(1.0/h - 1.0, -h*np.exp(-x))
7372  
7373 def f3(x, h, k):
7374 '''pdf = np.exp(-x-np.exp(-x))
7375 logpdf = ...
7376 '''
7377 return -x - np.exp(-x)
7378  
7379 return _lazyselect(condlist,
7380 [f0, f1, f2, f3],
7381 [x, h, k],
7382 default=np.nan)
7383  
7384 def _cdf(self, x, h, k):
7385 return np.exp(self._logcdf(x, h, k))
7386  
7387 def _logcdf(self, x, h, k):
7388 condlist = [np.logical_and(h != 0, k != 0),
7389 np.logical_and(h == 0, k != 0),
7390 np.logical_and(h != 0, k == 0),
7391 np.logical_and(h == 0, k == 0)]
7392  
7393 def f0(x, h, k):
7394 '''cdf = (1.0 - h*(1.0 - k*x)**(1.0/k))**(1.0/h)
7395 logcdf = ...
7396 '''
7397 return (1.0/h)*sc.log1p(-h*(1.0 - k*x)**(1.0/k))
7398  
7399 def f1(x, h, k):
7400 '''cdf = np.exp(-(1.0 - k*x)**(1.0/k))
7401 logcdf = ...
7402 '''
7403 return -(1.0 - k*x)**(1.0/k)
7404  
7405 def f2(x, h, k):
7406 '''cdf = (1.0 - h*np.exp(-x))**(1.0/h)
7407 logcdf = ...
7408 '''
7409 return (1.0/h)*sc.log1p(-h*np.exp(-x))
7410  
7411 def f3(x, h, k):
7412 '''cdf = np.exp(-np.exp(-x))
7413 logcdf = ...
7414 '''
7415 return -np.exp(-x)
7416  
7417 return _lazyselect(condlist,
7418 [f0, f1, f2, f3],
7419 [x, h, k],
7420 default=np.nan)
7421  
7422 def _ppf(self, q, h, k):
7423 condlist = [np.logical_and(h != 0, k != 0),
7424 np.logical_and(h == 0, k != 0),
7425 np.logical_and(h != 0, k == 0),
7426 np.logical_and(h == 0, k == 0)]
7427  
7428 def f0(q, h, k):
7429 return 1.0/k*(1.0 - ((1.0 - (q**h))/h)**k)
7430  
7431 def f1(q, h, k):
7432 return 1.0/k*(1.0 - (-np.log(q))**k)
7433  
7434 def f2(q, h, k):
7435 '''ppf = -np.log((1.0 - (q**h))/h)
7436 '''
7437 return -sc.log1p(-(q**h)) + np.log(h)
7438  
7439 def f3(q, h, k):
7440 return -np.log(-np.log(q))
7441  
7442 return _lazyselect(condlist,
7443 [f0, f1, f2, f3],
7444 [q, h, k],
7445 default=np.nan)
7446  
7447 def _get_stats_info(self, h, k):
7448 condlist = [
7449 np.logical_and(h < 0, k >= 0),
7450 k < 0,
7451 ]
7452  
7453 def f0(h, k):
7454 return (-1.0/h*k).astype(int)
7455  
7456 def f1(h, k):
7457 return (-1.0/k).astype(int)
7458  
7459 return _lazyselect(condlist, [f0, f1], [h, k], default=5)
7460  
7461 def _stats(self, h, k):
7462 maxr = self._get_stats_info(h, k)
7463 outputs = [None if np.any(r < maxr) else np.nan for r in range(1, 5)]
7464 return outputs[:]
7465  
7466 def _mom1_sc(self, m, *args):
7467 maxr = self._get_stats_info(args[0], args[1])
7468 if m >= maxr:
7469 return np.nan
7470 return integrate.quad(self._mom_integ1, 0, 1, args=(m,)+args)[0]
7471  
7472  
7473 kappa4 = kappa4_gen(name='kappa4')
7474  
7475  
7476 class kappa3_gen(rv_continuous):
7477 r"""Kappa 3 parameter distribution.
7478  
7479 %(before_notes)s
7480  
7481 Notes
7482 -----
7483 The probability density function for `kappa3` is:
7484  
7485 .. math::
7486  
7487 f(x, a) = a (a + x^a)^{-(a + 1)/a}
7488  
7489 for :math:`x > 0` and :math:`a > 0`.
7490  
7491 `kappa3` takes ``a`` as a shape parameter for :math:`a`.
7492  
7493 References
7494 ----------
7495 P.W. Mielke and E.S. Johnson, "Three-Parameter Kappa Distribution Maximum
7496 Likelihood and Likelihood Ratio Tests", Methods in Weather Research,
7497 701-707, (September, 1973),
7498 :doi:`10.1175/1520-0493(1973)101<0701:TKDMLE>2.3.CO;2`
7499  
7500 B. Kumphon, "Maximum Entropy and Maximum Likelihood Estimation for the
7501 Three-Parameter Kappa Distribution", Open Journal of Statistics, vol 2,
7502 415-419 (2012), :doi:`10.4236/ojs.2012.24050`
7503  
7504 %(after_notes)s
7505  
7506 %(example)s
7507  
7508 """
7509 def _shape_info(self):
7510 return [_ShapeInfo("a", False, (0, np.inf), (False, False))]
7511  
7512 def _pdf(self, x, a):
7513 # kappa3.pdf(x, a) = a*(a + x**a)**(-(a + 1)/a), for x > 0
7514 return a*(a + x**a)**(-1.0/a-1)
7515  
7516 def _cdf(self, x, a):
7517 return x*(a + x**a)**(-1.0/a)
7518  
7519 def _sf(self, x, a):
7520 x, a = np.broadcast_arrays(x, a) # some code paths pass scalars
7521 sf = super()._sf(x, a)
7522  
7523 # When the SF is small, another formulation is typically more accurate.
7524 # However, it blows up for large `a`, so use it only if it also returns
7525 # a small value of the SF.
7526 cutoff = 0.01
7527 i = sf < cutoff
7528 sf2 = -sc.expm1(sc.xlog1py(-1.0 / a[i], a[i] * x[i]**-a[i]))
7529 i2 = sf2 > cutoff
7530 sf2[i2] = sf[i][i2] # replace bad values with original values
7531  
7532 sf[i] = sf2
7533 return sf
7534  
7535 def _ppf(self, q, a):
7536 return (a/(q**-a - 1.0))**(1.0/a)
7537  
7538 def _isf(self, q, a):
7539 lg = sc.xlog1py(-a, -q)
7540 denom = sc.expm1(lg)
7541 return (a / denom)**(1.0 / a)
7542  
7543 def _stats(self, a):
7544 outputs = [None if np.any(i < a) else np.nan for i in range(1, 5)]
7545 return outputs[:]
7546  
7547 def _mom1_sc(self, m, *args):
7548 if np.any(m >= args[0]):
7549 return np.nan
7550 return integrate.quad(self._mom_integ1, 0, 1, args=(m,)+args)[0]
7551  
7552  
7553 kappa3 = kappa3_gen(a=0.0, name='kappa3')
7554  
7555  
7556 class moyal_gen(rv_continuous):
7557 r"""A Moyal continuous random variable.
7558  
7559 %(before_notes)s
7560  
7561 Notes
7562 -----
7563 The probability density function for `moyal` is:
7564  
7565 .. math::
7566  
7567 f(x) = \exp(-(x + \exp(-x))/2) / \sqrt{2\pi}
7568  
7569 for a real number :math:`x`.
7570  
7571 %(after_notes)s
7572  
7573 This distribution has utility in high-energy physics and radiation
7574 detection. It describes the energy loss of a charged relativistic
7575 particle due to ionization of the medium [1]_. It also provides an
7576 approximation for the Landau distribution. For an in depth description
7577 see [2]_. For additional description, see [3]_.
7578  
7579 References
7580 ----------
7581 .. [1] J.E. Moyal, "XXX. Theory of ionization fluctuations",
7582 The London, Edinburgh, and Dublin Philosophical Magazine
7583 and Journal of Science, vol 46, 263-280, (1955).
7584 :doi:`10.1080/14786440308521076` (gated)
7585 .. [2] G. Cordeiro et al., "The beta Moyal: a useful skew distribution",
7586 International Journal of Research and Reviews in Applied Sciences,
7587 vol 10, 171-192, (2012).
7588 http://www.arpapress.com/Volumes/Vol10Issue2/IJRRAS_10_2_02.pdf
7589 .. [3] C. Walck, "Handbook on Statistical Distributions for
7590 Experimentalists; International Report SUF-PFY/96-01", Chapter 26,
7591 University of Stockholm: Stockholm, Sweden, (2007).
7592 http://www.stat.rice.edu/~dobelman/textfiles/DistributionsHandbook.pdf
7593  
7594 .. versionadded:: 1.1.0
7595  
7596 %(example)s
7597  
7598 """
7599 def _shape_info(self):
7600 return []
7601  
7602 def _rvs(self, size=None, random_state=None):
7603 u1 = gamma.rvs(a=0.5, scale=2, size=size,
7604 random_state=random_state)
7605 return -np.log(u1)
7606  
7607 def _pdf(self, x):
7608 return np.exp(-0.5 * (x + np.exp(-x))) / np.sqrt(2*np.pi)
7609  
7610 def _cdf(self, x):
7611 return sc.erfc(np.exp(-0.5 * x) / np.sqrt(2))
7612  
7613 def _sf(self, x):
7614 return sc.erf(np.exp(-0.5 * x) / np.sqrt(2))
7615  
7616 def _ppf(self, x):
7617 return -np.log(2 * sc.erfcinv(x)**2)
7618  
7619 def _stats(self):
7620 mu = np.log(2) + np.euler_gamma
7621 mu2 = np.pi**2 / 2
7622 g1 = 28 * np.sqrt(2) * sc.zeta(3) / np.pi**3
7623 g2 = 4.
7624 return mu, mu2, g1, g2
7625  
7626 def _munp(self, n):
7627 if n == 1.0:
7628 return np.log(2) + np.euler_gamma
7629 elif n == 2.0:
7630 return np.pi**2 / 2 + (np.log(2) + np.euler_gamma)**2
7631 elif n == 3.0:
7632 tmp1 = 1.5 * np.pi**2 * (np.log(2)+np.euler_gamma)
7633 tmp2 = (np.log(2)+np.euler_gamma)**3
7634 tmp3 = 14 * sc.zeta(3)
7635 return tmp1 + tmp2 + tmp3
7636 elif n == 4.0:
7637 tmp1 = 4 * 14 * sc.zeta(3) * (np.log(2) + np.euler_gamma)
7638 tmp2 = 3 * np.pi**2 * (np.log(2) + np.euler_gamma)**2
7639 tmp3 = (np.log(2) + np.euler_gamma)**4
7640 tmp4 = 7 * np.pi**4 / 4
7641 return tmp1 + tmp2 + tmp3 + tmp4
7642 else:
7643 # return generic for higher moments
7644 # return rv_continuous._mom1_sc(self, n, b)
7645 return self._mom1_sc(n)
7646  
7647  
7648 moyal = moyal_gen(name="moyal")
7649  
7650  
7651 class nakagami_gen(rv_continuous):
7652 r"""A Nakagami continuous random variable.
7653  
7654 %(before_notes)s
7655  
7656 Notes
7657 -----
7658 The probability density function for `nakagami` is:
7659  
7660 .. math::
7661  
7662 f(x, \nu) = \frac{2 \nu^\nu}{\Gamma(\nu)} x^{2\nu-1} \exp(-\nu x^2)
7663  
7664 for :math:`x >= 0`, :math:`\nu > 0`. The distribution was introduced in
7665 [2]_, see also [1]_ for further information.
7666  
7667 `nakagami` takes ``nu`` as a shape parameter for :math:`\nu`.
7668  
7669 %(after_notes)s
7670  
7671 References
7672 ----------
7673 .. [1] "Nakagami distribution", Wikipedia
7674 https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nakagami_distribution
7675 .. [2] M. Nakagami, "The m-distribution - A general formula of intensity
7676 distribution of rapid fading", Statistical methods in radio wave
7677 propagation, Pergamon Press, 1960, 3-36.
7678 :doi:`10.1016/B978-0-08-009306-2.50005-4`
7679  
7680 %(example)s
7681  
7682 """
7683 def _argcheck(self, nu):
7684 return nu > 0
7685  
7686 def _shape_info(self):
7687 return [_ShapeInfo("nu", False, (0, np.inf), (False, False))]
7688  
7689 def _pdf(self, x, nu):
7690 return np.exp(self._logpdf(x, nu))
7691  
7692 def _logpdf(self, x, nu):
7693 # nakagami.pdf(x, nu) = 2 * nu**nu / gamma(nu) *
7694 # x**(2*nu-1) * exp(-nu*x**2)
7695 return (np.log(2) + sc.xlogy(nu, nu) - sc.gammaln(nu) +
7696 sc.xlogy(2*nu - 1, x) - nu*x**2)
7697  
7698 def _cdf(self, x, nu):
7699 return sc.gammainc(nu, nu*x*x)
7700  
7701 def _ppf(self, q, nu):
7702 return np.sqrt(1.0/nu*sc.gammaincinv(nu, q))
7703  
7704 def _sf(self, x, nu):

7754 # The function name ncx2 is an abbreviation for noncentral chi squared.
7755 def _ncx2_log_pdf(x, df, nc):
7756 # We use (xs**2 + ns**2)/2 = (xs - ns)**2/2 + xs*ns, and include the
7757 # factor of exp(-xs*ns) into the ive function to improve numerical
7758 # stability at large values of xs. See also `rice.pdf`.
7759 df2 = df/2.0 - 1.0
7760 xs, ns = np.sqrt(x), np.sqrt(nc)
7761 res = sc.xlogy(df2/2.0, x/nc) - 0.5*(xs - ns)**2
7762 corr = sc.ive(df2, xs*ns) / 2.0
7763 # Return res + np.log(corr) avoiding np.log(0)
7764 return xpx.apply_where(
7765 corr > 0,
7766 (res, corr),
7767 lambda r, c: r + np.log(c),
7768 fill_value=-np.inf)

7884 \lambda n_1 \frac{x}{2(n_1 x + n_2)}

7966 class t_gen(rv_continuous):
7967 r"""A Student's t continuous random variable.
7968  
7969 For the noncentral t distribution, see `nct`.
7970  
7971 %(before_notes)s
7972  
7973 See Also
7974 --------
7975 nct
7976  
7977 Notes
7978 -----
7979 The probability density function for `t` is:
7980  
7981 .. math::
7982  
7983 f(x, \nu) = \frac{\Gamma((\nu+1)/2)}
7984 {\sqrt{\pi \nu} \Gamma(\nu/2)}
7985 (1+x^2/\nu)^{-(\nu+1)/2}
7986  
7987 where :math:`x` is a real number and the degrees of freedom parameter
7988 :math:`\nu` (denoted ``df`` in the implementation) satisfies
7989 :math:`\nu > 0`. :math:`\Gamma` is the gamma function
7990 (`scipy.special.gamma`).
7991  
7992 %(after_notes)s
7993  
7994 %(example)s
7995  
7996 """
7997 def _shape_info(self):
7998 return [_ShapeInfo("df", False, (0, np.inf), (False, False))]
7999  
8000 def _rvs(self, df, size=None, random_state=None):
8001 return random_state.standard_t(df, size=size)
8002  
8003 def _pdf(self, x, df):
8004 return xpx.apply_where(
8005 df == np.inf, (x, df),
8006 lambda x, df: norm._pdf(x),
8007 lambda x, df: np.exp(self._logpdf(x, df)))
8008  
8009 def _logpdf(self, x, df):
8010  
8011 def t_logpdf(x, df):
8012 return (np.log(sc.poch(0.5 * df, 0.5))
8013 - 0.5 * (np.log(df) + np.log(np.pi))
8014 - (df + 1)/2*np.log1p(x * x/df))
8015  
8016 def norm_logpdf(x, df):
8017 return norm._logpdf(x)
8018  
8019 return xpx.apply_where(df == np.inf, (x, df), norm_logpdf, t_logpdf)
8020  
8021 def _cdf(self, x, df):
8022 return sc.stdtr(df, x)
8023  
8024 def _sf(self, x, df):
8025 return sc.stdtr(df, -x)
8026  
8027 def _ppf(self, q, df):
8028 return sc.stdtrit(df, q)
8029  
8030 def _isf(self, q, df):
8031 return -sc.stdtrit(df, q)
8032  
8033 def _stats(self, df):
8034 # infinite df -> normal distribution (0.0, 1.0, 0.0, 0.0)
8035 infinite_df = np.isposinf(df)
8036  
8037 mu = np.where(df > 1, 0.0, np.inf)
8038  
8039 condlist = ((df > 1) & (df <= 2),
8040 (df > 2) & np.isfinite(df),
8041 infinite_df)
8042 choicelist = (lambda df: np.broadcast_to(np.inf, df.shape),
8043 lambda df: df / (df-2.0),
8044 lambda df: np.broadcast_to(1, df.shape))
8045 mu2 = _lazyselect(condlist, choicelist, (df,), np.nan)
8046  
8047 g1 = np.where(df > 3, 0.0, np.nan)
8048  
8049 condlist = ((df > 2) & (df <= 4),
8050 (df > 4) & np.isfinite(df),
8051 infinite_df)
8052 choicelist = (lambda df: np.broadcast_to(np.inf, df.shape),
8053 lambda df: 6.0 / (df-4.0),
8054 lambda df: np.broadcast_to(0, df.shape))
8055 g2 = _lazyselect(condlist, choicelist, (df,), np.nan)
8056  
8057 return mu, mu2, g1, g2
8058  
8059 def _entropy(self, df):
8060 if df == np.inf:
8061 return norm._entropy()
8062  
8063 def regular(df):
8064 half = df/2
8065 half1 = (df + 1)/2
8066 return (half1*(sc.digamma(half1) - sc.digamma(half))
8067 + np.log(np.sqrt(df)*sc.beta(half, 0.5)))
8068  
8069 def asymptotic(df):
8070 # Formula from Wolfram Alpha:
8071 # "asymptotic expansion (d+1)/2 * (digamma((d+1)/2) - digamma(d/2))
8072 # + log(sqrt(d) * beta(d/2, 1/2))"
8073 h = (norm._entropy() + 1/df + (df**-2.)/4 - (df**-3.)/6
8074 - (df**-4.)/8 + 3/10*(df**-5.) + (df**-6.)/4)
8075 return h
8076  
8077 return xpx.apply_where(df >= 100, df, asymptotic, regular)
8078  
8079

8083 class nct_gen(rv_continuous):

8086 %(before_notes)s

8088 Notes
8089 -----
8090 If :math:`Y` is a standard normal random variable and :math:`V` is
8091 an independent chi-square random variable (`chi2`) with :math:`k` degrees
8092 of freedom, then
8093  
8094 .. math::
8095  
8096 X = \frac{Y + c}{\sqrt{V/k}}
8097  
8098 has a non-central Student's t distribution on the real line.
8099 The degrees of freedom parameter :math:`k` (denoted ``df`` in the
8100 implementation) satisfies :math:`k > 0` and the noncentrality parameter
8101 :math:`c` (denoted ``nc`` in the implementation) is a real number.
8102  
8103 This distribution uses routines from the Boost Math C++ library for
8104 the computation of the ``pdf``, ``cdf``, ``ppf``, ``sf`` and ``isf``
8105 methods. [1]_
8106  
8107 %(after_notes)s
8108  
8109 References
8110 ----------
8111 .. [1] The Boost Developers. "Boost C++ Libraries". https://www.boost.org/.
8112  
8113 %(example)s
8114  
8115 """
8116 def _argcheck(self, df, nc):
8117 return (df > 0) & (nc == nc)
8118  
8119 def _shape_info(self):
8120 idf = _ShapeInfo("df", False, (0, np.inf), (False, False))
8121 inc = _ShapeInfo("nc", False, (-np.inf, np.inf), (False, False))
8122 return [idf, inc]
8123  
8124 def _rvs(self, df, nc, size=None, random_state=None):
8125 n = norm.rvs(loc=nc, size=size, random_state=random_state)
8126 c2 = chi2.rvs(df, size=size, random_state=random_state)
8127 return n * np.sqrt(df) / np.sqrt(c2)
8128  
8129 def _pdf(self, x, df, nc):
8130 return scu._nct_pdf(x, df, nc)
8131  
8132 def _cdf(self, x, df, nc):
8133 return sc.nctdtr(df, nc, x)
8134  
8135 def _ppf(self, q, df, nc):
8136 return sc.nctdtrit(df, nc, q)
8137  
8138 def _sf(self, x, df, nc):
8139 with np.errstate(over='ignore'): # see gh-17432
8140 return np.clip(scu._nct_sf(x, df, nc), 0, 1)
8141  
8142 def _isf(self, x, df, nc):
8143 with np.errstate(over='ignore'): # see gh-17432
8144 return scu._nct_isf(x, df, nc)
8145  
8146 def _stats(self, df, nc, moments='mv'):
8147 mu = scu._nct_mean(df, nc)
8148 mu2 = scu._nct_variance(df, nc)
8149 g1 = scu._nct_skewness(df, nc) if 's' in moments else None
8150 g2 = scu._nct_kurtosis_excess(df, nc) if 'k' in moments else None

8242 # The first-order necessary condition on `shape` can be solved in
8243 # closed form
8244 return ndata / np.sum(np.log((data - location) / scale))
8245  
8246 if floc is fscale is None:
8247 # The support of the distribution is `(x - loc)/scale > 0`.
8248 # The method of Lagrange multipliers turns this constraint
8249 # into an equation that can be solved numerically.
8250 # See gh-12545 for details.
8251  
8252 def dL_dScale(shape, scale):
8253 # The partial derivative of the log-likelihood function w.r.t.
8254 # the scale.
8255 return ndata * shape / scale
8256  
8257 def dL_dLocation(shape, location):
8258 # The partial derivative of the log-likelihood function w.r.t.
8259 # the location.
8260 return (shape + 1) * np.sum(1 / (data - location))
8261  
8262 def fun_to_solve(scale):
8263 # optimize the scale by setting the partial derivatives
8264 # w.r.t. to location and scale equal and solving.
8265 location = np.min(data) - scale
8266 shape = fshape or get_shape(scale, location)
8267 return dL_dLocation(shape, location) - dL_dScale(shape, scale)
8268  
8269 def interval_contains_root(lbrack, rbrack):
8270 # return true if the signs disagree.
8271 return (np.sign(fun_to_solve(lbrack)) !=
8272 np.sign(fun_to_solve(rbrack)))
8273  
8274 # set brackets for `root_scalar` to use when optimizing over the
8275 # scale such that a root is likely between them. Use user supplied
8276 # guess or default 1.
8277 brack_start = float(kwds.get('scale', 1))
8278 lbrack, rbrack = brack_start / 2, brack_start * 2
8279 # if a root is not between the brackets, iteratively expand them
8280 # until they include a sign change, checking after each bracket is
8281 # modified.
8282 while (not interval_contains_root(lbrack, rbrack)
8283 and (lbrack > 0 or rbrack < np.inf)):
8284 lbrack /= 2
8285 rbrack *= 2
8286 res = root_scalar(fun_to_solve, bracket=[lbrack, rbrack])
8287 if res.converged:
8288 scale = res.root
8289 loc = np.min(data) - scale
8290 shape = fshape or get_shape(scale, loc)
8291  
8292 # The Pareto distribution requires that its parameters satisfy
8293 # the condition `fscale + floc <= min(data)`. However, to
8294 # avoid numerical issues, we require that `fscale + floc`
8295 # is strictly less than `min(data)`. If this condition
8296 # is not satisfied, reduce the scale with `np.nextafter` to
8297 # ensure that data does not fall outside of the support.
8298 if not (scale + loc) < np.min(data):
8299 scale = np.min(data) - loc
8300 scale = np.nextafter(scale, 0)
8301 return shape, loc, scale
8302 else:
8303 return super().fit(data, **kwds)
8304 elif floc is None:
8305 loc = np.min(data) - fscale
8306 else:
8307 loc = floc
8308 # Source: Evans, Hastings, and Peacock (2000), Statistical
8309 # Distributions, 3rd. Ed., John Wiley and Sons. Page 149.
8310 scale = fscale or np.min(data) - loc
8311 shape = fshape or get_shape(scale, loc)
8312 return shape, loc, scale
8313  
8314  
8315 pareto = pareto_gen(a=1.0, name="pareto")
8316  
8317  
8318 class lomax_gen(rv_continuous):
8319 r"""A Lomax (Pareto of the second kind) continuous random variable.
8320  
8321 %(before_notes)s
8322  
8323 Notes
8324 -----
8325 The probability density function for `lomax` is:
8326  
8327 .. math::
8328  
8329 f(x, c) = \frac{c}{(1+x)^{c+1}}
8330  
8331 for :math:`x \ge 0`, :math:`c > 0`.
8332  
8333 `lomax` takes ``c`` as a shape parameter for :math:`c`.
8334  
8335 `lomax` is a special case of `pareto` with ``loc=-1.0``.
8336  
8337 %(after_notes)s
8338  
8339 %(example)s
8340  
8341 """
8342 def _shape_info(self):
8343 return [_ShapeInfo("c", False, (0, np.inf), (False, False))]
8344  
8345 def _pdf(self, x, c):
8346 # lomax.pdf(x, c) = c / (1+x)**(c+1)
8347 return c*1.0/(1.0+x)**(c+1.0)
8348  
8349 def _logpdf(self, x, c):
8350 return np.log(c) - (c+1)*sc.log1p(x)
8351  
8352 def _cdf(self, x, c):
8353 return -sc.expm1(-c*sc.log1p(x))
8354  
8355 def _sf(self, x, c):
8356 return np.exp(-c*sc.log1p(x))
8357  
8358 def _logsf(self, x, c):
8359 return -c*sc.log1p(x)
8360  
8361 def _ppf(self, q, c):
8362 return sc.expm1(-sc.log1p(-q)/c)
8363  
8364 def _isf(self, q, c):
8365 return q**(-1.0 / c) - 1
8366  
8367 def _stats(self, c):
8368 mu, mu2, g1, g2 = pareto.stats(c, loc=-1.0, moments='mvsk')
8369 return mu, mu2, g1, g2
8370  
8371 def _entropy(self, c):
8372 return 1+1.0/c-np.log(c)
8373  
8374  
8375 lomax = lomax_gen(a=0.0, name="lomax")
8376  
8377  
8378 class pearson3_gen(rv_continuous):
8379 r"""A pearson type III continuous random variable.
8380  
8381 %(before_notes)s
8382  
8383 Notes
8384 -----
8385 The probability density function for `pearson3` is:
8386  
8387 .. math::
8388  
8389 f(x, \kappa) = \frac{|\beta|}{\Gamma(\alpha)}
8390 (\beta (x - \zeta))^{\alpha - 1}
8391 \exp(-\beta (x - \zeta))
8392  
8393 where:
8394  
8395 .. math::
8396  
8397 \beta = \frac{2}{\kappa}
8398  
8399 \alpha = \beta^2 = \frac{4}{\kappa^2}
8400  
8401 \zeta = -\frac{\alpha}{\beta} = -\beta
8402  
8403 :math:`\Gamma` is the gamma function (`scipy.special.gamma`).
8404 Pass the skew :math:`\kappa` into `pearson3` as the shape parameter
8405 ``skew``.
8406  
8407 %(after_notes)s
8408  
8409 %(example)s
8410  
8411 References
8412 ----------
8413 R.W. Vogel and D.E. McMartin, "Probability Plot Goodness-of-Fit and
8414 Skewness Estimation Procedures for the Pearson Type 3 Distribution", Water
8415 Resources Research, Vol.27, 3149-3158 (1991).
8416  
8417 L.R. Salvosa, "Tables of Pearson's Type III Function", Ann. Math. Statist.,
8418 Vol.1, 191-198 (1930).
8419  
8420 "Using Modern Computing Tools to Fit the Pearson Type III Distribution to
8421 Aviation Loads Data", Office of Aviation Research (2003).
8422  
8423 """
8424 def _preprocess(self, x, skew):
8425 # The real 'loc' and 'scale' are handled in the calling pdf(...). The
8426 # local variables 'loc' and 'scale' within pearson3._pdf are set to
8427 # the defaults just to keep them as part of the equations for
8428 # documentation.
8429 loc = 0.0
8430 scale = 1.0
8431  
8432 # If skew is small, return _norm_pdf. The divide between pearson3
8433 # and norm was found by brute force and is approximately a skew of
8434 # 0.000016. No one, I hope, would actually use a skew value even
8435 # close to this small.
8436 norm2pearson_transition = 0.000016
8437  
8438 ans, x, skew = np.broadcast_arrays(1.0, x, skew)
8439 ans = ans.copy()
8440  
8441 # mask is True where skew is small enough to use the normal approx.
8442 mask = np.absolute(skew) < norm2pearson_transition
8443 invmask = ~mask
8444  
8445 beta = 2.0 / (skew[invmask] * scale)
8446 alpha = (scale * beta)**2
8447 zeta = loc - alpha / beta
8448  
8449 transx = beta * (x[invmask] - zeta)
8450 return ans, x, transx, mask, invmask, beta, alpha, zeta
8451  
8452 def _argcheck(self, skew):
8453 # The _argcheck function in rv_continuous only allows positive
8454 # arguments. The skew argument for pearson3 can be zero (which I want
8455 # to handle inside pearson3._pdf) or negative. So just return True
8456 # for all skew args.
8457 return np.isfinite(skew)
8458  
8459 def _shape_info(self):
8460 return [_ShapeInfo("skew", False, (-np.inf, np.inf), (False, False))]
8461  
8462 def _stats(self, skew):
8463 m = 0.0
8464 v = 1.0
8465 s = skew
8466 k = 1.5*skew**2
8467 return m, v, s, k
8468  
8469 def _pdf(self, x, skew):
8470 # pearson3.pdf(x, skew) = abs(beta) / gamma(alpha) *
8471 # (beta * (x - zeta))**(alpha - 1) * exp(-beta*(x - zeta))
8472 # Do the calculation in _logpdf since helps to limit
8473 # overflow/underflow problems
8474 ans = np.exp(self._logpdf(x, skew))
8475 if ans.ndim == 0:
8476 if np.isnan(ans):
8477 return 0.0
8478 return ans
8479 ans[np.isnan(ans)] = 0.0
8480 return ans
8481  
8482 def _logpdf(self, x, skew):
8483 # PEARSON3 logpdf GAMMA logpdf
8484 # np.log(abs(beta))
8485 # + (alpha - 1)*np.log(beta*(x - zeta)) + (a - 1)*np.log(x)
8486 # - beta*(x - zeta) - x
8487 # - sc.gammalnalpha) - sc.gammalna)
8488 ans, x, transx, mask, invmask, beta, alpha, _ = (
8489 self._preprocess(x, skew))
8490  
8491 ans[mask] = np.log(_norm_pdf(x[mask]))
8492 # use logpdf instead of _logpdf to fix issue mentioned in gh-12640
8493 # (_logpdf does not return correct result for alpha = 1)
8494 ans[invmask] = np.log(abs(beta)) + gamma.logpdf(transx, alpha)
8495 return ans
8496  
8497 def _cdf(self, x, skew):
8498 ans, x, transx, mask, invmask, _, alpha, _ = (
8499 self._preprocess(x, skew))
8500  
8501 ans[mask] = _norm_cdf(x[mask])
8502  
8503 skew = np.broadcast_to(skew, invmask.shape)
8504 invmask1a = np.logical_and(invmask, skew > 0)
8505 invmask1b = skew[invmask] > 0
8506 # use cdf instead of _cdf to fix issue mentioned in gh-12640
8507 # (_cdf produces NaNs for inputs outside support)
8508 ans[invmask1a] = gamma.cdf(transx[invmask1b], alpha[invmask1b])
8509  
8510 # The gamma._cdf approach wasn't working with negative skew.
8511 # Note that multiplying the skew by -1 reflects about x=0.
8512 # So instead of evaluating the CDF with negative skew at x,
8513 # evaluate the SF with positive skew at -x.
8514 invmask2a = np.logical_and(invmask, skew < 0)
8515 invmask2b = skew[invmask] < 0
8516 # gamma._sf produces NaNs when transx < 0, so use gamma.sf
8517 ans[invmask2a] = gamma.sf(transx[invmask2b], alpha[invmask2b])
8518  
8519 return ans
8520  
8521 def _sf(self, x, skew):
8522 ans, x, transx, mask, invmask, _, alpha, _ = (
8523 self._preprocess(x, skew))
8524  
8525 ans[mask] = _norm_sf(x[mask])
8526  
8527 skew = np.broadcast_to(skew, invmask.shape)
8528 invmask1a = np.logical_and(invmask, skew > 0)
8529 invmask1b = skew[invmask] > 0
8530 ans[invmask1a] = gamma.sf(transx[invmask1b], alpha[invmask1b])
8531  
8532 invmask2a = np.logical_and(invmask, skew < 0)
8533 invmask2b = skew[invmask] < 0
8534 ans[invmask2a] = gamma.cdf(transx[invmask2b], alpha[invmask2b])
8535  
8536 return ans
8537  
8538 def _rvs(self, skew, size=None, random_state=None):
8539 skew = np.broadcast_to(skew, size)
8540 ans, _, _, mask, invmask, beta, alpha, zeta = (
8541 self._preprocess([0], skew))
8542  
8543 nsmall = mask.sum()
8544 nbig = mask.size - nsmall
8545 ans[mask] = random_state.standard_normal(nsmall)
8546 ans[invmask] = random_state.standard_gamma(alpha, nbig)/beta + zeta
8547  
8548 if size == ():
8549 ans = ans[0]
8550 return ans
8551  
8552 def _ppf(self, q, skew):
8553 ans, q, _, mask, invmask, beta, alpha, zeta = (
8554 self._preprocess(q, skew))
8555 ans[mask] = _norm_ppf(q[mask])
8556 q = q[invmask]
8557 q[beta < 0] = 1 - q[beta < 0] # for negative skew; see gh-17050
8558 ans[invmask] = sc.gammaincinv(alpha, q)/beta + zeta
8559 return ans
8560  
8561 @_call_super_mom
8562 @extend_notes_in_docstring(rv_continuous, notes="""\
8563 Note that method of moments (`method='MM'`) is not
8564 available for this distribution.\n\n""")
8565 def fit(self, data, *args, **kwds):
8566 if kwds.get("method", None) == 'MM':
8567 raise NotImplementedError("Fit `method='MM'` is not available for "
8568 "the Pearson3 distribution. Please try "
8569 "the default `method='MLE'`.")
8570 else:
8571 return super(type(self), self).fit(data, *args, **kwds)
8572  
8573  
8574 pearson3 = pearson3_gen(name="pearson3")
8575  
8576  
8577 class powerlaw_gen(rv_continuous):
8578 r"""A power-function continuous random variable.
8579  
8580 %(before_notes)s
8581  
8582 See Also
8583 --------
8584 pareto
8585  
8586 Notes
8587 -----
8588 The probability density function for `powerlaw` is:
8589  
8590 .. math::
8591  
8592 f(x, a) = a x^{a-1}
8593  
8594 for :math:`0 \le x \le 1`, :math:`a > 0`.
8595  
8596 `powerlaw` takes ``a`` as a shape parameter for :math:`a`.
8597  
8598 %(after_notes)s
8599  
8600 For example, the support of `powerlaw` can be adjusted from the default
8601 interval ``[0, 1]`` to the interval ``[c, c+d]`` by setting ``loc=c`` and
8602 ``scale=d``. For a power-law distribution with infinite support, see
8603 `pareto`.
8604  
8605 `powerlaw` is a special case of `beta` with ``b=1``.
8606  
8607 %(example)s
8608  
8609 """
8610 def _shape_info(self):
8611 return [_ShapeInfo("a", False, (0, np.inf), (False, False))]
8612  
8613 def _pdf(self, x, a):
8614 # powerlaw.pdf(x, a) = a * x**(a-1)
8615 return a*x**(a-1.0)
8616  
8617 def _logpdf(self, x, a):
8618 return np.log(a) + sc.xlogy(a - 1, x)
8619  
8620 def _cdf(self, x, a):
8621 return x**(a*1.0)
8622  
8623 def _logcdf(self, x, a):
8624 return a*np.log(x)
8625  
8626 def _ppf(self, q, a):
8627 return pow(q, 1.0/a)
8628  
8629 def _sf(self, p, a):
8630 return -sc.powm1(p, a)
8631  
8632 def _munp(self, n, a):
8633 # The following expression is correct for all real n (provided a > 0).
8634 return a / (a + n)
8635  
8636 def _stats(self, a):
8637 return (a / (a + 1.0),
8638 a / (a + 2.0) / (a + 1.0) ** 2,
8639 -2.0 * ((a - 1.0) / (a + 3.0)) * np.sqrt((a + 2.0) / a),
8640 6 * np.polyval([1, -1, -6, 2], a) / (a * (a + 3.0) * (a + 4)))
8641  
8642 def _entropy(self, a):
8643 return 1 - 1.0/a - np.log(a)
8644  
8645 def _support_mask(self, x, a):
8646 return (super()._support_mask(x, a)
8647 & ((x != 0) | (a >= 1)))
8648  
8649 @_call_super_mom
8650 @extend_notes_in_docstring(rv_continuous, notes="""\
8651 Notes specifically for ``powerlaw.fit``: If the location is a free
8652 parameter and the value returned for the shape parameter is less than
8653 one, the true maximum likelihood approaches infinity. This causes
8654 numerical difficulties, and the resulting estimates are approximate.
8655 \n\n""")
8656 def fit(self, data, *args, **kwds):
8657 # Summary of the strategy:
8658 #
8659 # 1) If the scale and location are fixed, return the shape according
8660 # to a formula.
8661 #
8662 # 2) If the scale is fixed, there are two possibilities for the other
8663 # parameters - one corresponding with shape less than one, and
8664 # another with shape greater than one. Calculate both, and return
8665 # whichever has the better log-likelihood.
8666 #
8667 # At this point, the scale is known to be free.
8668 #
8669 # 3) If the location is fixed, return the scale and shape according to
8670 # formulas (or, if the shape is fixed, the fixed shape).
8671 #
8672 # At this point, the location and scale are both free. There are
8673 # separate equations depending on whether the shape is less than one or
8674 # greater than one.
8675 #
8676 # 4a) If the shape is less than one, there are formulas for shape,
8677 # location, and scale.
8678 # 4b) If the shape is greater than one, there are formulas for shape
8679 # and scale, but there is a condition for location to be solved
8680 # numerically.
8681 #
8682 # If the shape is fixed and less than one, we use 4a.
8683 # If the shape is fixed and greater than one, we use 4b.
8684 # If the shape is also free, we calculate fits using both 4a and 4b
8685 # and choose the one that results a better log-likelihood.
8686 #
8687 # In many cases, the use of `np.nextafter` is used to avoid numerical
8688 # issues.
8689 if kwds.pop('superfit', False):
8690 return super().fit(data, *args, **kwds)
8691  
8692 if len(np.unique(data)) == 1:
8693 return super().fit(data, *args, **kwds)
8694  
8695 data, fshape, floc, fscale = _check_fit_input_parameters(self, data,
8696 args, kwds)
8697 penalized_nllf_args = [data, (self._fitstart(data),)]
8698 penalized_nllf = self._reduce_func(penalized_nllf_args, {})[1]
8699  
8700 # ensure that any fixed parameters don't violate constraints of the
8701 # distribution before continuing. The support of the distribution
8702 # is `0 < (x - loc)/scale < 1`.
8703 if floc is not None:
8704 if not data.min() > floc:
8705 raise FitDataError('powerlaw', 0, 1)
8706 if fscale is not None and not data.max() <= floc + fscale:
8707 raise FitDataError('powerlaw', 0, 1)
8708  
8709 if fscale is not None:
8710 if fscale <= 0:
8711 raise ValueError("Negative or zero `fscale` is outside the "
8712 "range allowed by the distribution.")
8713 if fscale <= np.ptp(data):
8714 msg = "`fscale` must be greater than the range of data."
8715 raise ValueError(msg)
8716  
8717 def get_shape(data, loc, scale):
8718 # The first-order necessary condition on `shape` can be solved in
8719 # closed form. It can be used no matter the assumption of the
8720 # value of the shape.
8721 N = len(data)
8722 return - N / (np.sum(np.log(data - loc)) - N*np.log(scale))
8723  
8724 def get_scale(data, loc):
8725 # analytical solution for `scale` based on the location.
8726 # It can be used no matter the assumption of the value of the
8727 # shape.
8728 return data.max() - loc
8729  
8730 # 1) The location and scale are both fixed. Analytically determine the
8731 # shape.
8732 if fscale is not None and floc is not None:
8733 return get_shape(data, floc, fscale), floc, fscale
8734  
8735 # 2) The scale is fixed. There are two possibilities for the other
8736 # parameters. Choose the option with better log-likelihood.
8737 if fscale is not None:
8738 # using `data.min()` as the optimal location
8739 loc_lt1 = np.nextafter(data.min(), -np.inf)
8740 shape_lt1 = fshape or get_shape(data, loc_lt1, fscale)
8741 ll_lt1 = penalized_nllf((shape_lt1, loc_lt1, fscale), data)
8742  
8743 # using `data.max() - scale` as the optimal location
8744 loc_gt1 = np.nextafter(data.max() - fscale, np.inf)
8745 shape_gt1 = fshape or get_shape(data, loc_gt1, fscale)
8746 ll_gt1 = penalized_nllf((shape_gt1, loc_gt1, fscale), data)
8747  
8748 if ll_lt1 < ll_gt1:
8749 return shape_lt1, loc_lt1, fscale
8750 else:
8751 return shape_gt1, loc_gt1, fscale
8752  
8753 # 3) The location is fixed. Return the analytical scale and the
8754 # analytical (or fixed) shape.
8755 if floc is not None:
8756 scale = get_scale(data, floc)
8757 shape = fshape or get_shape(data, floc, scale)
8758 return shape, floc, scale
8759  
8760 # 4) Location and scale are both free
8761 # 4a) Use formulas that assume `shape <= 1`.
8762  
8763 def fit_loc_scale_w_shape_lt_1():
8764 loc = np.nextafter(data.min(), -np.inf)
8765 if np.abs(loc) < np.finfo(loc.dtype).tiny:
8766 loc = np.sign(loc) * np.finfo(loc.dtype).tiny
8767 scale = np.nextafter(get_scale(data, loc), np.inf)
8768 shape = fshape or get_shape(data, loc, scale)
8769 return shape, loc, scale
8770  
8771 # 4b) Fit under the assumption that `shape > 1`. The support
8772 # of the distribution is `(x - loc)/scale <= 1`. The method of Lagrange
8773 # multipliers turns this constraint into the condition that
8774 # dL_dScale - dL_dLocation must be zero, which is solved numerically.
8775 # (Alternatively, substitute the constraint into the objective
8776 # function before deriving the likelihood equation for location.)
8777  
8778 def dL_dScale(data, shape, scale):
8779 # The partial derivative of the log-likelihood function w.r.t.
8780 # the scale.
8781 return -data.shape[0] * shape / scale
8782  
8783 def dL_dLocation(data, shape, loc):
8784 # The partial derivative of the log-likelihood function w.r.t.
8785 # the location.
8786 return (shape - 1) * np.sum(1 / (loc - data)) # -1/(data-loc)
8787  
8788 def dL_dLocation_star(loc):
8789 # The derivative of the log-likelihood function w.r.t.
8790 # the location, given optimal shape and scale
8791 scale = np.nextafter(get_scale(data, loc), -np.inf)
8792 shape = fshape or get_shape(data, loc, scale)
8793 return dL_dLocation(data, shape, loc)
8794  
8795 def fun_to_solve(loc):
8796 # optimize the location by setting the partial derivatives
8797 # w.r.t. to location and scale equal and solving.
8798 scale = np.nextafter(get_scale(data, loc), -np.inf)
8799 shape = fshape or get_shape(data, loc, scale)
8800 return (dL_dScale(data, shape, scale)
8801 - dL_dLocation(data, shape, loc))
8802  
8803 def fit_loc_scale_w_shape_gt_1():
8804 # set brackets for `root_scalar` to use when optimizing over the
8805 # location such that a root is likely between them.
8806 rbrack = np.nextafter(data.min(), -np.inf)
8807  
8808 # if the sign of `dL_dLocation_star` is positive at rbrack,
8809 # we're not going to find the root we're looking for
8810 delta = (data.min() - rbrack)
8811 while dL_dLocation_star(rbrack) > 0:
8812 rbrack = data.min() - delta
8813 delta *= 2
8814  
8815 def interval_contains_root(lbrack, rbrack):
8816 # Check if the interval (lbrack, rbrack) contains the root.
8817 return (np.sign(fun_to_solve(lbrack))
8818 != np.sign(fun_to_solve(rbrack)))
8819  
8820 lbrack = rbrack - 1
8821  
8822 # if the sign doesn't change between the brackets, move the left
8823 # bracket until it does. (The right bracket remains fixed at the
8824 # maximum permissible value.)
8825 i = 1.0
8826 while (not interval_contains_root(lbrack, rbrack)
8827 and lbrack != -np.inf):
8828 lbrack = (data.min() - i)
8829 i *= 2
8830  
8831 root = optimize.root_scalar(fun_to_solve, bracket=(lbrack, rbrack))
8832  
8833 loc = np.nextafter(root.root, -np.inf)
8834 scale = np.nextafter(get_scale(data, loc), np.inf)
8835 shape = fshape or get_shape(data, loc, scale)
8836 return shape, loc, scale
8837  
8838 # Shape is fixed - choose 4a or 4b accordingly.
8839 if fshape is not None and fshape <= 1:
8840 return fit_loc_scale_w_shape_lt_1()
8841 elif fshape is not None and fshape > 1:
8842 return fit_loc_scale_w_shape_gt_1()
8843  
8844 # Shape is free
8845 fit_shape_lt1 = fit_loc_scale_w_shape_lt_1()
8846 ll_lt1 = self.nnlf(fit_shape_lt1, data)
8847  
8848 fit_shape_gt1 = fit_loc_scale_w_shape_gt_1()
8849 ll_gt1 = self.nnlf(fit_shape_gt1, data)
8850  
8851 if ll_lt1 <= ll_gt1 and fit_shape_lt1[0] <= 1:
8852 return fit_shape_lt1
8853 elif ll_lt1 > ll_gt1 and fit_shape_gt1[0] > 1:
8854 return fit_shape_gt1
8855 else:
8856 return super().fit(data, *args, **kwds)
8857  
8858  
8859 powerlaw = powerlaw_gen(a=0.0, b=1.0, name="powerlaw")

8862 class powerlognorm_gen(rv_continuous):
8863 r"""A power log-normal continuous random variable.
8864  
8865 %(before_notes)s
8866  
8867 Notes
8868 -----
8869 The probability density function for `powerlognorm` is:
8870  
8871 .. math::
8872  
8873 f(x, c, s) = \frac{c}{x s} \phi(\log(x)/s)
8874 (\Phi(-\log(x)/s))^{c-1}
8875  
8876 where :math:`\phi` is the normal pdf, and :math:`\Phi` is the normal cdf,
8877 and :math:`x > 0`, :math:`s, c > 0`.
8878  
8879 `powerlognorm` takes :math:`c` and :math:`s` as shape parameters.
8880  
8881 %(after_notes)s
8882  
8883 %(example)s
8884  
8885 """
8886 _support_mask = rv_continuous._open_support_mask
8887  
8888 def _shape_info(self):
8889 ic = _ShapeInfo("c", False, (0, np.inf), (False, False))
8890 i_s = _ShapeInfo("s", False, (0, np.inf), (False, False))
8891 return [ic, i_s]
8892  
8893 def _pdf(self, x, c, s):
8894 return np.exp(self._logpdf(x, c, s))
8895  
8896 def _logpdf(self, x, c, s):
8897 return (np.log(c) - np.log(x) - np.log(s) +
8898 _norm_logpdf(np.log(x) / s) +
8899 _norm_logcdf(-np.log(x) / s) * (c - 1.))
8900  
8901 def _cdf(self, x, c, s):
8902 return -sc.expm1(self._logsf(x, c, s))
8903  
8904 def _ppf(self, q, c, s):
8905 return self._isf(1 - q, c, s)
8906  
8907 def _sf(self, x, c, s):
8908 return np.exp(self._logsf(x, c, s))
8909  
8910 def _logsf(self, x, c, s):
8911 return _norm_logcdf(-np.log(x) / s) * c
8912  
8913 def _isf(self, q, c, s):
8914 return np.exp(-_norm_ppf(q**(1/c)) * s)
8915  
8916  
8917 powerlognorm = powerlognorm_gen(a=0.0, name="powerlognorm")

8920 class powernorm_gen(rv_continuous):
8921 r"""A power normal continuous random variable.
8922  
8923 %(before_notes)s
8924  
8925 Notes
8926 -----
8927 The probability density function for `powernorm` is:
8928  
8929 .. math::
8930  
8931 f(x, c) = c \phi(x) (\Phi(-x))^{c-1}
8932  
8933 where :math:`\phi` is the normal pdf, :math:`\Phi` is the normal cdf,
8934 :math:`x` is any real, and :math:`c > 0` [1]_.
8935  
8936 `powernorm` takes ``c`` as a shape parameter for :math:`c`.
8937  
8938 %(after_notes)s
8939  
8940 References
8941 ----------
8942 .. [1] NIST Engineering Statistics Handbook, Section 1.3.6.6.13,
8943 https://www.itl.nist.gov/div898/handbook//eda/section3/eda366d.htm
8944  
8945 %(example)s
8946  
8947 """
8948 def _shape_info(self):
8949 return [_ShapeInfo("c", False, (0, np.inf), (False, False))]
8950  
8951 def _pdf(self, x, c):
8952 # powernorm.pdf(x, c) = c * phi(x) * (Phi(-x))**(c-1)
8953 return c*_norm_pdf(x) * (_norm_cdf(-x)**(c-1.0))
8954  
8955 def _logpdf(self, x, c):
8956 return np.log(c) + _norm_logpdf(x) + (c-1)*_norm_logcdf(-x)
8957  
8958 def _cdf(self, x, c):
8959 return -sc.expm1(self._logsf(x, c))
8960  
8961 def _ppf(self, q, c):
8962 return -_norm_ppf(pow(1.0 - q, 1.0 / c))
8963  
8964 def _sf(self, x, c):
8965 return np.exp(self._logsf(x, c))
8966  
8967 def _logsf(self, x, c):
8968 return c * _norm_logcdf(-x)
8969  
8970 def _isf(self, q, c):
8971 return -_norm_ppf(np.exp(np.log(q) / c))
8972  
8973  
8974 powernorm = powernorm_gen(name='powernorm')

8977 class rdist_gen(rv_continuous):
8978 r"""An R-distributed (symmetric beta) continuous random variable.
8979  
8980 %(before_notes)s
8981  
8982 Notes
8983 -----
8984 The probability density function for `rdist` is:
8985  
8986 .. math::
8987  
8988 f(x, c) = \frac{(1-x^2)^{c/2-1}}{B(1/2, c/2)}
8989  
8990 for :math:`-1 \le x \le 1`, :math:`c > 0`. `rdist` is also called the
8991 symmetric beta distribution: if B has a `beta` distribution with
8992 parameters (c/2, c/2), then X = 2*B - 1 follows a R-distribution with
8993 parameter c.
8994  
8995 `rdist` takes ``c`` as a shape parameter for :math:`c`.
8996  
8997 This distribution includes the following distribution kernels as
8998 special cases::
8999  
9000 c = 2: uniform
9001 c = 3: `semicircular`
9002 c = 4: Epanechnikov (parabolic)
9003 c = 6: quartic (biweight)
9004 c = 8: triweight
9005  
9006 %(after_notes)s
9007  
9008 %(example)s
9009  
9010 """
9011 def _shape_info(self):
9012 return [_ShapeInfo("c", False, (0, np.inf), (False, False))]
9013  
9014 # use relation to the beta distribution for pdf, cdf, etc
9015 def _pdf(self, x, c):
9016 return np.exp(self._logpdf(x, c))
9017  
9018 def _logpdf(self, x, c):
9019 return -np.log(2) + beta._logpdf((x + 1)/2, c/2, c/2)
9020  
9021 def _cdf(self, x, c):
9022 return beta._cdf((x + 1)/2, c/2, c/2)
9023  
9024 def _sf(self, x, c):
9025 return beta._sf((x + 1)/2, c/2, c/2)
9026  
9027 def _ppf(self, q, c):
9028 return 2*beta._ppf(q, c/2, c/2) - 1
9029  
9030 def _rvs(self, c, size=None, random_state=None):
9031 return 2 * random_state.beta(c/2, c/2, size) - 1
9032  
9033 def _munp(self, n, c):
9034 numerator = (1 - (n % 2)) * sc.beta((n + 1.0) / 2, c / 2.0)
9035 return numerator / sc.beta(1. / 2, c / 2.)
9036  
9037  
9038 rdist = rdist_gen(a=-1.0, b=1.0, name="rdist")
9039  
9040  
9041 class rayleigh_gen(rv_continuous):
9042 r"""A Rayleigh continuous random variable.
9043  
9044 %(before_notes)s
9045  
9046 Notes
9047 -----
9048 The probability density function for `rayleigh` is:
9049  
9050 .. math::
9051  
9052 f(x) = x \exp(-x^2/2)
9053  
9054 for :math:`x \ge 0`.
9055  
9056 `rayleigh` is a special case of `chi` with ``df=2``.
9057  
9058 %(after_notes)s
9059  
9060 %(example)s
9061  
9062 """
9063 _support_mask = rv_continuous._open_support_mask
9064  
9065 def _shape_info(self):
9066 return []
9067  
9068 def _rvs(self, size=None, random_state=None):
9069 return chi.rvs(2, size=size, random_state=random_state)
9070  
9071 def _pdf(self, r):
9072 # rayleigh.pdf(r) = r * exp(-r**2/2)
9073 return np.exp(self._logpdf(r))
9074  
9075 def _logpdf(self, r):
9076 return np.log(r) - 0.5 * r * r
9077  
9078 def _cdf(self, r):
9079 return -sc.expm1(-0.5 * r**2)
9080  
9081 def _ppf(self, q):
9082 return np.sqrt(-2 * sc.log1p(-q))
9083  
9084 def _sf(self, r):
9085 return np.exp(self._logsf(r))
9086  
9087 def _logsf(self, r):
9088 return -0.5 * r * r
9089  
9090 def _isf(self, q):
9091 return np.sqrt(-2 * np.log(q))
9092  
9093 def _stats(self):
9094 val = 4 - np.pi
9095 return (np.sqrt(np.pi/2),
9096 val/2,
9097 2*(np.pi-3)*np.sqrt(np.pi)/val**1.5,
9098 6*np.pi/val-16/val**2)
9099  
9100 def _entropy(self):
9101 return _EULER/2.0 + 1 - 0.5*np.log(2)
9102  
9103 @_call_super_mom
9104 @extend_notes_in_docstring(rv_continuous, notes="""\
9105 Notes specifically for ``rayleigh.fit``: If the location is fixed with
9106 the `floc` parameter, this method uses an analytical formula to find
9107 the scale. Otherwise, this function uses a numerical root finder on
9108 the first order conditions of the log-likelihood function to find the
9109 MLE. Only the (optional) `loc` parameter is used as the initial guess
9110 for the root finder; the `scale` parameter and any other parameters
9111 for the optimizer are ignored.\n\n""")
9112 def fit(self, data, *args, **kwds):
9113 if kwds.pop('superfit', False):
9114 return super().fit(data, *args, **kwds)
9115 data, floc, fscale = _check_fit_input_parameters(self, data,
9116 args, kwds)
9117  
9118 def scale_mle(loc):
9119 # Source: Statistical Distributions, 3rd Edition. Evans, Hastings,
9120 # and Peacock (2000), Page 175
9121 return (np.sum((data - loc) ** 2) / (2 * len(data))) ** .5
9122  
9123 def loc_mle(loc):
9124 # This implicit equation for `loc` is used when
9125 # both `loc` and `scale` are free.
9126 xm = data - loc
9127 s1 = xm.sum()
9128 s2 = (xm**2).sum()
9129 s3 = (1/xm).sum()
9130 return s1 - s2/(2*len(data))*s3
9131  
9132 def loc_mle_scale_fixed(loc, scale=fscale):
9133 # This implicit equation for `loc` is used when
9134 # `scale` is fixed but `loc` is not.
9135 xm = data - loc
9136 return xm.sum() - scale**2 * (1/xm).sum()
9137  
9138 if floc is not None:
9139 # `loc` is fixed, analytically determine `scale`.
9140 if np.any(data - floc <= 0):
9141 raise FitDataError("rayleigh", lower=1, upper=np.inf)
9142 else:
9143 return floc, scale_mle(floc)
9144  
9145 # Account for user provided guess of `loc`.
9146 loc0 = kwds.get('loc')
9147 if loc0 is None:
9148 # Use _fitstart to estimate loc; ignore the returned scale.
9149 loc0 = self._fitstart(data)[0]
9150  
9151 fun = loc_mle if fscale is None else loc_mle_scale_fixed
9152 rbrack = np.nextafter(np.min(data), -np.inf)
9153 lbrack = _get_left_bracket(fun, rbrack)
9154 res = optimize.root_scalar(fun, bracket=(lbrack, rbrack))
9155 if not res.converged:
9156 raise FitSolverError(res.flag)
9157 loc = res.root
9158 scale = fscale or scale_mle(loc)
9159 return loc, scale
9160  
9161  
9162 rayleigh = rayleigh_gen(a=0.0, name="rayleigh")
9163

9165 class reciprocal_gen(rv_continuous):
9166 r"""A loguniform or reciprocal continuous random variable.
9167  
9168 %(before_notes)s
9169  
9170 Notes
9171 -----
9172 The probability density function for this class is:
9173  
9174 .. math::
9175  
9176 f(x, a, b) = \frac{1}{x \log(b/a)}
9177  
9178 for :math:`a \le x \le b`, :math:`b > a > 0`. This class takes
9179 :math:`a` and :math:`b` as shape parameters.
9180  
9181 %(after_notes)s
9182  
9183 %(example)s
9184  
9185 This doesn't show the equal probability of ``0.01``, ``0.1`` and
9186 ``1``. This is best when the x-axis is log-scaled:
9187  
9188 >>> import numpy as np
9189 >>> import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
9190 >>> fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 1)
9191 >>> ax.hist(np.log10(r))
9192 >>> ax.set_ylabel("Frequency")
9193 >>> ax.set_xlabel("Value of random variable")
9194 >>> ax.xaxis.set_major_locator(plt.FixedLocator([-2, -1, 0]))
9195 >>> ticks = ["$10^{{ {} }}$".format(i) for i in [-2, -1, 0]]
9196 >>> ax.set_xticklabels(ticks) # doctest: +SKIP
9197 >>> plt.show()
9198  
9199 This random variable will be log-uniform regardless of the base chosen for
9200 ``a`` and ``b``. Let's specify with base ``2`` instead:
9201  
9202 >>> rvs = %(name)s(2**-2, 2**0).rvs(size=1000)
9203  
9204 Values of ``1/4``, ``1/2`` and ``1`` are equally likely with this random
9205 variable. Here's the histogram:
9206  
9207 >>> fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 1)
9208 >>> ax.hist(np.log2(rvs))
9209 >>> ax.set_ylabel("Frequency")
9210 >>> ax.set_xlabel("Value of random variable")
9211 >>> ax.xaxis.set_major_locator(plt.FixedLocator([-2, -1, 0]))
9212 >>> ticks = ["$2^{{ {} }}$".format(i) for i in [-2, -1, 0]]
9213 >>> ax.set_xticklabels(ticks) # doctest: +SKIP
9214 >>> plt.show()
9215  
9216 """
9217 def _argcheck(self, a, b):
9218 return (a > 0) & (b > a)
9219  
9220 def _shape_info(self):
9221 ia = _ShapeInfo("a", False, (0, np.inf), (False, False))
9222 ib = _ShapeInfo("b", False, (0, np.inf), (False, False))
9223 return [ia, ib]
9224  
9225 def _fitstart(self, data):
9226 if isinstance(data, CensoredData):
9227 data = data._uncensor()
9228 # Reasonable, since support is [a, b]
9229 return super()._fitstart(data, args=(np.min(data), np.max(data)))
9230  
9231 def _get_support(self, a, b):
9232 return a, b
9233  
9234 def _pdf(self, x, a, b):
9235 # reciprocal.pdf(x, a, b) = 1 / (x*(log(b) - log(a)))
9236 return np.exp(self._logpdf(x, a, b))
9237  
9238 def _logpdf(self, x, a, b):
9239 return -np.log(x) - np.log(np.log(b) - np.log(a))
9240  
9241 def _cdf(self, x, a, b):
9242 return (np.log(x)-np.log(a)) / (np.log(b) - np.log(a))
9243  
9244 def _ppf(self, q, a, b):
9245 return np.exp(np.log(a) + q*(np.log(b) - np.log(a)))
9246  
9247 def _munp(self, n, a, b):
9248 if n == 0:
9249 return 1.0
9250 t1 = 1 / (np.log(b) - np.log(a)) / n
9251 t2 = np.real(np.exp(_log_diff(n * np.log(b), n*np.log(a))))
9252 return t1 * t2
9253  
9254 def _entropy(self, a, b):
9255 return 0.5*(np.log(a) + np.log(b)) + np.log(np.log(b) - np.log(a))
9256  
9257 fit_note = """\
9258 `loguniform`/`reciprocal` is over-parameterized. `fit` automatically
9259 fixes `scale` to 1 unless `fscale` is provided by the user.\n\n"""
9260  
9261 @extend_notes_in_docstring(rv_continuous, notes=fit_note)
9262 def fit(self, data, *args, **kwds):
9263 fscale = kwds.pop('fscale', 1)
9264 return super().fit(data, *args, fscale=fscale, **kwds)
9265  
9266 # Details related to the decision of not defining
9267 # the survival function for this distribution can be
9268 # found in the PR: https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/18614
9269  
9270  
9271 loguniform = reciprocal_gen(name="loguniform")
9272 reciprocal = reciprocal_gen(name="reciprocal")
9273 loguniform._support = ('a', 'b')
9274 reciprocal._support = ('a', 'b')
9275  
9276  
9277 class rice_gen(rv_continuous):
9278 r"""A Rice continuous random variable.
9279  
9280 %(before_notes)s
9281  
9282 Notes
9283 -----
9284 The probability density function for `rice` is:
9285  
9286 .. math::
9287  
9288 f(x, b) = x \exp(- \frac{x^2 + b^2}{2}) I_0(x b)
9289  
9290 for :math:`x >= 0`, :math:`b > 0`. :math:`I_0` is the modified Bessel
9291 function of order zero (`scipy.special.i0`).
9292  
9293 `rice` takes ``b`` as a shape parameter for :math:`b`.
9294  
9295 %(after_notes)s
9296  
9297 The Rice distribution describes the length, :math:`r`, of a 2-D vector with
9298 components :math:`(U+u, V+v)`, where :math:`U, V` are constant, :math:`u,
9299 v` are independent Gaussian random variables with standard deviation
9300 :math:`s`. Let :math:`R = \sqrt{U^2 + V^2}`. Then the pdf of :math:`r` is
9301 ``rice.pdf(x, R/s, scale=s)``.
9302  
9303 %(example)s
9304  
9305 """
9306 def _argcheck(self, b):
9307 return b >= 0
9308  
9309 def _shape_info(self):
9310 return [_ShapeInfo("b", False, (0, np.inf), (True, False))]
9311  
9312 def _rvs(self, b, size=None, random_state=None):
9313 # https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rice_distribution
9314 t = b/np.sqrt(2) + random_state.standard_normal(size=(2,) + size)
9315 return np.sqrt((t*t).sum(axis=0))
9316  
9317 def _cdf(self, x, b):
9318 return sc.chndtr(np.square(x), 2, np.square(b))
9319  
9320 def _ppf(self, q, b):
9321 return np.sqrt(sc.chndtrix(q, 2, np.square(b)))
9322  
9323 def _pdf(self, x, b):
9324 # rice.pdf(x, b) = x * exp(-(x**2+b**2)/2) * I[0](x*b)
9325 #
9326 # We use (x**2 + b**2)/2 = ((x-b)**2)/2 + xb.
9327 # The factor of np.exp(-xb) is then included in the i0e function
9328 # in place of the modified Bessel function, i0, improving
9329 # numerical stability for large values of xb.
9330 return x * np.exp(-(x-b)*(x-b)/2.0) * sc.i0e(x*b)
9331  
9332 def _munp(self, n, b):
9333 nd2 = n/2.0
9334 n1 = 1 + nd2
9335 b2 = b*b/2.0
9336 return (2.0**(nd2) * np.exp(-b2) * sc.gamma(n1) *
9337 sc.hyp1f1(n1, 1, b2))
9338  
9339  
9340 rice = rice_gen(a=0.0, name="rice")
9341

9342 class irwinhall_gen(rv_continuous):
9343 r"""An Irwin-Hall (Uniform Sum) continuous random variable.
9344  
9345 An `Irwin-Hall <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irwin-Hall_distribution/>`_
9346 continuous random variable is the sum of :math:`n` independent
9347 standard uniform random variables [1]_ [2]_.
9348  
9349 %(before_notes)s
9350  
9351 Notes
9352 -----
9353 Applications include `Rao's Spacing Test
9354 <https://jammalam.faculty.pstat.ucsb.edu/html/favorite/test.htm>`_,
9355 a more powerful alternative to the Rayleigh test
9356 when the data are not unimodal, and radar [3]_.
9357  
9358 Conveniently, the pdf and cdf are the :math:`n`-fold convolution of
9359 the ones for the standard uniform distribution, which is also the
9360 definition of the cardinal B-splines of degree :math:`n-1`
9361 having knots evenly spaced from :math:`1` to :math:`n` [4]_ [5]_.
9362  
9363 The Bates distribution, which represents the *mean* of statistically
9364 independent, uniformly distributed random variables, is simply the
9365 Irwin-Hall distribution scaled by :math:`1/n`. For example, the frozen
9366 distribution ``bates = irwinhall(10, scale=1/10)`` represents the
9367 distribution of the mean of 10 uniformly distributed random variables.
  • W293 Blank line contains whitespace
9368
9369 %(after_notes)s
9370  
9371 References
9372 ----------
9373 .. [1] P. Hall, "The distribution of means for samples of size N drawn
9374 from a population in which the variate takes values between 0 and 1,
9375 all such values being equally probable",
9376 Biometrika, Volume 19, Issue 3-4, December 1927, Pages 240-244,
9377 :doi:`10.1093/biomet/19.3-4.240`.
9378 .. [2] J. O. Irwin, "On the frequency distribution of the means of samples
9379 from a population having any law of frequency with finite moments,
9380 with special reference to Pearson's Type II,
9381 Biometrika, Volume 19, Issue 3-4, December 1927, Pages 225-239,
9382 :doi:`0.1093/biomet/19.3-4.225`.
  • W291 Trailing whitespace
9383 .. [3] K. Buchanan, T. Adeyemi, C. Flores-Molina, S. Wheeland and D. Overturf,
9384 "Sidelobe behavior and bandwidth characteristics
9385 of distributed antenna arrays,"
9386 2018 United States National Committee of
9387 URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM),
9388 Boulder, CO, USA, 2018, pp. 1-2.
9389 https://www.usnc-ursi-archive.org/nrsm/2018/papers/B15-9.pdf.
9390 .. [4] Amos Ron, "Lecture 1: Cardinal B-splines and convolution operators", p. 1
9391 https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~deboor/887/lec1new.pdf.
  • W291 Trailing whitespace
9392 .. [5] Trefethen, N. (2012, July). B-splines and convolution. Chebfun.

9474 class recipinvgauss_gen(rv_continuous):
9475 r"""A reciprocal inverse Gaussian continuous random variable.
9476  
9477 %(before_notes)s
9478  
9479 Notes
9480 -----
9481 The probability density function for `recipinvgauss` is:
9482  
9483 .. math::
9484  
9485 f(x, \mu) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi x}}
9486 \exp\left(\frac{-(1-\mu x)^2}{2\mu^2x}\right)
9487  
9488 for :math:`x \ge 0`.
9489  
9490 `recipinvgauss` takes ``mu`` as a shape parameter for :math:`\mu`.
9491  
9492 %(after_notes)s
9493  
9494 %(example)s
9495

9497 def _shape_info(self):
9498 return [_ShapeInfo("mu", False, (0, np.inf), (False, False))]
9499  
9500 def _pdf(self, x, mu):
9501 # recipinvgauss.pdf(x, mu) =
9502 # 1/sqrt(2*pi*x) * exp(-(1-mu*x)**2/(2*x*mu**2))
9503 return np.exp(self._logpdf(x, mu))
9504  
9505 def _logpdf(self, x, mu):
9506 return xpx.apply_where(
9507 x > 0, (x, mu),
9508 lambda x, mu: (-(1 - mu*x)**2.0 / (2*x*mu**2.0)
9509 - 0.5*np.log(2*np.pi*x)),
9510 fill_value=-np.inf)

9512 def _cdf(self, x, mu):
9513 trm1 = 1.0/mu - x
9514 trm2 = 1.0/mu + x
9515 isqx = 1.0/np.sqrt(x)
9516 return _norm_cdf(-isqx*trm1) - np.exp(2.0/mu)*_norm_cdf(-isqx*trm2)
9517

9520 trm2 = 1.0/mu + x
9521 isqx = 1.0/np.sqrt(x)
9522 return _norm_cdf(isqx*trm1) + np.exp(2.0/mu)*_norm_cdf(-isqx*trm2)
9523  
9524 def _rvs(self, mu, size=None, random_state=None):
9525 return 1.0/random_state.wald(mu, 1.0, size=size)

9594 class skewcauchy_gen(rv_continuous):
9595 r"""A skewed Cauchy random variable.
9596  
9597 %(before_notes)s
9598  
9599 See Also
9600 --------
9601 cauchy : Cauchy distribution
9602  
9603 Notes
9604 -----
9605  
9606 The probability density function for `skewcauchy` is:
9607  
9608 .. math::
9609  
9610 f(x) = \frac{1}{\pi \left(\frac{x^2}{\left(a\, \text{sign}(x) + 1
9611 \right)^2} + 1 \right)}
9612  
9613 for a real number :math:`x` and skewness parameter :math:`-1 < a < 1`.
9614  
9615 When :math:`a=0`, the distribution reduces to the usual Cauchy
9616 distribution.
9617  
9618 %(after_notes)s
9619  
9620 References
9621 ----------
9622 .. [1] "Skewed generalized *t* distribution", Wikipedia
9623 https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skewed_generalized_t_distribution#Skewed_Cauchy_distribution
9624  
9625 %(example)s
9626  
9627 """
9628 def _argcheck(self, a):
9629 return np.abs(a) < 1
9630  
9631 def _shape_info(self):
9632 return [_ShapeInfo("a", False, (-1.0, 1.0), (False, False))]
9633  
9634 def _pdf(self, x, a):
9635 return 1 / (np.pi * (x**2 / (a * np.sign(x) + 1)**2 + 1))
9636  
9637 def _cdf(self, x, a):
9638 return np.where(x <= 0,
9639 (1 - a) / 2 + (1 - a) / np.pi * np.arctan(x / (1 - a)),
9640 (1 - a) / 2 + (1 + a) / np.pi * np.arctan(x / (1 + a)))
9641  
9642 def _ppf(self, x, a):
9643 i = x < self._cdf(0, a)
9644 return np.where(i,
9645 np.tan(np.pi / (1 - a) * (x - (1 - a) / 2)) * (1 - a),
9646 np.tan(np.pi / (1 + a) * (x - (1 - a) / 2)) * (1 + a))
9647  
9648 def _stats(self, a, moments='mvsk'):
9649 return np.nan, np.nan, np.nan, np.nan
9650  
9651 def _fitstart(self, data):
9652 # Use 0 as the initial guess of the skewness shape parameter.
9653 # For the location and scale, estimate using the median and
9654 # quartiles.
9655 if isinstance(data, CensoredData):
9656 data = data._uncensor()
9657 p25, p50, p75 = np.percentile(data, [25, 50, 75])
9658 return 0.0, p50, (p75 - p25)/2

9664 class skewnorm_gen(rv_continuous):
9665 r"""A skew-normal random variable.
9666  
9667 %(before_notes)s
9668  
9669 Notes
9670 -----
9671 The pdf is::
9672  
9673 skewnorm.pdf(x, a) = 2 * norm.pdf(x) * norm.cdf(a*x)
9674  
9675 `skewnorm` takes a real number :math:`a` as a skewness parameter
9676 When ``a = 0`` the distribution is identical to a normal distribution
9677 (`norm`). `rvs` implements the method of [1]_.
9678  
9679 This distribution uses routines from the Boost Math C++ library for
9680 the computation of ``cdf``, ``ppf`` and ``isf`` methods. [2]_
9681  
9682 %(after_notes)s
9683  
9684 References
9685 ----------
9686 .. [1] A. Azzalini and A. Capitanio (1999). Statistical applications of
9687 the multivariate skew-normal distribution. J. Roy. Statist. Soc.,
9688 B 61, 579-602. :arxiv:`0911.2093`
9689 .. [2] The Boost Developers. "Boost C++ Libraries". https://www.boost.org/.
9690  
9691 %(example)s
9692  
9693 """
9694 def _argcheck(self, a):
9695 return np.isfinite(a)
9696  
9697 def _shape_info(self):
9698 return [_ShapeInfo("a", False, (-np.inf, np.inf), (False, False))]
9699  
9700 def _pdf(self, x, a):
9701 return xpx.apply_where(
9702 a == 0, (x, a),
9703 lambda x, a: _norm_pdf(x),
9704 lambda x, a: 2.*_norm_pdf(x)*_norm_cdf(a*x))
9705  
9706 def _logpdf(self, x, a):
9707 return xpx.apply_where(
9708 a == 0, (x, a),
9709 lambda x, a: _norm_logpdf(x),
9710 lambda x, a: np.log(2)+_norm_logpdf(x)+_norm_logcdf(a*x))
9711  
9712 def _cdf(self, x, a):
9713 a = np.atleast_1d(a)
9714 cdf = scu._skewnorm_cdf(x, 0.0, 1.0, a)
9715 # for some reason, a isn't broadcasted if some of x are invalid
9716 a = np.broadcast_to(a, cdf.shape)
9717 # Boost is not accurate in left tail when a > 0
9718 i_small_cdf = (cdf < 1e-6) & (a > 0)
9719 cdf[i_small_cdf] = super()._cdf(x[i_small_cdf], a[i_small_cdf])
9720 return np.clip(cdf, 0, 1)
9721  
9722 def _ppf(self, x, a):
9723 return scu._skewnorm_ppf(x, 0.0, 1.0, a)
9724  
9725 def _sf(self, x, a):
9726 # Boost's SF is implemented this way. Use whatever customizations
9727 # we made in the _cdf.
9728 return self._cdf(-x, -a)
9729  
9730 def _isf(self, x, a):
9731 return scu._skewnorm_isf(x, 0.0, 1.0, a)
9732  
9733 def _rvs(self, a, size=None, random_state=None):
9734 u0 = random_state.normal(size=size)
9735 v = random_state.normal(size=size)
9736 d = a/np.sqrt(1 + a**2)
9737 u1 = d*u0 + v*np.sqrt(1 - d**2)
9738 return np.where(u0 >= 0, u1, -u1)
9739  
9740 def _stats(self, a, moments='mvsk'):
9741 output = [None, None, None, None]
9742 const = np.sqrt(2/np.pi) * a/np.sqrt(1 + a**2)
9743  
9744 if 'm' in moments:
9745 output[0] = const
9746 if 'v' in moments:
9747 output[1] = 1 - const**2
9748 if 's' in moments:
9749 output[2] = ((4 - np.pi)/2) * (const/np.sqrt(1 - const**2))**3
9750 if 'k' in moments:
9751 output[3] = (2*(np.pi - 3)) * (const**4/(1 - const**2)**2)
9752  
9753 return output
9754  
9755 # For odd order, the each noncentral moment of the skew-normal distribution
9756 # with location 0 and scale 1 can be expressed as a polynomial in delta,
9757 # where delta = a/sqrt(1 + a**2) and `a` is the skew-normal shape
9758 # parameter. The dictionary _skewnorm_odd_moments defines those
9759 # polynomials for orders up to 19. The dict is implemented as a cached
9760 # property to reduce the impact of the creation of the dict on import time.
9761 @cached_property
9762 def _skewnorm_odd_moments(self):
9763 skewnorm_odd_moments = {
9764 1: Polynomial([1]),
9765 3: Polynomial([3, -1]),
9766 5: Polynomial([15, -10, 3]),
9767 7: Polynomial([105, -105, 63, -15]),
9768 9: Polynomial([945, -1260, 1134, -540, 105]),
9769 11: Polynomial([10395, -17325, 20790, -14850, 5775, -945]),
9770 13: Polynomial([135135, -270270, 405405, -386100, 225225, -73710,
9771 10395]),
9772 15: Polynomial([2027025, -4729725, 8513505, -10135125, 7882875,
9773 -3869775, 1091475, -135135]),
9774 17: Polynomial([34459425, -91891800, 192972780, -275675400,
9775 268017750, -175429800, 74220300, -18378360,
9776 2027025]),
9777 19: Polynomial([654729075, -1964187225, 4714049340, -7856748900,
9778 9166207050, -7499623950, 4230557100, -1571349780,
9779 346621275, -34459425]),
9780 }
9781 return skewnorm_odd_moments
9782  
9783 def _munp(self, order, a):
9784 if order % 2:
9785 if order > 19:
9786 raise NotImplementedError("skewnorm noncentral moments not "
9787 "implemented for odd orders greater "
9788 "than 19.")
9789 # Use the precomputed polynomials that were derived from the
9790 # moment generating function.
9791 delta = a/np.sqrt(1 + a**2)
9792 return (delta * self._skewnorm_odd_moments[order](delta**2)
9793 * _SQRT_2_OVER_PI)
9794 else:
9795 # For even order, the moment is just (order-1)!!, where !! is the
9796 # notation for the double factorial; for an odd integer m, m!! is
9797 # m*(m-2)*...*3*1.
9798 # We could use special.factorial2, but we know the argument is odd,
9799 # so avoid the overhead of that function and compute the result
9800 # directly here.
9801 return sc.gamma((order + 1)/2) * 2**(order/2) / _SQRT_PI
9802  
9803 @extend_notes_in_docstring(rv_continuous, notes="""\
9804 If ``method='mm'``, parameters fixed by the user are respected, and the
9805 remaining parameters are used to match distribution and sample moments
9806 where possible. For example, if the user fixes the location with
9807 ``floc``, the parameters will only match the distribution skewness and
9808 variance to the sample skewness and variance; no attempt will be made
9809 to match the means or minimize a norm of the errors.
9810 Note that the maximum possible skewness magnitude of a
9811 `scipy.stats.skewnorm` distribution is approximately 0.9952717; if the
9812 magnitude of the data's sample skewness exceeds this, the returned
9813 shape parameter ``a`` will be infinite.
9814 \n\n""")
9815 def fit(self, data, *args, **kwds):
9816 if kwds.pop("superfit", False):
9817 return super().fit(data, *args, **kwds)
9818 if isinstance(data, CensoredData):
9819 if data.num_censored() == 0:
9820 data = data._uncensor()
9821 else:
9822 return super().fit(data, *args, **kwds)
9823  
9824 # this extracts fixed shape, location, and scale however they
9825 # are specified, and also leaves them in `kwds`
9826 data, fa, floc, fscale = _check_fit_input_parameters(self, data,
9827 args, kwds)
9828 method = kwds.get("method", "mle").lower()
9829  
9830 # See https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skew_normal_distribution for
9831 # moment formulas.
9832 def skew_d(d): # skewness in terms of delta
9833 return (4-np.pi)/2 * ((d * np.sqrt(2 / np.pi))**3
9834 / (1 - 2*d**2 / np.pi)**(3/2))
9835  
9836 def d_skew(skew): # delta in terms of skewness
9837 s_23 = np.abs(skew)**(2/3)
9838 return np.sign(skew) * np.sqrt(
9839 np.pi/2 * s_23 / (s_23 + ((4 - np.pi)/2)**(2/3))
9840 )
9841  
9842 # If method is method of moments, we don't need the user's guesses.
9843 # Otherwise, extract the guesses from args and kwds.
9844 if method == "mm":
9845 a, loc, scale = None, None, None
9846 else:
9847 a = args[0] if len(args) else None
9848 loc = kwds.pop('loc', None)
9849 scale = kwds.pop('scale', None)
9850  
9851 if fa is None and a is None: # not fixed and no guess: use MoM
9852 # Solve for a that matches sample distribution skewness to sample
9853 # skewness.
9854 s = stats.skew(data)
9855 if method == 'mle':
9856 # For MLE initial conditions, clip skewness to a large but
9857 # reasonable value in case the data skewness is out-of-range.
9858 s = np.clip(s, -0.99, 0.99)
9859 else:
9860 s_max = skew_d(1)
9861 s = np.clip(s, -s_max, s_max)
9862 d = d_skew(s)
9863 with np.errstate(divide='ignore'):
9864 a = np.sqrt(np.divide(d**2, (1-d**2)))*np.sign(s)
9865 else:
9866 a = fa if fa is not None else a
9867 d = a / np.sqrt(1 + a**2)
9868  
9869 if fscale is None and scale is None:
9870 v = np.var(data)
9871 scale = np.sqrt(v / (1 - 2*d**2/np.pi))
9872 elif fscale is not None:
9873 scale = fscale
9874  
9875 if floc is None and loc is None:
9876 m = np.mean(data)
9877 loc = m - scale*d*np.sqrt(2/np.pi)
9878 elif floc is not None:
9879 loc = floc
9880  
9881 if method == 'mm':
9882 return a, loc, scale
9883 else:
9884 # At this point, parameter "guesses" may equal the fixed parameters
9885 # in kwds. No harm in passing them as guesses, too.
9886 return super().fit(data, a, loc=loc, scale=scale, **kwds)
9887  
9888  
9889 skewnorm = skewnorm_gen(name='skewnorm')
9890  
9891  
9892 class trapezoid_gen(rv_continuous):
9893 r"""A trapezoidal continuous random variable.
9894  
9895 %(before_notes)s
9896  
9897 Notes
9898 -----
9899 The trapezoidal distribution can be represented with an up-sloping line
9900 from ``loc`` to ``(loc + c*scale)``, then constant to ``(loc + d*scale)``
9901 and then downsloping from ``(loc + d*scale)`` to ``(loc+scale)``. This
9902 defines the trapezoid base from ``loc`` to ``(loc+scale)`` and the flat
9903 top from ``c`` to ``d`` proportional to the position along the base
9904 with ``0 <= c <= d <= 1``. When ``c=d``, this is equivalent to `triang`
9905 with the same values for `loc`, `scale` and `c`.
9906 The method of [1]_ is used for computing moments.
9907  
9908 `trapezoid` takes :math:`c` and :math:`d` as shape parameters.
9909  
9910 %(after_notes)s
9911  
9912 The standard form is in the range [0, 1] with c the mode.
9913 The location parameter shifts the start to `loc`.
9914 The scale parameter changes the width from 1 to `scale`.
9915  
9916 %(example)s
9917  
9918 References
9919 ----------
9920 .. [1] Kacker, R.N. and Lawrence, J.F. (2007). Trapezoidal and triangular
9921 distributions for Type B evaluation of standard uncertainty.
9922 Metrologia 44, 117-127. :doi:`10.1088/0026-1394/44/2/003`
9923  
9924  
9925 """
9926 def _argcheck(self, c, d):
9927 return (c >= 0) & (c <= 1) & (d >= 0) & (d <= 1) & (d >= c)
9928  
9929 def _shape_info(self):
9930 ic = _ShapeInfo("c", False, (0, 1.0), (True, True))
9931 id = _ShapeInfo("d", False, (0, 1.0), (True, True))
9932 return [ic, id]
9933  
9934 def _pdf(self, x, c, d):
9935 u = 2 / (d-c+1)
9936  
9937 return _lazyselect([x < c,
9938 (c <= x) & (x <= d),
9939 x > d],
9940 [lambda x, c, d, u: u * x / c,
9941 lambda x, c, d, u: u,
9942 lambda x, c, d, u: u * (1-x) / (1-d)],
9943 (x, c, d, u))
9944  
9945 def _cdf(self, x, c, d):
9946 return _lazyselect([x < c,
9947 (c <= x) & (x <= d),
9948 x > d],
9949 [lambda x, c, d: x**2 / c / (d-c+1),
9950 lambda x, c, d: (c + 2 * (x-c)) / (d-c+1),
9951 lambda x, c, d: 1-((1-x) ** 2
9952 / (d-c+1) / (1-d))],
9953 (x, c, d))
9954  
9955 def _ppf(self, q, c, d):
9956 qc, qd = self._cdf(c, c, d), self._cdf(d, c, d)
9957 condlist = [q < qc, q <= qd, q > qd]
9958 choicelist = [np.sqrt(q * c * (1 + d - c)),
9959 0.5 * q * (1 + d - c) + 0.5 * c,
9960 1 - np.sqrt((1 - q) * (d - c + 1) * (1 - d))]
9961 return np.select(condlist, choicelist)
9962  
9963 def _munp(self, n, c, d):
9964 # Using the parameterization from Kacker, 2007, with
9965 # a=bottom left, c=top left, d=top right, b=bottom right, then
9966 # E[X^n] = h/(n+1)/(n+2) [(b^{n+2}-d^{n+2})/(b-d)
9967 # - ((c^{n+2} - a^{n+2})/(c-a)]
9968 # with h = 2/((b-a) - (d-c)). The corresponding parameterization
9969 # in scipy, has a'=loc, c'=loc+c*scale, d'=loc+d*scale, b'=loc+scale,
9970 # which for standard form reduces to a'=0, b'=1, c'=c, d'=d.
9971 # Substituting into E[X^n] gives the bd' term as (1 - d^{n+2})/(1 - d)
9972 # and the ac' term as c^{n-1} for the standard form. The bd' term has
9973 # numerical difficulties near d=1, so replace (1 - d^{n+2})/(1-d)
9974 # with expm1((n+2)*log(d))/(d-1).
9975 # Testing with n=18 for c=(1e-30,1-eps) shows that this is stable.
9976 # We still require an explicit test for d=1 to prevent divide by zero,
9977 # and now a test for d=0 to prevent log(0).
9978 ab_term = c**(n+1)
9979 dc_term = _lazyselect(
9980 [d == 0.0, (0.0 < d) & (d < 1.0), d == 1.0],
9981 [lambda d: 1.0,
9982 lambda d: np.expm1((n+2) * np.log(d)) / (d-1.0),
9983 lambda d: n+2],
9984 [d])
9985 val = 2.0 / (1.0+d-c) * (dc_term - ab_term) / ((n+1) * (n+2))
9986 return val
9987  
9988 def _entropy(self, c, d):
9989 # Using the parameterization from Wikipedia (van Dorp, 2003)
9990 # with a=bottom left, c=top left, d=top right, b=bottom right
9991 # gives a'=loc, b'=loc+c*scale, c'=loc+d*scale, d'=loc+scale,
9992 # which for loc=0, scale=1 is a'=0, b'=c, c'=d, d'=1.
9993 # Substituting into the entropy formula from Wikipedia gives
9994 # the following result.
9995 return 0.5 * (1.0-d+c) / (1.0+d-c) + np.log(0.5 * (1.0+d-c))
9996  
9997  
9998 trapezoid = trapezoid_gen(a=0.0, b=1.0, name="trapezoid")
9999  
10000  
10001 class triang_gen(rv_continuous):

10003  
10004 %(before_notes)s
10005  
10006 Notes
10007 -----
10008 The triangular distribution can be represented with an up-sloping line from
10009 ``loc`` to ``(loc + c*scale)`` and then downsloping for ``(loc + c*scale)``
10010 to ``(loc + scale)``.
10011  
10012 `triang` takes ``c`` as a shape parameter for :math:`0 \le c \le 1`.
10013  
10014 %(after_notes)s
10015  
10016 The standard form is in the range [0, 1] with c the mode.
10017 The location parameter shifts the start to `loc`.
10018 The scale parameter changes the width from 1 to `scale`.
10019  
10020 %(example)s

10022 """
10023 def _rvs(self, c, size=None, random_state=None):

10025  
10026 def _argcheck(self, c):

10029 def _shape_info(self):
