10031  
10032 def _pdf(self, x, c):
10033 # 0: edge case where c=0
10034 # 1: generalised case for x < c, don't use x <= c, as it doesn't cope
10035 # with c = 0.
10036 # 2: generalised case for x >= c, but doesn't cope with c = 1
10037 # 3: edge case where c=1
10038 r = _lazyselect([c == 0,
10039 x < c,
10040 (x >= c) & (c != 1),
10041 c == 1],
10042 [lambda x, c: 2 - 2 * x,
10043 lambda x, c: 2 * x / c,
10044 lambda x, c: 2 * (1 - x) / (1 - c),
10045 lambda x, c: 2 * x],
10046 (x, c))
10047 return r
10048  
10049 def _cdf(self, x, c):
10050 r = _lazyselect([c == 0,
10051 x < c,
10052 (x >= c) & (c != 1),
10053 c == 1],
10054 [lambda x, c: 2*x - x*x,
10055 lambda x, c: x * x / c,
10056 lambda x, c: (x*x - 2*x + c) / (c-1),
10057 lambda x, c: x * x],
10058 (x, c))
10059 return r

10061 def _ppf(self, q, c):
10062 return np.where(q < c, np.sqrt(c * q), 1-np.sqrt((1-c) * (1-q)))
10063  
10064 def _stats(self, c):
10065 return ((c+1.0)/3.0,
10066 (1.0-c+c*c)/18,
  • E501 Line too long (80 > 79 characters)
10067 np.sqrt(2)*(2*c-1)*(c+1)*(c-2) / (5*np.power((1.0-c+c*c), 1.5)),
10068 -3.0/5.0)
10069  
10070 def _entropy(self, c):
10071 return 0.5-np.log(2)

10077 class truncexpon_gen(rv_continuous):
10078 r"""A truncated exponential continuous random variable.
10079  
10080 %(before_notes)s
10081  
10082 Notes
10083 -----
10084 The probability density function for `truncexpon` is:
10085  
10086 .. math::
10087  
10088 f(x, b) = \frac{\exp(-x)}{1 - \exp(-b)}
10089  
10090 for :math:`0 <= x <= b`.
10091  
10092 `truncexpon` takes ``b`` as a shape parameter for :math:`b`.
10093  
10094 %(after_notes)s
10095  
10096 %(example)s
10097  
10098 """
10099 def _shape_info(self):
10100 return [_ShapeInfo("b", False, (0, np.inf), (False, False))]
10101  
10102 def _get_support(self, b):
10103 return self.a, b
10104  
10105 def _pdf(self, x, b):
10106 # truncexpon.pdf(x, b) = exp(-x) / (1-exp(-b))
10107 return np.exp(-x)/(-sc.expm1(-b))
10108  
10109 def _logpdf(self, x, b):
10110 return -x - np.log(-sc.expm1(-b))
10111  
10112 def _cdf(self, x, b):
10113 return sc.expm1(-x)/sc.expm1(-b)
10114  
10115 def _ppf(self, q, b):
10116 return -sc.log1p(q*sc.expm1(-b))
10117  
10118 def _sf(self, x, b):
10119 return (np.exp(-b) - np.exp(-x))/sc.expm1(-b)
10120  
10121 def _isf(self, q, b):
10122 return -np.log(np.exp(-b) - q * sc.expm1(-b))
10123  
10124 def _munp(self, n, b):
10125 # wrong answer with formula, same as in continuous.pdf
10126 # return sc.gamman+1)-sc.gammainc1+n, b)
10127 if n == 1:
10128 return (1-(b+1)*np.exp(-b))/(-sc.expm1(-b))
10129 elif n == 2:
10130 return 2*(1-0.5*(b*b+2*b+2)*np.exp(-b))/(-sc.expm1(-b))
10131 else:
10132 # return generic for higher moments
10133 return super()._munp(n, b)
10134  
10135 def _entropy(self, b):
10136 eB = np.exp(b)
10137 return np.log(eB-1)+(1+eB*(b-1.0))/(1.0-eB)
10138  
10139  
10140 truncexpon = truncexpon_gen(a=0.0, name='truncexpon')
10141 truncexpon._support = (0.0, 'b')
10142  
10143  
10144 # logsumexp trick for log(p + q) with only log(p) and log(q)
10145 def _log_sum(log_p, log_q):
10146 return sc.logsumexp([log_p, log_q], axis=0)
10147  
10148  
10149 # same as above, but using -exp(x) = exp(x + πi)
10150 def _log_diff(log_p, log_q):
10151 return sc.logsumexp([log_p, log_q+np.pi*1j], axis=0)
10152  
10153  
10154 def _log_gauss_mass(a, b):
10155 """Log of Gaussian probability mass within an interval"""
10156 a, b = np.broadcast_arrays(a, b)
10157  
10158 # Calculations in right tail are inaccurate, so we'll exploit the
10159 # symmetry and work only in the left tail
10160 case_left = b <= 0
10161 case_right = a > 0
10162 case_central = ~(case_left | case_right)
10163  
10164 def mass_case_left(a, b):
10165 return _log_diff(_norm_logcdf(b), _norm_logcdf(a))
10166  
10167 def mass_case_right(a, b):
10168 return mass_case_left(-b, -a)
10169  
10170 def mass_case_central(a, b):
10171 # Previously, this was implemented as:
10172 # left_mass = mass_case_left(a, 0)
10173 # right_mass = mass_case_right(0, b)
10174 # return _log_sum(left_mass, right_mass)
10175 # Catastrophic cancellation occurs as np.exp(log_mass) approaches 1.
10176 # Correct for this with an alternative formulation.
10177 # We're not concerned with underflow here: if only one term
10178 # underflows, it was insignificant; if both terms underflow,
10179 # the result can't accurately be represented in logspace anyway
10180 # because sc.log1p(x) ~ x for small x.
10181 return sc.log1p(-_norm_cdf(a) - _norm_cdf(-b))
10182  
10183 # _lazyselect not working; don't care to debug it
10184 out = np.full_like(a, fill_value=np.nan, dtype=np.complex128)
10185 if a[case_left].size:
10186 out[case_left] = mass_case_left(a[case_left], b[case_left])
10187 if a[case_right].size:
10188 out[case_right] = mass_case_right(a[case_right], b[case_right])
10189 if a[case_central].size:
10190 out[case_central] = mass_case_central(a[case_central], b[case_central])
10191 return np.real(out) # discard ~0j
10192  
10193  
10194 class truncnorm_gen(rv_continuous):
10195 r"""A truncated normal continuous random variable.
10196  
10197 %(before_notes)s
10198  
10199 Notes
10200 -----
10201 This distribution is the normal distribution centered on ``loc`` (default
10202 0), with standard deviation ``scale`` (default 1), and truncated at ``a``
10203 and ``b`` *standard deviations* from ``loc``. For arbitrary ``loc`` and
10204 ``scale``, ``a`` and ``b`` are *not* the abscissae at which the shifted
10205 and scaled distribution is truncated.
10206  
10207 .. note::
10208 If ``a_trunc`` and ``b_trunc`` are the abscissae at which we wish
10209 to truncate the distribution (as opposed to the number of standard
10210 deviations from ``loc``), then we can calculate the distribution
10211 parameters ``a`` and ``b`` as follows::
10212  
10213 a, b = (a_trunc - loc) / scale, (b_trunc - loc) / scale
10214  
10215 This is a common point of confusion. For additional clarification,
10216 please see the example below.
10217  
10218 %(example)s
10219  
10220 In the examples above, ``loc=0`` and ``scale=1``, so the plot is truncated
10221 at ``a`` on the left and ``b`` on the right. However, suppose we were to
10222 produce the same histogram with ``loc = 1`` and ``scale=0.5``.
10223  
10224 >>> loc, scale = 1, 0.5
10225 >>> rv = truncnorm(a, b, loc=loc, scale=scale)
10226 >>> x = np.linspace(truncnorm.ppf(0.01, a, b),
10227 ... truncnorm.ppf(0.99, a, b), 100)
10228 >>> r = rv.rvs(size=1000)
10229  
10230 >>> fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 1)
10231 >>> ax.plot(x, rv.pdf(x), 'k-', lw=2, label='frozen pdf')
10232 >>> ax.hist(r, density=True, bins='auto', histtype='stepfilled', alpha=0.2)
10233 >>> ax.set_xlim(a, b)
10234 >>> ax.legend(loc='best', frameon=False)
10235 >>> plt.show()
10236  
10237 Note that the distribution is no longer appears to be truncated at
10238 abscissae ``a`` and ``b``. That is because the *standard* normal
10239 distribution is first truncated at ``a`` and ``b``, *then* the resulting
10240 distribution is scaled by ``scale`` and shifted by ``loc``. If we instead
10241 want the shifted and scaled distribution to be truncated at ``a`` and
10242 ``b``, we need to transform these values before passing them as the
10243 distribution parameters.
10244  
10245 >>> a_transformed, b_transformed = (a - loc) / scale, (b - loc) / scale
10246 >>> rv = truncnorm(a_transformed, b_transformed, loc=loc, scale=scale)
10247 >>> x = np.linspace(truncnorm.ppf(0.01, a, b),
10248 ... truncnorm.ppf(0.99, a, b), 100)
10249 >>> r = rv.rvs(size=10000)
10250  
10251 >>> fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 1)
10252 >>> ax.plot(x, rv.pdf(x), 'k-', lw=2, label='frozen pdf')
10253 >>> ax.hist(r, density=True, bins='auto', histtype='stepfilled', alpha=0.2)
10254 >>> ax.set_xlim(a-0.1, b+0.1)
10255 >>> ax.legend(loc='best', frameon=False)
10256 >>> plt.show()
10257 """
10258  
10259 def _argcheck(self, a, b):
10260 return a < b
10261  
10262 def _shape_info(self):
10263 ia = _ShapeInfo("a", False, (-np.inf, np.inf), (True, False))
10264 ib = _ShapeInfo("b", False, (-np.inf, np.inf), (False, True))
10265 return [ia, ib]
10266  
10267 def _fitstart(self, data):
10268 # Reasonable, since support is [a, b]
10269 if isinstance(data, CensoredData):
10270 data = data._uncensor()
10271 return super()._fitstart(data, args=(np.min(data), np.max(data)))
10272  
10273 def _get_support(self, a, b):
10274 return a, b
10275  
10276 def _pdf(self, x, a, b):
10277 return np.exp(self._logpdf(x, a, b))
10278  
10279 def _logpdf(self, x, a, b):
10280 return _norm_logpdf(x) - _log_gauss_mass(a, b)
10281  
10282 def _cdf(self, x, a, b):
10283 return np.exp(self._logcdf(x, a, b))
10284  
10285 def _logcdf(self, x, a, b):
10286 x, a, b = np.broadcast_arrays(x, a, b)
10287 logcdf = np.asarray(_log_gauss_mass(a, x) - _log_gauss_mass(a, b))
10288 i = logcdf > -0.1 # avoid catastrophic cancellation
10289 if np.any(i):
10290 logcdf[i] = np.log1p(-np.exp(self._logsf(x[i], a[i], b[i])))
10291 return logcdf
10292  
10293 def _sf(self, x, a, b):
10294 return np.exp(self._logsf(x, a, b))
10295  
10296 def _logsf(self, x, a, b):
10297 x, a, b = np.broadcast_arrays(x, a, b)
10298 logsf = np.asarray(_log_gauss_mass(x, b) - _log_gauss_mass(a, b))
10299 i = logsf > -0.1 # avoid catastrophic cancellation
10300 if np.any(i):
10301 logsf[i] = np.log1p(-np.exp(self._logcdf(x[i], a[i], b[i])))
10302 return logsf
10303  
10304 def _entropy(self, a, b):
10305 A = _norm_cdf(a)
10306 B = _norm_cdf(b)
10307 Z = B - A
10308 C = np.log(np.sqrt(2 * np.pi * np.e) * Z)
10309 D = (a * _norm_pdf(a) - b * _norm_pdf(b)) / (2 * Z)
10310 h = C + D
10311 return h
10312  
10313 def _ppf(self, q, a, b):
10314 q, a, b = np.broadcast_arrays(q, a, b)
10315  
10316 case_left = a < 0
10317 case_right = ~case_left
10318  
10319 def ppf_left(q, a, b):
10320 log_Phi_x = _log_sum(_norm_logcdf(a),
10321 np.log(q) + _log_gauss_mass(a, b))
10322 return sc.ndtri_exp(log_Phi_x)
10323  
10324 def ppf_right(q, a, b):
10325 log_Phi_x = _log_sum(_norm_logcdf(-b),
10326 np.log1p(-q) + _log_gauss_mass(a, b))
10327 return -sc.ndtri_exp(log_Phi_x)
10328  
10329 out = np.empty_like(q)
10330  
10331 q_left = q[case_left]
10332 q_right = q[case_right]
10333  
10334 if q_left.size:
10335 out[case_left] = ppf_left(q_left, a[case_left], b[case_left])
10336 if q_right.size:
10337 out[case_right] = ppf_right(q_right, a[case_right], b[case_right])
10338  
10339 return out
10340  
10341 def _isf(self, q, a, b):
10342 # Mostly copy-paste of _ppf, but I think this is simpler than combining
10343 q, a, b = np.broadcast_arrays(q, a, b)
10344  
10345 case_left = b < 0
10346 case_right = ~case_left
10347  
10348 def isf_left(q, a, b):
10349 log_Phi_x = _log_diff(_norm_logcdf(b),
10350 np.log(q) + _log_gauss_mass(a, b))
10351 return sc.ndtri_exp(np.real(log_Phi_x))
10352  
10353 def isf_right(q, a, b):
10354 log_Phi_x = _log_diff(_norm_logcdf(-a),
10355 np.log1p(-q) + _log_gauss_mass(a, b))
10356 return -sc.ndtri_exp(np.real(log_Phi_x))
10357  
10358 out = np.empty_like(q)
10359  
10360 q_left = q[case_left]
10361 q_right = q[case_right]
10362  
10363 if q_left.size:
10364 out[case_left] = isf_left(q_left, a[case_left], b[case_left])
10365 if q_right.size:
10366 out[case_right] = isf_right(q_right, a[case_right], b[case_right])
10367  
10368 return out
10369  
10370 def _munp(self, n, a, b):
10371 def n_th_moment(n, a, b):
10372 """
10373 Returns n-th moment. Defined only if n >= 0.
10374 Function cannot broadcast due to the loop over n
10375 """
10376 ab = np.asarray([a, b])
10377 pA, pB = self._pdf(ab, a, b)
10378 probs = np.asarray([pA, -pB])
10379 cond = probs != 0
10380 moments = [0, 1]
10381 for k in range(1, n+1):
10382 # a or b might be infinite, and the corresponding pdf value
10383 # is 0 in that case, but nan is returned for the
10384 # multiplication. However, as b->infinity, pdf(b)*b**k -> 0.
10385 # So it is safe to use xpx.apply_where to avoid the nan.
10386 vals = xpx.apply_where(cond, (probs, ab),
10387 lambda x, y: x * y**(k-1),
10388 fill_value=0)
10389 mk = np.sum(vals) + (k-1) * moments[-2]
10390 moments.append(mk)
10391 return moments[-1]
10392  
10393 return xpx.apply_where((n >= 0) & (a == a) & (b == b), (n, a, b),
10394 np.vectorize(n_th_moment, otypes=[np.float64]),
10395 fill_value=np.nan)
10396  
10397 def _stats(self, a, b, moments='mv'):
10398 pA, pB = self.pdf(np.array([a, b]), a, b)
10399  
10400 def _truncnorm_stats_scalar(a, b, pA, pB):
10401 ab = np.asarray([a, b])
10402 m1 = pA - pB
10403 mu = m1
10404 # use xpx.apply_where to avoid nan (See detailed comment in _munp)
10405 probs = np.asarray([pA, -pB])
10406 cond = probs != 0
10407 vals = xpx.apply_where(cond, (probs, ab), lambda x, y: x*y,
10408 fill_value=0)
10409 m2 = 1 + np.sum(vals)
10410 vals = xpx.apply_where(cond, (probs, ab - mu), lambda x, y: x*y,
10411 fill_value=0)
10412 # mu2 = m2 - mu**2, but not as numerically stable as:
10413 # mu2 = (a-mu)*pA - (b-mu)*pB + 1
10414 mu2 = 1 + np.sum(vals)
10415 vals = xpx.apply_where(cond, (probs, ab), lambda x, y: x*y**2,
10416 fill_value=0)
10417 m3 = 2*m1 + np.sum(vals)
10418 vals = xpx.apply_where(cond, (probs, ab), lambda x, y: x*y**3,
10419 fill_value=0)
10420 m4 = 3*m2 + np.sum(vals)
10421  
10422 mu3 = m3 + m1 * (-3*m2 + 2*m1**2)
10423 g1 = mu3 / np.power(mu2, 1.5)
10424 mu4 = m4 + m1*(-4*m3 + 3*m1*(2*m2 - m1**2))
10425 g2 = mu4 / mu2**2 - 3
10426 return mu, mu2, g1, g2
10427  
10428 _truncnorm_stats = np.vectorize(_truncnorm_stats_scalar)
10429 return _truncnorm_stats(a, b, pA, pB)
10430  
10431  
10432 truncnorm = truncnorm_gen(name='truncnorm', momtype=1)
10433 truncnorm._support = ('a', 'b')
10434  
10435  
10436 class truncpareto_gen(rv_continuous):
10437 r"""An upper truncated Pareto continuous random variable.
10438  
10439 %(before_notes)s
10440  
10441 See Also
10442 --------
10443 pareto : Pareto distribution
10444  
10445 Notes
10446 -----
10447 The probability density function for `truncpareto` is:
10448  
10449 .. math::
10450  
10451 f(x, b, c) = \frac{b}{1 - c^{-b}} \frac{1}{x^{b+1}}
10452  
10453 for :math:`b > 0`, :math:`c > 1` and :math:`1 \le x \le c`.
10454  
10455 `truncpareto` takes `b` and `c` as shape parameters for :math:`b` and
10456 :math:`c`.
10457  
10458 Notice that the upper truncation value :math:`c` is defined in
10459 standardized form so that random values of an unscaled, unshifted variable
10460 are within the range ``[1, c]``.
10461 If ``u_r`` is the upper bound to a scaled and/or shifted variable,
10462 then ``c = (u_r - loc) / scale``. In other words, the support of the
10463 distribution becomes ``(scale + loc) <= x <= (c*scale + loc)`` when
10464 `scale` and/or `loc` are provided.
10465  
10466 %(after_notes)s
10467  
10468 References
10469 ----------
10470 .. [1] Burroughs, S. M., and Tebbens S. F.
10471 "Upper-truncated power laws in natural systems."
10472 Pure and Applied Geophysics 158.4 (2001): 741-757.
10473  
10474 %(example)s
10475  
10476 """
10477  
10478 def _shape_info(self):
10479 ib = _ShapeInfo("b", False, (0.0, np.inf), (False, False))
10480 ic = _ShapeInfo("c", False, (1.0, np.inf), (False, False))
10481 return [ib, ic]
10482  
10483 def _argcheck(self, b, c):
10484 return (b > 0.) & (c > 1.)
10485  
10486 def _get_support(self, b, c):
10487 return self.a, c
10488  
10489 def _pdf(self, x, b, c):
10490 return b * x**-(b+1) / (1 - 1/c**b)
10491  
10492 def _logpdf(self, x, b, c):
10493 return np.log(b) - np.log(-np.expm1(-b*np.log(c))) - (b+1)*np.log(x)
10494  
10495 def _cdf(self, x, b, c):
10496 return (1 - x**-b) / (1 - 1/c**b)
10497  
10498 def _logcdf(self, x, b, c):
10499 return np.log1p(-x**-b) - np.log1p(-1/c**b)
10500  
10501 def _ppf(self, q, b, c):
10502 return pow(1 - (1 - 1/c**b)*q, -1/b)
10503

10829 class uniform_gen(rv_continuous):
10830 r"""A uniform continuous random variable.
10831  
10832 In the standard form, the distribution is uniform on ``[0, 1]``. Using
10833 the parameters ``loc`` and ``scale``, one obtains the uniform distribution
10834 on ``[loc, loc + scale]``.
10835  
10836 %(before_notes)s
10837  
10838 %(example)s
10839  
10840 """
10841 def _shape_info(self):
10842 return []
10843  
10844 def _rvs(self, size=None, random_state=None):
10845 return random_state.uniform(0.0, 1.0, size)
10846  
10847 def _pdf(self, x):
10848 return 1.0*(x == x)
10849  
10850 def _cdf(self, x):
10851 return x
10852  
10853 def _ppf(self, q):
10854 return q
10855  
10856 def _stats(self):
10857 return 0.5, 1.0/12, 0, -1.2
10858  
10859 def _entropy(self):
10860 return 0.0
10861  
10862 @_call_super_mom
10863 def fit(self, data, *args, **kwds):
10864 """
10865 Maximum likelihood estimate for the location and scale parameters.
10866  
10867 `uniform.fit` uses only the following parameters. Because exact
10868 formulas are used, the parameters related to optimization that are
10869 available in the `fit` method of other distributions are ignored
10870 here. The only positional argument accepted is `data`.
10871  
10872 Parameters
10873 ----------
10874 data : array_like
10875 Data to use in calculating the maximum likelihood estimate.
10876 floc : float, optional
10877 Hold the location parameter fixed to the specified value.
10878 fscale : float, optional
10879 Hold the scale parameter fixed to the specified value.
10880  
10881 Returns
10882 -------
10883 loc, scale : float
10884 Maximum likelihood estimates for the location and scale.
10885  
10886 Notes
10887 -----
10888 An error is raised if `floc` is given and any values in `data` are
10889 less than `floc`, or if `fscale` is given and `fscale` is less
10890 than ``data.max() - data.min()``. An error is also raised if both
10891 `floc` and `fscale` are given.
10892  
10893 Examples
10894 --------
10895 >>> import numpy as np
10896 >>> from scipy.stats import uniform
10897  
10898 We'll fit the uniform distribution to `x`:
10899  
10900 >>> x = np.array([2, 2.5, 3.1, 9.5, 13.0])
10901  
10902 For a uniform distribution MLE, the location is the minimum of the
10903 data, and the scale is the maximum minus the minimum.
10904  
10905 >>> loc, scale = uniform.fit(x)
10906 >>> loc
10907 2.0
10908 >>> scale
10909 11.0
10910  
10911 If we know the data comes from a uniform distribution where the support
10912 starts at 0, we can use ``floc=0``:
10913  
10914 >>> loc, scale = uniform.fit(x, floc=0)
10915 >>> loc
10916 0.0
10917 >>> scale
10918 13.0
10919  
10920 Alternatively, if we know the length of the support is 12, we can use
10921 ``fscale=12``:
10922  
10923 >>> loc, scale = uniform.fit(x, fscale=12)
10924 >>> loc
10925 1.5
10926 >>> scale
10927 12.0
10928  
10929 In that last example, the support interval is [1.5, 13.5]. This
10930 solution is not unique. For example, the distribution with ``loc=2``
10931 and ``scale=12`` has the same likelihood as the one above. When
10932 `fscale` is given and it is larger than ``data.max() - data.min()``,
10933 the parameters returned by the `fit` method center the support over
10934 the interval ``[data.min(), data.max()]``.
10935  
10936 """
10937 if len(args) > 0:
10938 raise TypeError("Too many arguments.")
10939  
10940 floc = kwds.pop('floc', None)
10941 fscale = kwds.pop('fscale', None)
10942  
10943 _remove_optimizer_parameters(kwds)
10944  
10945 if floc is not None and fscale is not None:
10946 # This check is for consistency with `rv_continuous.fit`.
10947 raise ValueError("All parameters fixed. There is nothing to "
10948 "optimize.")
10949  
10950 data = np.asarray(data)
10951  
10952 if not np.isfinite(data).all():
10953 raise ValueError("The data contains non-finite values.")
10954  
10955 # MLE for the uniform distribution
10956 # --------------------------------
10957 # The PDF is
10958 #
10959 # f(x, loc, scale) = {1/scale for loc <= x <= loc + scale
10960 # {0 otherwise}
10961 #
10962 # The likelihood function is
10963 # L(x, loc, scale) = (1/scale)**n
10964 # where n is len(x), assuming loc <= x <= loc + scale for all x.
10965 # The log-likelihood is
10966 # l(x, loc, scale) = -n*log(scale)
10967 # The log-likelihood is maximized by making scale as small as possible,
10968 # while keeping loc <= x <= loc + scale. So if neither loc nor scale
10969 # are fixed, the log-likelihood is maximized by choosing
10970 # loc = x.min()
10971 # scale = np.ptp(x)
10972 # If loc is fixed, it must be less than or equal to x.min(), and then
10973 # the scale is
10974 # scale = x.max() - loc
10975 # If scale is fixed, it must not be less than np.ptp(x). If scale is
10976 # greater than np.ptp(x), the solution is not unique. Note that the
10977 # likelihood does not depend on loc, except for the requirement that
10978 # loc <= x <= loc + scale. All choices of loc for which
10979 # x.max() - scale <= loc <= x.min()
10980 # have the same log-likelihood. In this case, we choose loc such that
10981 # the support is centered over the interval [data.min(), data.max()]:
10982 # loc = x.min() = 0.5*(scale - np.ptp(x))
10983  
10984 if fscale is None:
10985 # scale is not fixed.
10986 if floc is None:
10987 # loc is not fixed, scale is not fixed.
10988 loc = data.min()
10989 scale = np.ptp(data)
10990 else:
10991 # loc is fixed, scale is not fixed.
10992 loc = floc
10993 scale = data.max() - loc
10994 if data.min() < loc:
10995 raise FitDataError("uniform", lower=loc, upper=loc + scale)
10996 else:
10997 # loc is not fixed, scale is fixed.
10998 ptp = np.ptp(data)
10999 if ptp > fscale:
11000 raise FitUniformFixedScaleDataError(ptp=ptp, fscale=fscale)
11001 # If ptp < fscale, the ML estimate is not unique; see the comments
11002 # above. We choose the distribution for which the support is
11003 # centered over the interval [data.min(), data.max()].
11004 loc = data.min() - 0.5*(fscale - ptp)
11005 scale = fscale
11006  
11007 # We expect the return values to be floating point, so ensure it
11008 # by explicitly converting to float.
11009 return float(loc), float(scale)
11010  
11011  
11012 uniform = uniform_gen(a=0.0, b=1.0, name='uniform')
11013  
11014  
11015 class vonmises_gen(rv_continuous):
11016 r"""A Von Mises continuous random variable.
11017  
11018 %(before_notes)s
11019  
11020 See Also
11021 --------
11022 scipy.stats.vonmises_fisher : Von-Mises Fisher distribution on a
11023 hypersphere
11024  
11025 Notes
11026 -----
11027 The probability density function for `vonmises` and `vonmises_line` is:
11028  
11029 .. math::
11030  
11031 f(x, \kappa) = \frac{ \exp(\kappa \cos(x)) }{ 2 \pi I_0(\kappa) }
11032  
11033 for :math:`-\pi \le x \le \pi`, :math:`\kappa \ge 0`. :math:`I_0` is the
11034 modified Bessel function of order zero (`scipy.special.i0`).
11035  
11036 `vonmises` is a circular distribution which does not restrict the
11037 distribution to a fixed interval. Currently, there is no circular
11038 distribution framework in SciPy. The ``cdf`` is implemented such that
11039 ``cdf(x + 2*np.pi) == cdf(x) + 1``.
11040  
11041 `vonmises_line` is the same distribution, defined on :math:`[-\pi, \pi]`
11042 on the real line. This is a regular (i.e. non-circular) distribution.
11043  
11044 Note about distribution parameters: `vonmises` and `vonmises_line` take
11045 ``kappa`` as a shape parameter (concentration) and ``loc`` as the location
11046 (circular mean). A ``scale`` parameter is accepted but does not have any
11047 effect.
11048  
11049 Examples
11050 --------
11051 Import the necessary modules.
11052  
11053 >>> import numpy as np
11054 >>> import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
11055 >>> from scipy.stats import vonmises
11056  
11057 Define distribution parameters.
11058  
11059 >>> loc = 0.5 * np.pi # circular mean
11060 >>> kappa = 1 # concentration
11061  
11062 Compute the probability density at ``x=0`` via the ``pdf`` method.
11063  
11064 >>> vonmises.pdf(0, loc=loc, kappa=kappa)
11065 0.12570826359722018
11066  
11067 Verify that the percentile function ``ppf`` inverts the cumulative
11068 distribution function ``cdf`` up to floating point accuracy.
11069  
11070 >>> x = 1
11071 >>> cdf_value = vonmises.cdf(x, loc=loc, kappa=kappa)
11072 >>> ppf_value = vonmises.ppf(cdf_value, loc=loc, kappa=kappa)
11073 >>> x, cdf_value, ppf_value
11074 (1, 0.31489339900904967, 1.0000000000000004)
11075  
11076 Draw 1000 random variates by calling the ``rvs`` method.
11077  
11078 >>> sample_size = 1000
11079 >>> sample = vonmises(loc=loc, kappa=kappa).rvs(sample_size)
11080  
11081 Plot the von Mises density on a Cartesian and polar grid to emphasize
11082 that it is a circular distribution.
11083  
11084 >>> fig = plt.figure(figsize=(12, 6))
11085 >>> left = plt.subplot(121)
11086 >>> right = plt.subplot(122, projection='polar')
11087 >>> x = np.linspace(-np.pi, np.pi, 500)
11088 >>> vonmises_pdf = vonmises.pdf(x, loc=loc, kappa=kappa)
11089 >>> ticks = [0, 0.15, 0.3]
11090  
11091 The left image contains the Cartesian plot.
11092  
11093 >>> left.plot(x, vonmises_pdf)
11094 >>> left.set_yticks(ticks)
11095 >>> number_of_bins = int(np.sqrt(sample_size))
11096 >>> left.hist(sample, density=True, bins=number_of_bins)
11097 >>> left.set_title("Cartesian plot")
11098 >>> left.set_xlim(-np.pi, np.pi)
11099 >>> left.grid(True)
11100  
11101 The right image contains the polar plot.
11102  
11103 >>> right.plot(x, vonmises_pdf, label="PDF")
11104 >>> right.set_yticks(ticks)
11105 >>> right.hist(sample, density=True, bins=number_of_bins,
11106 ... label="Histogram")
11107 >>> right.set_title("Polar plot")
11108 >>> right.legend(bbox_to_anchor=(0.15, 1.06))
11109  
11110 """
11111 def _shape_info(self):
11112 return [_ShapeInfo("kappa", False, (0, np.inf), (True, False))]
11113  
11114 def _argcheck(self, kappa):
11115 return kappa >= 0
11116  
11117 def _rvs(self, kappa, size=None, random_state=None):

11125 def _pdf(self, x, kappa):
11126 # vonmises.pdf(x, kappa) = exp(kappa * cos(x)) / (2*pi*I[0](kappa))
11127 # = exp(kappa * (cos(x) - 1)) /
11128 # (2*pi*exp(-kappa)*I[0](kappa))
11129 # = exp(kappa * cosm1(x)) / (2*pi*i0e(kappa))
11130 return np.exp(kappa*sc.cosm1(x)) / (2*np.pi*sc.i0e(kappa))
11131  
11132 def _logpdf(self, x, kappa):
11133 # vonmises.pdf(x, kappa) = exp(kappa * cosm1(x)) / (2*pi*i0e(kappa))
11134 return kappa * sc.cosm1(x) - np.log(2*np.pi) - np.log(sc.i0e(kappa))
11135  
11136 def _cdf(self, x, kappa):
11137 return _stats.von_mises_cdf(kappa, x)

11139 def _stats_skip(self, kappa):
11140 return 0, None, 0, None
11141  
11142 def _entropy(self, kappa):
11143 # vonmises.entropy(kappa) = -kappa * I[1](kappa) / I[0](kappa) +
11144 # log(2 * np.pi * I[0](kappa))
11145 # = -kappa * I[1](kappa) * exp(-kappa) /
11146 # (I[0](kappa) * exp(-kappa)) +
11147 # log(2 * np.pi *
11148 # I[0](kappa) * exp(-kappa) / exp(-kappa))
11149 # = -kappa * sc.i1e(kappa) / sc.i0e(kappa) +
11150 # log(2 * np.pi * i0e(kappa)) + kappa
11151 return (-kappa * sc.i1e(kappa) / sc.i0e(kappa) +
11152 np.log(2 * np.pi * sc.i0e(kappa)) + kappa)

11158 def expect(self, func=None, args=(), loc=0, scale=1, lb=None, ub=None,

11161

11163 lb = loc + _a

11170 @_call_super_mom
11171 @extend_notes_in_docstring(rv_continuous, notes="""\
11172 Fit data is assumed to represent angles and will be wrapped onto the
11173 unit circle. `f0` and `fscale` are ignored; the returned shape is
11174 always the maximum likelihood estimate and the scale is always
11175 1. Initial guesses are ignored.\n\n""")
11176 def fit(self, data, *args, **kwds):
11177 if kwds.pop('superfit', False):
11178 return super().fit(data, *args, **kwds)
11179  
11180 data, fshape, floc, fscale = _check_fit_input_parameters(self, data,
11181 args, kwds)
11182 if self.a == -np.pi:
11183 # vonmises line case, here the default fit method will be used
11184 return super().fit(data, *args, **kwds)
11185  
11186 # wrap data to interval [0, 2*pi]
11187 data = np.mod(data, 2 * np.pi)
11188  
11189 def find_mu(data):
11190 return stats.circmean(data)
11191  
11192 def find_kappa(data, loc):
11193 # Usually, sources list the following as the equation to solve for
11194 # the MLE of the shape parameter:
11195 # r = I[1](kappa)/I[0](kappa), where r = mean resultant length
11196 # This is valid when the location is the MLE of location.
11197 # More generally, when the location may be fixed at an arbitrary
11198 # value, r should be defined as follows:
11199 r = np.sum(np.cos(loc - data))/len(data)
11200 # See gh-18128 for more information.
11201  
11202 # The function r[0](kappa) := I[1](kappa)/I[0](kappa) is monotonic
11203 # increasing from r[0](0) = 0 to r[0](+inf) = 1. The partial
11204 # derivative of the log likelihood function with respect to kappa
11205 # is monotonic decreasing in kappa.
11206 if r == 1:
11207 # All observations are (almost) equal to the mean. Return
11208 # some large kappa such that r[0](kappa) = 1.0 numerically.
11209 return 1e16
11210 elif r > 0:
11211 def solve_for_kappa(kappa):
11212 return sc.i1e(kappa)/sc.i0e(kappa) - r
11213  
11214 # The bounds of the root of r[0](kappa) = r are derived from
11215 # selected bounds of r[0](x) given in [1, Eq. 11 & 16]. See
11216 # gh-20102 for details.
11217 #
11218 # [1] Amos, D. E. (1973). Computation of Modified Bessel
11219 # Functions and Their Ratios. Mathematics of Computation,
11220 # 28(125): 239-251.
11221 lower_bound = r/(1-r)/(1+r)
11222 upper_bound = 2*lower_bound
11223  
11224 # The bounds are violated numerically for certain values of r,
11225 # where solve_for_kappa evaluated at the bounds have the same
11226 # sign. This indicates numerical imprecision of i1e()/i0e().
11227 # Return the violated bound in this case as it's more accurate.
11228 if solve_for_kappa(lower_bound) >= 0:
11229 return lower_bound
11230 elif solve_for_kappa(upper_bound) <= 0:
11231 return upper_bound
11232 else:
11233 root_res = root_scalar(solve_for_kappa, method="brentq",
11234 bracket=(lower_bound, upper_bound))
11235 return root_res.root
11236 else:
11237 # if the provided floc is very far from the circular mean,
11238 # the mean resultant length r can become negative.
11239 # In that case, the equation
11240 # I[1](kappa)/I[0](kappa) = r does not have a solution.
11241 # The maximum likelihood kappa is then 0 which practically
11242 # results in the uniform distribution on the circle. As
11243 # vonmises is defined for kappa > 0, return instead the
11244 # smallest floating point value.
11245 # See gh-18190 for more information
11246 return np.finfo(float).tiny
11247  
11248 # location likelihood equation has a solution independent of kappa
11249 loc = floc if floc is not None else find_mu(data)
11250 # shape likelihood equation depends on location
11251 shape = fshape if fshape is not None else find_kappa(data, loc)
11252  
11253 loc = np.mod(loc + np.pi, 2 * np.pi) - np.pi # ensure in [-pi, pi]
11254 return shape, loc, 1 # scale is not handled
11255  
11256  
11257 vonmises = vonmises_gen(name='vonmises')
11258 vonmises_line = vonmises_gen(a=-np.pi, b=np.pi, name='vonmises_line')
11259

11330 Notes
11331 -----

11338 for :math:`0 \le x \le 2\pi`, :math:`0 < c < 1`.
11339  
11340 `wrapcauchy` takes ``c`` as a shape parameter for :math:`c`.

11395 class gennorm_gen(rv_continuous):
11396 r"""A generalized normal continuous random variable.
11397  
11398 %(before_notes)s
11399  
11400 See Also
11401 --------
11402 laplace : Laplace distribution
11403 norm : normal distribution
11404  
11405 Notes
11406 -----
11407 The probability density function for `gennorm` is [1]_:
11408  
11409 .. math::
11410  
11411 f(x, \beta) = \frac{\beta}{2 \Gamma(1/\beta)} \exp(-|x|^\beta),
11412  
11413 where :math:`x` is a real number, :math:`\beta > 0` and
11414 :math:`\Gamma` is the gamma function (`scipy.special.gamma`).
11415  
11416 `gennorm` takes ``beta`` as a shape parameter for :math:`\beta`.
11417 For :math:`\beta = 1`, it is identical to a Laplace distribution.
11418 For :math:`\beta = 2`, it is identical to a normal distribution
11419 (with ``scale=1/sqrt(2)``).
11420  
11421 References
11422 ----------
11423  
11424 .. [1] "Generalized normal distribution, Version 1",
11425 https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generalized_normal_distribution#Version_1
11426  
11427 .. [2] Nardon, Martina, and Paolo Pianca. "Simulation techniques for
11428 generalized Gaussian densities." Journal of Statistical
11429 Computation and Simulation 79.11 (2009): 1317-1329
11430  
11431 .. [3] Wicklin, Rick. "Simulate data from a generalized Gaussian
11432 distribution" in The DO Loop blog, September 21, 2016,
11433 https://blogs.sas.com/content/iml/2016/09/21/simulate-generalized-gaussian-sas.html
11434  
11435 %(example)s
11436  
11437 """
11438 def _shape_info(self):
11439 return [_ShapeInfo("beta", False, (0, np.inf), (False, False))]
11440  
11441 def _pdf(self, x, beta):
11442 return np.exp(self._logpdf(x, beta))
11443  
11444 def _logpdf(self, x, beta):
11445 return np.log(0.5*beta) - sc.gammaln(1.0/beta) - abs(x)**beta
11446  
11447 def _cdf(self, x, beta):
11448 c = 0.5 * np.sign(x)
11449 # evaluating (.5 + c) first prevents numerical cancellation
11450 return (0.5 + c) - c * sc.gammaincc(1.0/beta, abs(x)**beta)
11451  
11452 def _ppf(self, x, beta):
11453 c = np.sign(x - 0.5)
11454 # evaluating (1. + c) first prevents numerical cancellation
11455 return c * sc.gammainccinv(1.0/beta, (1.0 + c) - 2.0*c*x)**(1.0/beta)
11456  
11457 def _sf(self, x, beta):
11458 return self._cdf(-x, beta)
11459  
11460 def _isf(self, x, beta):
11461 return -self._ppf(x, beta)
11462  
11463 def _munp(self, n, beta):
11464 if n == 0:
11465 return 1.
11466 if n % 2 == 0:
11467 c1, cn = sc.gammaln([1.0/beta, (n + 1.0)/beta])
11468 return np.exp(cn - c1)
11469 else:
11470 return 0.
11471  
11472 def _stats(self, beta):
11473 c1, c3, c5 = sc.gammaln([1.0/beta, 3.0/beta, 5.0/beta])
11474 return 0., np.exp(c3 - c1), 0., np.exp(c5 + c1 - 2.0*c3) - 3.
11475  
11476 def _entropy(self, beta):
11477 return 1. / beta - np.log(.5 * beta) + sc.gammaln(1. / beta)
11478  
11479 def _rvs(self, beta, size=None, random_state=None):
11480 # see [2]_ for the algorithm
11481 # see [3]_ for reference implementation in SAS
11482 z = random_state.gamma(1/beta, size=size)
11483 y = z ** (1/beta)
11484 # convert y to array to ensure masking support
11485 y = np.asarray(y)
11486 mask = random_state.random(size=y.shape) < 0.5
11487 y[mask] = -y[mask]
11488 return y
11489  
11490  
11491 gennorm = gennorm_gen(name='gennorm')
11492  
11493

11561 class crystalball_gen(rv_continuous):
11562 r"""
11563 Crystalball distribution
11564  
11565 %(before_notes)s
11566  
11567 Notes
11568 -----
11569 The probability density function for `crystalball` is:
11570  
11571 .. math::
11572  
11573 f(x, \beta, m) = \begin{cases}
11574 N \exp(-x^2 / 2), &\text{for } x > -\beta\\
11575 N A (B - x)^{-m} &\text{for } x \le -\beta
11576 \end{cases}
11577  
11578 where :math:`A = (m / |\beta|)^m \exp(-\beta^2 / 2)`,
11579 :math:`B = m/|\beta| - |\beta|` and :math:`N` is a normalisation constant.
11580  
11581 `crystalball` takes :math:`\beta > 0` and :math:`m > 1` as shape
11582 parameters. :math:`\beta` defines the point where the pdf changes
11583 from a power-law to a Gaussian distribution. :math:`m` is the power
11584 of the power-law tail.
11585  
11586 %(after_notes)s
11587  
11588 .. versionadded:: 0.19.0
11589  
11590 References
11591 ----------
11592 .. [1] "Crystal Ball Function",
11593 https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crystal_Ball_function
11594  
11595 %(example)s
11596 """
11597 def _argcheck(self, beta, m):
11598 """
11599 Shape parameter bounds are m > 1 and beta > 0.
11600 """
11601 return (m > 1) & (beta > 0)
11602  
11603 def _shape_info(self):
11604 ibeta = _ShapeInfo("beta", False, (0, np.inf), (False, False))
11605 im = _ShapeInfo("m", False, (1, np.inf), (False, False))
11606 return [ibeta, im]
11607  
11608 def _fitstart(self, data):
11609 # Arbitrary, but the default m=1 is not valid
11610 return super()._fitstart(data, args=(1, 1.5))
11611  
11612 def _pdf(self, x, beta, m):
11613 """
11614 Return PDF of the crystalball function.
11615  
11616 --
11617 | exp(-x**2 / 2), for x > -beta
11618 crystalball.pdf(x, beta, m) = N * |
11619 | A * (B - x)**(-m), for x <= -beta
11620 --
11621 """
11622 N = 1.0 / (m/beta / (m-1) * np.exp(-beta**2 / 2.0) +
11623 _norm_pdf_C * _norm_cdf(beta))
11624  
11625 def rhs(x, beta, m):
11626 return np.exp(-x**2 / 2)
11627  
11628 def lhs(x, beta, m):
11629 return ((m/beta)**m * np.exp(-beta**2 / 2.0) *
11630 (m/beta - beta - x)**(-m))
11631  
11632 return N * xpx.apply_where(x > -beta, (x, beta, m), rhs, lhs)
11633  
11634 def _logpdf(self, x, beta, m):
11635 """
11636 Return the log of the PDF of the crystalball function.
11637 """
11638 N = 1.0 / (m/beta / (m-1) * np.exp(-beta**2 / 2.0) +
11639 _norm_pdf_C * _norm_cdf(beta))
11640  
11641 def rhs(x, beta, m):
11642 return -x**2/2
11643  
11644 def lhs(x, beta, m):
11645 return m*np.log(m/beta) - beta**2/2 - m*np.log(m/beta - beta - x)
11646  
11647 return np.log(N) + xpx.apply_where(x > -beta, (x, beta, m), rhs, lhs)
11648  
11649 def _cdf(self, x, beta, m):
11650 """
11651 Return CDF of the crystalball function
11652 """
11653 N = 1.0 / (m/beta / (m-1) * np.exp(-beta**2 / 2.0) +
11654 _norm_pdf_C * _norm_cdf(beta))
11655  
11656 def rhs(x, beta, m):
11657 return ((m/beta) * np.exp(-beta**2 / 2.0) / (m-1) +
11658 _norm_pdf_C * (_norm_cdf(x) - _norm_cdf(-beta)))
11659  
11660 def lhs(x, beta, m):
11661 return ((m/beta)**m * np.exp(-beta**2 / 2.0) *
11662 (m/beta - beta - x)**(-m+1) / (m-1))
11663  
11664 return N * xpx.apply_where(x > -beta, (x, beta, m), rhs, lhs)
11665  
11666 def _sf(self, x, beta, m):
11667 """
11668 Survival function of the crystalball distribution.
11669 """
11670  
11671 def rhs(x, beta, m):
11672 # M is the same as 1/N used elsewhere.
11673 M = m/beta/(m - 1)*np.exp(-beta**2/2) + _norm_pdf_C*_norm_cdf(beta)
11674 return _norm_pdf_C*_norm_sf(x)/M
11675  
11676 def lhs(x, beta, m):
11677 # Default behavior is OK in the left tail of the SF.
11678 return 1 - self._cdf(x, beta, m)
11679  
11680 return xpx.apply_where(x > -beta, (x, beta, m), rhs, lhs)
11681  
11682 def _ppf(self, p, beta, m):
11683 N = 1.0 / (m/beta / (m-1) * np.exp(-beta**2 / 2.0) +
11684 _norm_pdf_C * _norm_cdf(beta))
11685 pbeta = N * (m/beta) * np.exp(-beta**2/2) / (m - 1)
11686  
11687 def ppf_less(p, beta, m):
11688 eb2 = np.exp(-beta**2/2)
11689 C = (m/beta) * eb2 / (m-1)
11690 N = 1/(C + _norm_pdf_C * _norm_cdf(beta))
11691 return (m/beta - beta -
11692 ((m - 1)*(m/beta)**(-m)/eb2*p/N)**(1/(1-m)))
11693  
11694 def ppf_greater(p, beta, m):
11695 eb2 = np.exp(-beta**2/2)
11696 C = (m/beta) * eb2 / (m-1)
11697 N = 1/(C + _norm_pdf_C * _norm_cdf(beta))

11732 def _argus_phi(chi):
11733 """
11734 Utility function for the argus distribution used in the pdf, sf and
11735 moment calculation.
11736 Note that for all x > 0:
11737 gammainc(1.5, x**2/2) = 2 * (_norm_cdf(x) - x * _norm_pdf(x) - 0.5).
11738 This can be verified directly by noting that the cdf of Gamma(1.5) can
11739 be written as erf(sqrt(x)) - 2*sqrt(x)*exp(-x)/sqrt(Pi).
11740 We use gammainc instead of the usual definition because it is more precise
11741 for small chi.
11742 """
11743 return sc.gammainc(1.5, chi**2/2) / 2

11746 class argus_gen(rv_continuous):
11747 r"""
11748 Argus distribution
11749  
11750 %(before_notes)s
11751  
11752 Notes
11753 -----
11754 The probability density function for `argus` is:
11755  
11756 .. math::
11757  
11758 f(x, \chi) = \frac{\chi^3}{\sqrt{2\pi} \Psi(\chi)} x \sqrt{1-x^2}
11759 \exp(-\chi^2 (1 - x^2)/2)
11760  
11761 for :math:`0 < x < 1` and :math:`\chi > 0`, where
11762  
11763 .. math::
11764  
11765 \Psi(\chi) = \Phi(\chi) - \chi \phi(\chi) - 1/2
11766  
11767 with :math:`\Phi` and :math:`\phi` being the CDF and PDF of a standard
11768 normal distribution, respectively.
11769  
11770 `argus` takes :math:`\chi` as shape a parameter. Details about sampling
11771 from the ARGUS distribution can be found in [2]_.
11772  
11773 %(after_notes)s
11774  
11775 References
11776 ----------
11777 .. [1] "ARGUS distribution",
11778 https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ARGUS_distribution
11779 .. [2] Christoph Baumgarten "Random variate generation by fast numerical
11780 inversion in the varying parameter case." Research in Statistics,
11781 vol. 1, 2023, doi:10.1080/27684520.2023.2279060.
11782  
11783 .. versionadded:: 0.19.0
11784  
11785 %(example)s
11786 """
11787 def _shape_info(self):
11788 return [_ShapeInfo("chi", False, (0, np.inf), (False, False))]
11789  
11790 def _logpdf(self, x, chi):
11791 # for x = 0 or 1, logpdf returns -np.inf
11792 with np.errstate(divide='ignore'):
11793 y = 1.0 - x*x
11794 A = 3*np.log(chi) - _norm_pdf_logC - np.log(_argus_phi(chi))
11795 return A + np.log(x) + 0.5*np.log1p(-x*x) - chi**2 * y / 2
11796  
11797 def _pdf(self, x, chi):
11798 return np.exp(self._logpdf(x, chi))
11799  
11800 def _cdf(self, x, chi):
11801 return 1.0 - self._sf(x, chi)
11802  
11803 def _sf(self, x, chi):
11804 return _argus_phi(chi * np.sqrt((1 - x)*(1 + x))) / _argus_phi(chi)
11805  
11806 def _rvs(self, chi, size=None, random_state=None):
11807 chi = np.asarray(chi)
11808 if chi.size == 1:
11809 out = self._rvs_scalar(chi, numsamples=size,
11810 random_state=random_state)
11811 else:
11812 shp, bc = _check_shape(chi.shape, size)
11813 numsamples = int(np.prod(shp))
11814 out = np.empty(size)
11815 it = np.nditer([chi],
11816 flags=['multi_index'],
11817 op_flags=[['readonly']])
11818 while not it.finished:
11819 idx = tuple((it.multi_index[j] if not bc[j] else slice(None))
11820 for j in range(-len(size), 0))
11821 r = self._rvs_scalar(it[0], numsamples=numsamples,
11822 random_state=random_state)
11823 out[idx] = r.reshape(shp)
11824 it.iternext()
11825  
11826 if size == ():
11827 out = out[()]
11828 return out
11829  
11830 def _rvs_scalar(self, chi, numsamples=None, random_state=None):
11831 # if chi <= 1.8:
11832 # use rejection method, see Devroye:
11833 # Non-Uniform Random Variate Generation, 1986, section II.3.2.
11834 # write: PDF f(x) = c * g(x) * h(x), where
11835 # h is [0,1]-valued and g is a density
11836 # we use two ways to write f
11837 #
11838 # Case 1:
11839 # write g(x) = 3*x*sqrt(1-x**2), h(x) = exp(-chi**2 (1-x**2) / 2)
11840 # If X has a distribution with density g its ppf G_inv is given by:
11841 # G_inv(u) = np.sqrt(1 - u**(2/3))
11842 #
11843 # Case 2:
11844 # g(x) = chi**2 * x * exp(-chi**2 * (1-x**2)/2) / (1 - exp(-chi**2 /2))
11845 # h(x) = sqrt(1 - x**2), 0 <= x <= 1
11846 # one can show that
11847 # G_inv(u) = np.sqrt(2*np.log(u*(np.exp(chi**2/2)-1)+1))/chi
11848 # = np.sqrt(1 + 2*np.log(np.exp(-chi**2/2)*(1-u)+u)/chi**2)
11849 # the latter expression is used for precision with small chi
11850 #
11851 # In both cases, the inverse cdf of g can be written analytically, and
11852 # we can apply the rejection method:
11853 #
11854 # REPEAT
11855 # Generate U uniformly distributed on [0, 1]
11856 # Generate X with density g (e.g. via inverse transform sampling:
11857 # X = G_inv(V) with V uniformly distributed on [0, 1])
11858 # UNTIL X <= h(X)
11859 # RETURN X
11860 #
11861 # We use case 1 for chi <= 0.5 as it maintains precision for small chi
11862 # and case 2 for 0.5 < chi <= 1.8 due to its speed for moderate chi.
11863 #
11864 # if chi > 1.8:
11865 # use relation to the Gamma distribution: if X is ARGUS with parameter
11866 # chi), then Y = chi**2 * (1 - X**2) / 2 has density proportional to
11867 # sqrt(u) * exp(-u) on [0, chi**2 / 2], i.e. a Gamma(3/2) distribution
11868 # conditioned on [0, chi**2 / 2]). Therefore, to sample X from the
11869 # ARGUS distribution, we sample Y from the gamma distribution, keeping
11870 # only samples on [0, chi**2 / 2], and apply the inverse
11871 # transformation X = (1 - 2*Y/chi**2)**(1/2). Since we only
11872 # look at chi > 1.8, gamma(1.5).cdf(chi**2/2) is large enough such
11873 # Y falls in the interval [0, chi**2 / 2] with a high probability:
11874 # stats.gamma(1.5).cdf(1.8**2/2) = 0.644...
11875 #
11876 # The points to switch between the different methods are determined
11877 # by a comparison of the runtime of the different methods. However,
11878 # the runtime is platform-dependent. The implemented values should
11879 # ensure a good overall performance and are supported by an analysis
11880 # of the rejection constants of different methods.
11881  
11882 size1d = tuple(np.atleast_1d(numsamples))
11883 N = int(np.prod(size1d))
11884 x = np.zeros(N)
11885 simulated = 0
11886 chi2 = chi * chi
11887 if chi <= 0.5:
11888 d = -chi2 / 2
11889 while simulated < N:
11890 k = N - simulated
11891 u = random_state.uniform(size=k)
11892 v = random_state.uniform(size=k)
11893 z = v**(2/3)
11894 # acceptance condition: u <= h(G_inv(v)). This simplifies to
11895 accept = (np.log(u) <= d * z)
11896 num_accept = np.sum(accept)
11897 if num_accept > 0:
11898 # we still need to transform z=v**(2/3) to X = G_inv(v)
11899 rvs = np.sqrt(1 - z[accept])
11900 x[simulated:(simulated + num_accept)] = rvs
11901 simulated += num_accept
11902 elif chi <= 1.8:
11903 echi = np.exp(-chi2 / 2)
11904 while simulated < N:
11905 k = N - simulated
11906 u = random_state.uniform(size=k)
11907 v = random_state.uniform(size=k)
11908 z = 2 * np.log(echi * (1 - v) + v) / chi2
11909 # as in case one, simplify u <= h(G_inv(v)) and then transform
11910 # z to the target distribution X = G_inv(v)
11911 accept = (u**2 + z <= 0)
11912 num_accept = np.sum(accept)
11913 if num_accept > 0:
11914 rvs = np.sqrt(1 + z[accept])
11915 x[simulated:(simulated + num_accept)] = rvs
11916 simulated += num_accept
11917 else:
11918 # conditional Gamma for chi > 1.8
11919 while simulated < N:
11920 k = N - simulated
11921 g = random_state.standard_gamma(1.5, size=k)
11922 accept = (g <= chi2 / 2)
11923 num_accept = np.sum(accept)
11924 if num_accept > 0:
11925 x[simulated:(simulated + num_accept)] = g[accept]
11926 simulated += num_accept
11927 x = np.sqrt(1 - 2 * x / chi2)
11928  
11929 return np.reshape(x, size1d)
11930  
11931 def _stats(self, chi):
11932 # need to ensure that dtype is float
11933 # otherwise the mask below does not work for integers
11934 chi = np.asarray(chi, dtype=float)
11935 phi = _argus_phi(chi)
11936 m = np.sqrt(np.pi/8) * chi * sc.ive(1, chi**2/4) / phi
11937 # compute second moment, use Taylor expansion for small chi (<= 0.1)
11938 mu2 = np.empty_like(chi)
11939 mask = chi > 0.1
11940 c = chi[mask]
11941 mu2[mask] = 1 - 3 / c**2 + c * _norm_pdf(c) / phi[mask]
11942 c = chi[~mask]
11943 coef = [-358/65690625, 0, -94/1010625, 0, 2/2625, 0, 6/175, 0, 0.4]
11944 mu2[~mask] = np.polyval(coef, c)
11945 return m, mu2 - m**2, None, None
11946  
11947  
11948 argus = argus_gen(name='argus', longname="An Argus Function", a=0.0, b=1.0)
11949  
11950  
11951 class rv_histogram(rv_continuous):
11952 """
11953 Generates a distribution given by a histogram.
11954 This is useful to generate a template distribution from a binned
11955 datasample.
11956  
11957 As a subclass of the `rv_continuous` class, `rv_histogram` inherits from it
11958 a collection of generic methods (see `rv_continuous` for the full list),
11959 and implements them based on the properties of the provided binned
11960 datasample.
11961  
11962 Parameters
11963 ----------
11964 histogram : tuple of array_like
11965 Tuple containing two array_like objects.
11966 The first containing the content of n bins,
11967 the second containing the (n+1) bin boundaries.
11968 In particular, the return value of `numpy.histogram` is accepted.
11969  
11970 density : bool, optional
11971 If False, assumes the histogram is proportional to counts per bin;
11972 otherwise, assumes it is proportional to a density.
11973 For constant bin widths, these are equivalent, but the distinction
11974 is important when bin widths vary (see Notes).
11975 If None (default), sets ``density=True`` for backwards compatibility,
11976 but warns if the bin widths are variable. Set `density` explicitly
11977 to silence the warning.
11978  
11979 .. versionadded:: 1.10.0
11980  
11981 Notes
11982 -----
11983 When a histogram has unequal bin widths, there is a distinction between
11984 histograms that are proportional to counts per bin and histograms that are
11985 proportional to probability density over a bin. If `numpy.histogram` is
11986 called with its default ``density=False``, the resulting histogram is the
11987 number of counts per bin, so ``density=False`` should be passed to
11988 `rv_histogram`. If `numpy.histogram` is called with ``density=True``, the
11989 resulting histogram is in terms of probability density, so ``density=True``
11990 should be passed to `rv_histogram`. To avoid warnings, always pass
11991 ``density`` explicitly when the input histogram has unequal bin widths.
11992  
11993 There are no additional shape parameters except for the loc and scale.
11994 The pdf is defined as a stepwise function from the provided histogram.
11995 The cdf is a linear interpolation of the pdf.
11996  
11997 .. versionadded:: 0.19.0
11998  
11999 Examples
12000 --------
12001  
12002 Create a scipy.stats distribution from a numpy histogram
12003  
12004 >>> import scipy.stats
12005 >>> import numpy as np
12006 >>> data = scipy.stats.norm.rvs(size=100000, loc=0, scale=1.5,
12007 ... random_state=123)
12008 >>> hist = np.histogram(data, bins=100)
12009 >>> hist_dist = scipy.stats.rv_histogram(hist, density=False)
12010  
12011 Behaves like an ordinary scipy rv_continuous distribution
12012  
12013 >>> hist_dist.pdf(1.0)
12014 0.20538577847618705
12015 >>> hist_dist.cdf(2.0)
12016 0.90818568543056499
12017  
12018 PDF is zero above (below) the highest (lowest) bin of the histogram,
12019 defined by the max (min) of the original dataset
12020  
12021 >>> hist_dist.pdf(np.max(data))
12022 0.0
12023 >>> hist_dist.cdf(np.max(data))
12024 1.0
12025 >>> hist_dist.pdf(np.min(data))
12026 7.7591907244498314e-05
12027 >>> hist_dist.cdf(np.min(data))
12028 0.0
12029  
12030 PDF and CDF follow the histogram
12031  
12032 >>> import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
12033 >>> X = np.linspace(-5.0, 5.0, 100)
12034 >>> fig, ax = plt.subplots()
12035 >>> ax.set_title("PDF from Template")
12036 >>> ax.hist(data, density=True, bins=100)
12037 >>> ax.plot(X, hist_dist.pdf(X), label='PDF')
12038 >>> ax.plot(X, hist_dist.cdf(X), label='CDF')
12039 >>> ax.legend()
12040 >>> fig.show()
12041  
12042 """
12043 _support_mask = rv_continuous._support_mask
12044  
12045 def __init__(self, histogram, *args, density=None, **kwargs):
12046 """
12047 Create a new distribution using the given histogram
12048  
12049 Parameters
12050 ----------
12051 histogram : tuple of array_like
12052 Tuple containing two array_like objects.
12053 The first containing the content of n bins,
12054 the second containing the (n+1) bin boundaries.
12055 In particular, the return value of np.histogram is accepted.
12056 density : bool, optional
12057 If False, assumes the histogram is proportional to counts per bin;
12058 otherwise, assumes it is proportional to a density.
12059 For constant bin widths, these are equivalent.
12060 If None (default), sets ``density=True`` for backward
12061 compatibility, but warns if the bin widths are variable. Set
12062 `density` explicitly to silence the warning.
12063 """
12064 self._histogram = histogram
12065 self._density = density
12066 if len(histogram) != 2:
12067 raise ValueError("Expected length 2 for parameter histogram")
12068 self._hpdf = np.asarray(histogram[0])
12069 self._hbins = np.asarray(histogram[1])
12070 if len(self._hpdf) + 1 != len(self._hbins):
12071 raise ValueError("Number of elements in histogram content "
12072 "and histogram boundaries do not match, "
12073 "expected n and n+1.")
12074 self._hbin_widths = self._hbins[1:] - self._hbins[:-1]
12075 bins_vary = not np.allclose(self._hbin_widths, self._hbin_widths[0])
12076 if density is None and bins_vary:
12077 message = ("Bin widths are not constant. Assuming `density=True`."
12078 "Specify `density` explicitly to silence this warning.")
12079 warnings.warn(message, RuntimeWarning, stacklevel=2)
12080 density = True
12081 elif not density:
12082 self._hpdf = self._hpdf / self._hbin_widths
12083  
12084 self._hpdf = self._hpdf / float(np.sum(self._hpdf * self._hbin_widths))
12085 self._hcdf = np.cumsum(self._hpdf * self._hbin_widths)
12086 self._hpdf = np.hstack([0.0, self._hpdf, 0.0])
12087 self._hcdf = np.hstack([0.0, self._hcdf])
12088 # Set support
12089 kwargs['a'] = self.a = self._hbins[0]
12090 kwargs['b'] = self.b = self._hbins[-1]
12091 super().__init__(*args, **kwargs)
12092  
12093 def _pdf(self, x):
12094 """
12095 PDF of the histogram
12096 """
12097 return self._hpdf[np.searchsorted(self._hbins, x, side='right')]
12098  
12099 def _cdf(self, x):
12100 """
12101 CDF calculated from the histogram
12102 """
12103 return np.interp(x, self._hbins, self._hcdf)
12104  
12105 def _ppf(self, x):
12106 """
12107 Percentile function calculated from the histogram
12108 """
12109 return np.interp(x, self._hcdf, self._hbins)
12110  
12111 def _munp(self, n):
12112 """Compute the n-th non-central moment."""
12113 integrals = (self._hbins[1:]**(n+1) - self._hbins[:-1]**(n+1)) / (n+1)
12114 return np.sum(self._hpdf[1:-1] * integrals)
12115  
12116 def _entropy(self):
12117 """Compute entropy of distribution"""
12118 hpdf = self._hpdf[1:-1]
12119 res = xpx.apply_where(hpdf > 0.0, hpdf, np.log, fill_value=0.0)
12120 return -np.sum(hpdf * res * self._hbin_widths)
12121  
12122 def _updated_ctor_param(self):
12123 """
12124 Set the histogram as additional constructor argument
12125 """
12126 dct = super()._updated_ctor_param()
12127 dct['histogram'] = self._histogram
12128 dct['density'] = self._density
12129 return dct
12130  
12131  
12132 class studentized_range_gen(rv_continuous):
12133 r"""A studentized range continuous random variable.
12134  
12135 %(before_notes)s
12136  
12137 See Also
12138 --------
12139 t: Student's t distribution
12140  
12141 Notes
12142 -----
12143 The probability density function for `studentized_range` is:
12144  
12145 .. math::
12146  
12147 f(x; k, \nu) = \frac{k(k-1)\nu^{\nu/2}}{\Gamma(\nu/2)
12148 2^{\nu/2-1}} \int_{0}^{\infty} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}
12149 s^{\nu} e^{-\nu s^2/2} \phi(z) \phi(sx + z)
12150 [\Phi(sx + z) - \Phi(z)]^{k-2} \,dz \,ds
12151  
12152 for :math:`x ≥ 0`, :math:`k > 1`, and :math:`\nu > 0`.
12153  
12154 `studentized_range` takes ``k`` for :math:`k` and ``df`` for :math:`\nu`
12155 as shape parameters.
12156  
12157 When :math:`\nu` exceeds 100,000, an asymptotic approximation (infinite
12158 degrees of freedom) is used to compute the cumulative distribution
12159 function [4]_ and probability distribution function.
12160  
12161 %(after_notes)s
12162  
12163 References
12164 ----------
12165  
12166 .. [1] "Studentized range distribution",
12167 https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Studentized_range_distribution
12168 .. [2] Batista, Ben Dêivide, et al. "Externally Studentized Normal Midrange
12169 Distribution." Ciência e Agrotecnologia, vol. 41, no. 4, 2017, pp.
12170 378-389., doi:10.1590/1413-70542017414047716.
12171 .. [3] Harter, H. Leon. "Tables of Range and Studentized Range." The Annals
12172 of Mathematical Statistics, vol. 31, no. 4, 1960, pp. 1122-1147.
12173 JSTOR, www.jstor.org/stable/2237810. Accessed 18 Feb. 2021.
12174 .. [4] Lund, R. E., and J. R. Lund. "Algorithm AS 190: Probabilities and
12175 Upper Quantiles for the Studentized Range." Journal of the Royal
12176 Statistical Society. Series C (Applied Statistics), vol. 32, no. 2,
12177 1983, pp. 204-210. JSTOR, www.jstor.org/stable/2347300. Accessed 18
12178 Feb. 2021.
12179  
12180 Examples
12181 --------
12182 >>> import numpy as np
12183 >>> from scipy.stats import studentized_range
12184 >>> import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
12185 >>> fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 1)
12186  
12187 Display the probability density function (``pdf``):
12188  
12189 >>> k, df = 3, 10
12190 >>> x = np.linspace(studentized_range.ppf(0.01, k, df),
12191 ... studentized_range.ppf(0.99, k, df), 100)
12192 >>> ax.plot(x, studentized_range.pdf(x, k, df),
12193 ... 'r-', lw=5, alpha=0.6, label='studentized_range pdf')
12194  
12195 Alternatively, the distribution object can be called (as a function)
12196 to fix the shape, location and scale parameters. This returns a "frozen"
12197 RV object holding the given parameters fixed.
12198  
12199 Freeze the distribution and display the frozen ``pdf``:
12200  
12201 >>> rv = studentized_range(k, df)
12202 >>> ax.plot(x, rv.pdf(x), 'k-', lw=2, label='frozen pdf')
12203  
12204 Check accuracy of ``cdf`` and ``ppf``:
12205  
12206 >>> vals = studentized_range.ppf([0.001, 0.5, 0.999], k, df)
12207 >>> np.allclose([0.001, 0.5, 0.999], studentized_range.cdf(vals, k, df))
12208 True
12209  
12210 Rather than using (``studentized_range.rvs``) to generate random variates,
12211 which is very slow for this distribution, we can approximate the inverse
12212 CDF using an interpolator, and then perform inverse transform sampling
12213 with this approximate inverse CDF.
12214  
12215 This distribution has an infinite but thin right tail, so we focus our
12216 attention on the leftmost 99.9 percent.
12217  
12218 >>> a, b = studentized_range.ppf([0, .999], k, df)
12219 >>> a, b
12220 0, 7.41058083802274
12221  
12222 >>> from scipy.interpolate import interp1d
12223 >>> rng = np.random.default_rng()
12224 >>> xs = np.linspace(a, b, 50)
12225 >>> cdf = studentized_range.cdf(xs, k, df)
12226 # Create an interpolant of the inverse CDF
12227 >>> ppf = interp1d(cdf, xs, fill_value='extrapolate')
12228 # Perform inverse transform sampling using the interpolant
12229 >>> r = ppf(rng.uniform(size=1000))
12230  
12231 And compare the histogram:
12232  
12233 >>> ax.hist(r, density=True, histtype='stepfilled', alpha=0.2)
12234 >>> ax.legend(loc='best', frameon=False)
12235 >>> plt.show()
12236  
12237 """
12238  
12239 def _argcheck(self, k, df):
12240 return (k > 1) & (df > 0)
12241  
12242 def _shape_info(self):
12243 ik = _ShapeInfo("k", False, (1, np.inf), (False, False))
12244 idf = _ShapeInfo("df", False, (0, np.inf), (False, False))
12245 return [ik, idf]
12246  
12247 def _fitstart(self, data):
12248 # Default is k=1, but that is not a valid value of the parameter.
12249 return super()._fitstart(data, args=(2, 1))
12250  
12251 def _munp(self, K, k, df):
12252 cython_symbol = '_studentized_range_moment'
12253 _a, _b = self._get_support()
12254 # all three of these are used to create a numpy array so they must
12255 # be the same shape.
12256  
12257 def _single_moment(K, k, df):
12258 log_const = _stats._studentized_range_pdf_logconst(k, df)
12259 arg = [K, k, df, log_const]
12260 usr_data = np.array(arg, float).ctypes.data_as(ctypes.c_void_p)
12261  
12262 llc = LowLevelCallable.from_cython(_stats, cython_symbol, usr_data)
12263  
12264 ranges = [(-np.inf, np.inf), (0, np.inf), (_a, _b)]
12265 opts = dict(epsabs=1e-11, epsrel=1e-12)
12266  
12267 return integrate.nquad(llc, ranges=ranges, opts=opts)[0]
12268  
12269 ufunc = np.frompyfunc(_single_moment, 3, 1)
12270 return np.asarray(ufunc(K, k, df), dtype=np.float64)[()]
12271  
12272 def _pdf(self, x, k, df):
12273  
12274 def _single_pdf(q, k, df):
12275 # The infinite form of the PDF is derived from the infinite
12276 # CDF.
12277 if df < 100000:
12278 cython_symbol = '_studentized_range_pdf'
12279 log_const = _stats._studentized_range_pdf_logconst(k, df)
12280 arg = [q, k, df, log_const]
12281 usr_data = np.array(arg, float).ctypes.data_as(ctypes.c_void_p)
12282 ranges = [(-np.inf, np.inf), (0, np.inf)]
12283  
12284 else:
12285 cython_symbol = '_studentized_range_pdf_asymptotic'
12286 arg = [q, k]
12287 usr_data = np.array(arg, float).ctypes.data_as(ctypes.c_void_p)
12288 ranges = [(-np.inf, np.inf)]
12289  
12290 llc = LowLevelCallable.from_cython(_stats, cython_symbol, usr_data)
12291 opts = dict(epsabs=1e-11, epsrel=1e-12)
12292 return integrate.nquad(llc, ranges=ranges, opts=opts)[0]
12293  
12294 ufunc = np.frompyfunc(_single_pdf, 3, 1)
12295 return np.asarray(ufunc(x, k, df), dtype=np.float64)[()]
12296  
12297 def _cdf(self, x, k, df):
12298  
12299 def _single_cdf(q, k, df):
12300 # "When the degrees of freedom V are infinite the probability
12301 # integral takes [on a] simpler form," and a single asymptotic
12302 # integral is evaluated rather than the standard double integral.
12303 # (Lund, Lund, page 205)
12304 if df < 100000:
12305 cython_symbol = '_studentized_range_cdf'
12306 log_const = _stats._studentized_range_cdf_logconst(k, df)
12307 arg = [q, k, df, log_const]
12308 usr_data = np.array(arg, float).ctypes.data_as(ctypes.c_void_p)
12309 ranges = [(-np.inf, np.inf), (0, np.inf)]
12310  
12311 else:
12312 cython_symbol = '_studentized_range_cdf_asymptotic'
12313 arg = [q, k]
12314 usr_data = np.array(arg, float).ctypes.data_as(ctypes.c_void_p)
12315 ranges = [(-np.inf, np.inf)]
12316  
12317 llc = LowLevelCallable.from_cython(_stats, cython_symbol, usr_data)
12318 opts = dict(epsabs=1e-11, epsrel=1e-12)
12319 return integrate.nquad(llc, ranges=ranges, opts=opts)[0]
12320  
12321 ufunc = np.frompyfunc(_single_cdf, 3, 1)
12322  
12323 # clip p-values to ensure they are in [0, 1].
12324 return np.clip(np.asarray(ufunc(x, k, df), dtype=np.float64)[()], 0, 1)
12325

12328 b=np.inf)

12331 class rel_breitwigner_gen(rv_continuous):
12332 r"""A relativistic Breit-Wigner random variable.
12333  
12334 %(before_notes)s
12335  
12336 See Also
12337 --------
12338 cauchy: Cauchy distribution, also known as the Breit-Wigner distribution.
12339  
12340 Notes
12341 -----
12342  
12343 The probability density function for `rel_breitwigner` is
12344  
12345 .. math::
12346  
12347 f(x, \rho) = \frac{k}{(x^2 - \rho^2)^2 + \rho^2}
12348  
12349 where
12350  
12351 .. math::
12352 k = \frac{2\sqrt{2}\rho^2\sqrt{\rho^2 + 1}}
12353 {\pi\sqrt{\rho^2 + \rho\sqrt{\rho^2 + 1}}}
12354  
12355 The relativistic Breit-Wigner distribution is used in high energy physics
12356 to model resonances [1]_. It gives the uncertainty in the invariant mass,
12357 :math:`M` [2]_, of a resonance with characteristic mass :math:`M_0` and
12358 decay-width :math:`\Gamma`, where :math:`M`, :math:`M_0` and :math:`\Gamma`
12359 are expressed in natural units. In SciPy's parametrization, the shape
12360 parameter :math:`\rho` is equal to :math:`M_0/\Gamma` and takes values in
12361 :math:`(0, \infty)`.
12362  
12363 Equivalently, the relativistic Breit-Wigner distribution is said to give
12364 the uncertainty in the center-of-mass energy :math:`E_{\text{cm}}`. In
12365 natural units, the speed of light :math:`c` is equal to 1 and the invariant
12366 mass :math:`M` is equal to the rest energy :math:`Mc^2`. In the
12367 center-of-mass frame, the rest energy is equal to the total energy [3]_.
12368  
12369 %(after_notes)s
12370  
12371 :math:`\rho = M/\Gamma` and :math:`\Gamma` is the scale parameter. For
12372 example, if one seeks to model the :math:`Z^0` boson with :math:`M_0
12373 \approx 91.1876 \text{ GeV}` and :math:`\Gamma \approx 2.4952\text{ GeV}`
12374 [4]_ one can set ``rho=91.1876/2.4952`` and ``scale=2.4952``.
12375  
12376 To ensure a physically meaningful result when using the `fit` method, one
12377 should set ``floc=0`` to fix the location parameter to 0.
12378  
12379 References
12380 ----------
12381 .. [1] Relativistic Breit-Wigner distribution, Wikipedia,
12382 https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Relativistic_Breit-Wigner_distribution
12383 .. [2] Invariant mass, Wikipedia,
12384 https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Invariant_mass
12385 .. [3] Center-of-momentum frame, Wikipedia,
12386 https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Center-of-momentum_frame
12387 .. [4] M. Tanabashi et al. (Particle Data Group) Phys. Rev. D 98, 030001 -
12388 Published 17 August 2018
12389  
12390 %(example)s
12391  
12392 """
12393 def _argcheck(self, rho):
12394 return rho > 0
12395  
12396 def _shape_info(self):
12397 return [_ShapeInfo("rho", False, (0, np.inf), (False, False))]
12398  
12399 def _pdf(self, x, rho):
12400 # C = k / rho**2
12401 C = np.sqrt(
12402 2 * (1 + 1/rho**2) / (1 + np.sqrt(1 + 1/rho**2))
12403 ) * 2 / np.pi
12404 with np.errstate(over='ignore'):
12405 return C / (((x - rho)*(x + rho)/rho)**2 + 1)
12406  
12407 def _cdf(self, x, rho):
12408 # C = k / (2 * rho**2) / np.sqrt(1 + 1/rho**2)
12409 C = np.sqrt(2/(1 + np.sqrt(1 + 1/rho**2)))/np.pi
12410 result = (
12411 np.sqrt(-1 + 1j/rho)
12412 * np.arctan(x/np.sqrt(-rho*(rho + 1j)))
12413 )
12414 result = C * 2 * np.imag(result)
12415 # Sometimes above formula produces values greater than 1.
12416 return np.clip(result, None, 1)
12417  
12418 def _munp(self, n, rho):
12419 if n == 0:
12420 return 1.
12421 if n == 1:
12422 # C = k / (2 * rho)
12423 C = np.sqrt(
12424 2 * (1 + 1/rho**2) / (1 + np.sqrt(1 + 1/rho**2))
12425 ) / np.pi * rho
12426 return C * (np.pi/2 + np.arctan(rho))
12427 if n == 2:
12428 # C = pi * k / (4 * rho)
12429 C = np.sqrt(
12430 (1 + 1/rho**2) / (2 * (1 + np.sqrt(1 + 1/rho**2)))
12431 ) * rho
12432 result = (1 - rho * 1j) / np.sqrt(-1 - 1j/rho)
12433 return 2 * C * np.real(result)
12434 else:
12435 return np.inf
12436  
12437 def _stats(self, rho):
12438 # Returning None from stats makes public stats use _munp.
12439 # nan values will be omitted from public stats. Skew and
12440 # kurtosis are actually infinite.
12441 return None, None, np.nan, np.nan
12442  
12443 @inherit_docstring_from(rv_continuous)
12444 def fit(self, data, *args, **kwds):
12445 # Override rv_continuous.fit to better handle case where floc is set.
12446 data, _, floc, fscale = _check_fit_input_parameters(
12447 self, data, args, kwds
12448 )
12449  
12450 censored = isinstance(data, CensoredData)
12451 if censored:
12452 if data.num_censored() == 0:
12453 # There are no censored values in data, so replace the
12454 # CensoredData instance with a regular array.
12455 data = data._uncensored
12456 censored = False
12457  
12458 if floc is None or censored:
12459 return super().fit(data, *args, **kwds)
12460  
12461 if fscale is None:
12462 # The interquartile range approximates the scale parameter gamma.
12463 # The median approximates rho * gamma.
12464 p25, p50, p75 = np.quantile(data - floc, [0.25, 0.5, 0.75])
12465 scale_0 = p75 - p25
12466 rho_0 = p50 / scale_0
12467 if not args:
12468 args = [rho_0]
12469 if "scale" not in kwds:
12470 kwds["scale"] = scale_0
12471 else:
12472 M_0 = np.median(data - floc)
12473 rho_0 = M_0 / fscale
12474 if not args:
12475 args = [rho_0]
12476 return super().fit(data, *args, **kwds)
12477  
12478  
12479 rel_breitwigner = rel_breitwigner_gen(a=0.0, name="rel_breitwigner")
12480  
12481  
12482 # Collect names of classes and objects in this module.
12483 pairs = list(globals().copy().items())
12484 _distn_names, _distn_gen_names = get_distribution_names(pairs, rv_continuous)
12485  
12486 __all__ = _distn_names + _distn_gen_names + ['rv_histogram']
